items.speaker: PESETA SAM LOTU-IIGA
items.text: It is a pleasure to
participate in this, the Address in Repl y debate. May I first congratulate you, Mr
Speaker, on your reappointment to the o ffice of Speaker, and, secondly, may I
congratulate all new members who are part of this, the 50th Parliament of New Zealand.
The Prime Minister has laid out clearly our Government’s four priorities. The first of
these is to responsibly manage the Governme nt’s finances. In a world as it is today—
and last night we saw Moody’s downgrade both Spain and Portugal, and we saw the
Greek Parliament pass austerity measures in order to combat the evils of debt—it is
important that our Government controls the debt path our c ountry is heading on. It is
about budgeting carefully and deciding which things are important and which things to
prioritise. As with our own personal finances and our household finances, we would not
go for years spending more that we earn. So this Government is committed to returning
to surplus in the 2014-15 financial year.
Secondly, we are about building a more  productive and competitive economy. We
have seen under this Governme nt, for the first time in many years, a trade surplus, and
when we look at the record of the last Government, we see 5 consecutive years of
diminishing export levels. We know that the fo cus of a brighter future and the focus on
jobs and opportunities must come through the export-focused economy. What does it
322 Address in Reply 14 Feb 2012
mean? It means selling more of what the wo rld wants. It means selling at a competitive
price and building on a solid base of i nnovation. In both 2012 and 2013 our economy is
forecast to grow more strongly than the eurozone, the UK, Japan, the United States—

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Still!

items.speaker: PESETA SAM LOTU-IIGA
items.text: —as well as Canada. It is good to see you back in the
House, Mr Cunliffe. I do not know about the beard, but it is good to see you, anyway.
Again, the European crisis offers some lessons. It offers lessons because it is about—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I would actually like to hear what
the member is saying, so keep the interjections low.

items.speaker: PESETA SAM LOTU-IIGA
items.text: It is about competitiveness, as I was saying. The
second reason is that our comp etitiveness has declined over the period of the 2000s. As
a result, industries and sectors that were competing internationally have gone into
recession, and we have to do something about that. So what has this Government done?
It has turned that r ound with a 120-point economic plan. I hold here, in my hand, some
of the answers to peeling back some of  the poor performance that the Labour
Government gave us over the 9 years. What does it include? It  includes a Future
Investment Fund. It means investing in our future and investing in our kids. The schools
and the early childhood centres that have been  built across this count ry are part of the
solution going forward. It is about a 120-poi nt plan that will bring us into the 21 st
century.

items.speaker: Simon Bridges
items.text: What’s it about?

items.speaker: PESETA SAM LOTU-IIGA
items.text: Mr Bridges wants to know what it is about. It is about
some of the roads that go into Tauranga, Mr Bridges.

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: And Hamilton.

items.speaker: PESETA SAM LOTU-IIGA
items.text: That is right; and Hamilton. What else is it about? It
is about broadband and connect ivity between our cities as  well as with the world. We
are able to live in this country and make goods and services, and export these across the
world. That is what it is about.
When I talk to our businesses in Maungakiekie, they ask about the exchange rate and
they ask about access to capital. This Governme nt in the last 3 years has reformed so
much of the capital markets. We created the Financial Markets Authority—admittedly
with the help of the whole House; it was a policy that had cross-party support. We
created a regulator that actually has teeth, has resources, and will enforce some of the
really dreaded parts of financial markets where so many mum and dad investors were
taken for a ride.
We will reform the Securities Act, which is 34 years old and needs refining. We will
ensure that our capital markets operate with  confidence and trust,  but also that the
regulatory authority has the resources to enforce those matters in our capital markets.
We are also looking at furthering our Res ource Management Act reforms. When we
talk to users of council facilities, they say that  one of things about c onsents is that they
take too long, they cost too much, and there is so much un certainty as to when and how
a resource or building consent may be issu ed. So we are introducing a 6-month time
limit for some of the consenting of medium-sized projects.
We are encouraging oil and gas explorati on, and that is with a new system of
processing permits. Whereas Opposition partie s will look at our Australian cousins,
brothers, and sisters, and they  will compare us with that country, when you look at that
country, though, you see how effectively they us e their minerals and their resources. If
we are going to be competitive not just with Australia but with the rest of the world, we
really need to get our act together in term s of exploration and in terms of using our
minerals, oil, and gas resources in this country.
14 Feb 2012 Address in Reply 323
We are also negotiating free-trade agreements. Although I admit that we are carrying
on the good work of the last Government , we are working on the Trans-Pacific
Partnership, including the United States, as well as other free -trade agreements that will
increase our access to markets around the wo rld and increase our opportunities for job
growth in our export sector. Of course, we are talking also about the mixed-ownership
model, and extending th at to four State-owned enterpri se companies, which will make
better use of New Zealand’s balance sh eet. It is about providing investment
opportunities for our mum and da d investors, because they cannot just invest in
Telecom. They cannot just invest in a few top public companies. But these investment
opportunities will provide some solid returns going into the future.
Also for a company like Mighty River Power, which needs access to more resources
with its geothermal technological expertise, and its ability to expand across the globe—
it is in Chile, in Germany, and in the US, but  it is looking to get further into South-east
Asia—these investments will provide Mighty River Power with the capital and
expertise to extend those exports overseas.
The final bit of reform that will be importa nt, especially this year—and I sit as the
chair of the Social Services Committee—wi ll be reforming welfare. Welfare is about
getting people who can work to work. Welfar e will be about providing a safety net for
those who need help, but providing incentives  for those who need to go out and earn a
living.
I have set out the Government’s priorities . I am proud to represent this second-term
National Government. It is a Government that is about action, it is a Government that is
about producing jobs and opportunities, and it is about a Government that will deliver
on its promises. Thank you very much.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: I could spend 10 minut es deconstructing the
arguments around the State-owned enterprise sale s. They are just ridiculous. This idea
that New Zealand will somehow become wealthier by changing who owns what already
exists is an absolute nonsense. I will leave that to others of my colleagues.
This is the Address in Reply debate, which is the first formal set of speeches after the
election. I suppose I should start by saying congr atulations to the National Party and its
colleagues in Government. You have won th e Treasury benches again, but I would note
that New Zealanders are very fair-minded, and in my lifetime there has never been a
one-term Government—indeed, except once. Th at was when the th en sitting Prime
Minister Norman Kirk died in office.
So the fact that National ha s won a second term should not  be seen as some great
endorsement of the National Government. Indeed, to achieve that, National has gobbled
up all of its coalition partners. All of them ar e either at 1 percent or lower, if you round
them. The M āori Party got slightly more than 1 per cent, but closer to 1 percent than 2
percent. The ACT Party is decimated. It is here only because of John Banks. Its vote has
collapsed to 1 percent. Why? There was this litany of disasters around the ACT Party. It
was seen by the electorate to be bankrupt.
What happened? Well, we had the perk- buster Rodney Hide busted for perks. We
had the ultimate act of hypocrisy of Davi d Garrett, having railed against shorter
sentences and name suppression, being found out to have sought name suppression and
a discharge without conviction for his earlier passport fraud. We th en had the takeover
of the ACT Party from outside its ranks  by John Banks and Don Brash. Despite the
endorsement that we had of th is cosy little deal, with Pa ul Goldsmith for the National

items.speaker: Party saying
items.text: “Please don’t vote for me; vote for John Banks.”—that was essentially his
campaign—it looked like Paul Goldsmith was still going to win.
So what did they do? They had this tea pa rty, and within the tea party were planted
seeds of discontent in the minds of the me dia and wider New Zealand that the Prime
324 Address in Reply 14 Feb 2012
Minister was not quite all the smiles, good na ture, and goodwill that he had previously
pretended were his making. In the tea party we  saw this act of political engineering. In
fact, someone said to me it was an act of political pornography, where they went and
they showed themselves off to 30 or 40 cam eras. But the problem is when you agree to
be a centrefold in an act of political pornography you lose your right to privacy. So New
Zealanders and the media started to look aska nce at the Prime Minister when he called
in the police. He had the temerity to say that the police had the time to inquire into this
because the police had lower burglary rates.  Well, we know that around New Zealand
there are lots of uninvestigated burglaries a nd other crimes, but the Prime Minister used
an arm of the State. The media were under at tack by the police, who were called in by
the Prime Minister to witch-hun t as a consequence of this ta pe, which was taken at this
public event.
Since then, following the election, we have had the Prime Minister saying that the
rosy promises he was making just a few weeks ago he now no longer will be held to.
That was the first act of the Prime Minister  in this new Government, backed up by the
Prime Minister saying that he went to the election with the Government’s own forecast,
but now he is coming back, weeks later, and saying it is going to be even worse than
that. As a consequence of that , we have now seen, in the Sunday Star-Times  in the
weekend, a slow declin e in the popularity of  the Prime Minister, because this forever
telling people “It’s rosy, it’s rosy, it’s rosy.” and then saying “Oh, look, it’s all too hard;
it’s not going to be that good.”, is starting  to wear thin with middle-class New
Zealanders. They are tired of waiting for this  nirvana, which never arrives but which is
forever promised by the Prime Minister.
In the last term of Government we had B ill English saying that all that went wrong
was the fault of the Labour Government. The Labour Government was blamed for
increasing Government debt. Let us have a look  at those figures. Do es history bear that
out to be true? Well, in 1999 New Zealand’s gross Government debt was 35 percent of
GDP. That is when the Labour Government cam e to office. By the time we left office
we had reduced that figure to 17 percen t of GDP—an incredible decrease in
Government debt. Every one of those Budget surpluses that the La bour Party ran under
Michael Cullen was opposed by National.
Net debt went down even further, and, depe nding on the measure, it was either zero
percent or 5 percent of GDP. It went down because the Government was investing in
assets like State-owned enterprises a nd Air New Zealand, and was pre-funding
superannuation. We were building up the assets of the Government at the same time that
we were reducing Government debt.
Since that time, Government debt has in creased—up from 17 percent of GDP to, in
2011, 36 percent of GDP. Where does it go from here? Can the National Party members
tell me whether it gets better or worse from  here? Silence! Well, I can tell you that
National, in its own Treasury forecasts, show that that debt continues to increase and, by
2014, the end of this parliamentary term, Govern ment debt is projected to increase by
another $16 billion—$16 billon more of Government debt.
Now, if there was some hope in terms of so me of the structural imbalances in the
economy being unwound, and New Zealand making economic progress by then, then
maybe New Zealanders would forgive that . But the reason that middle-class New
Zealanders are starting to go off the Government was amply illustrated by Steven Joyce
when he answered on behalf of the Mini ster of Finance in the House today. The
question the Government asked of itself—the first question—was to Mr Joyce on behalf
of the Minister of Finance,  and asked what progress th e Government is making in
implementing its economic growth agenda. We ll, you would think on that basis that
there was good news there, but the reality is—and we explored this in our questions—
14 Feb 2012 Address in Reply 325
that New Zealand’s structural economic probl ems remain, so much so that if this
Government was still in office in 2016, by which time it would have been in office for 8
years, what would be happening to New Zeala nd? Well, in that eighth year, and in the
years prior, New Zealand gets poorer, becau se every year New Zealand runs a current
account deficit, and we effectively impor t more goods and services, and pay more
interest out overseas, than we earn. And every year we do that—every year that we have
a current account deficit—we get poorer, because we bridge that gap and we bridge that
gap through more borrowing.
So what happens? This year the current acc ount deficit is projected  to be $5 billion.
Bill English pretends that the Government has changed structural imbalances in our
economy to improve exports. Well, you would th ink if that was th e case, then that
balance would get better, but it does not. Ev ery year from here, the current account
deficit is projected to get hi gher, so much so that by 2016, th e current account deficit is
projected to be $17 billion in that year  alone—$17 billion of current account deficit,
which can be bridged in only one of two ways: selling more  of our assets, which the
Government is big on, whether it is land sa les or State-owned enterprise sales, or
borrowing more money, which the Government is also big on.
So what does that mean in terms of New Zealand’s balance sheet? Well, our balance
sheet is measured by what we call our net liabilities, and, again, it is bad news. By 2016
New Zealand’s net international liabilities relative to now—not years past, but now; the
Government is responsible for now, and it has been in power for 3 years—increase by
10 percent of GDP. New Zealand’s net international liabilities go up from $140 billion
now—it is already a big number—to $200 billion in 2016.
The Government responds and says “Oh, we have got a 120-point plan.” You look
through that plan and about most of those th ings it says “Oh, we’ve already done that.”
In the list are things like investing in transmi ssion infrastructure. That is part of its 120-
point plan. Look, there is nothing wrong with investing in transmission infrastructure—
that is how we get electricity—but it was going to happen a nyway; it is not the
Government that has changed that. There is no thing substantial in its plan to address the
structural imbalances in the economy. Why not? Treasury says it should. The briefing to
the incoming Minister from Treasury says, according to the New Zealand Herald
interpretation of it, that it was calling fo r an introduction of a capital gains tax—a
Labour Party policy that the Government re fuses to adopt, despite recommendations
from Treasury, the OECD, the IMF, and just about every other country in the world. It
recommends changes to savings and it reco mmends raising the age of superannuation.
These are structural change s that only the Government can bring about, but this
National Government refuses to acknowledge them, and we go backwards until 2016 as
a consequence.

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: Can I just begin my
contribution by congratulating you, Mr A ssistant Speaker Tisch, and your fellow
presiding officers on your re-election to your roles, and can I welcome all new members
to the House.
That last contribution, from Mr Parker, te lls us very clearly that Labour is still
labouring under the illusion that somehow New Zealand got it wrong: they did not
really mean to vote National; it  kind of somehow slipped by them when they were not
looking. The reality is that New Zealand has once more comprehensively rejected the
Labour programme of debt and disarray. Wh at New Zealand actually told us on 26
November was that they wanted a National- led Government with John Key at the helm,
and that they understood that in challeng ing times you need the sort of economically
responsible, strong, stable Government that we have proven ourselves to be over the last
3 years, and that we will continue to be over this next term.
326 Address in Reply 14 Feb 2012
The last 12 months in particular have  seen the global situation continue to
deteriorate. I know that over the break in January I was looking at one of the reports that
came out of Europe that had been entitled “Euro-geddon”. That is certainly a graphic
way of describing the very real and very seri ous nature of the dete riorating situation in
Europe and around the world. We cannot put our heads in the sand on this. We cannot
keep continuing to believe that we can ju st keep spending and say “Don’t worry about
where it will come from; it will all come out all right.” We have to take the necessary
steps to protect ourselves from these international shock waves and we have to continue
to diversify our trade routes. Excellent work has been done—and I acknowledge that
that work has been done by a number of Governments—on diversifying those
alternative trade routes, making sure we ar e not as heavily reliant on the traditional
European and US markets, and recognising that  the great growth area s for us are in the
Asia-Pacific region. And all the work we are doing in that area is certainly fundamental.
We have to also reflect on our domestic situation, and recognise that when you are a
country the size of New Zealand, we have to be better, leaner, and more resilient than
perhaps our larger neighbours. If we are going to move towards the sort of New Zealand
that this Government wants to deliv er—one of higher incomes and better
opportunities—we have to have a plan in pl ace to weather this situation and build
towards our future, and that is what this Government is focused on. It is not always
going to be easy. Some of the decisions and some of the discussions will challenge
some people, but we cannot keep carrying on pretending everything is rosy while the
world gets weaker and weaker around us.
Looking across the 3 years of this term, the Prime Minister set out in his introductory
statements to the House that in this term  there are four key areas in which we see
important progress needing to be made. The first of those is around the management of
Government finances. Both this Nationa l Government and National Governments
historically have proven themselves to  be Governments of economic rationality,
economic prudence, and very careful mana gement of taxpayers’ money. We understand
that every cent we spend, we take out of th e pocket of a hard-wor king New Zealander.
We are very, very mindful of that. We are not going to throw money away or throw it
around recklessly. We have to respect the pe ople who have earned that money, and we
owe them the courtesy of ensuring we spend it well. So we have to manage the
Government finances well.
We are focused on getting New Zealand b ack to surplus by 2014-15, and we are still
on track to do that, even though the times are getting tougher. Why is that so important?
It is important because being in surplus means we have choices. We cannot keep
spending money we have not got. You have  got to earn money before you spend it.
Now, that sounds pretty simple; it sounds pret ty trite. Every family and every business
in New Zealand knows that, but for too l ong Labour and left-wing Governments have
forgotten that. We are going to get back to a basis that you have to earn money before
you spend it. So we have to keep the Crown debt to a manageable level.
Debt has become an issue over years gone by, and dealing with  the impact of the
Christchurch earthquakes and ot her disasters, we are going to keep debt peaking under
30 percent. The Labour Opposition, over th e campaign, went out and promised $15
billion more in spending than this Gove rnment did. Labour did not worry about the
debt, it did not worry about the long-term resilience of this economy; it just kept
promising to spend your money and rack up more debt, which your future generations
were going to have to cover. This Govern ment will not do that. We will keep debt
peaking below 30 percent.
Let us look back on the legacy of the Labour Government. We hear Labour members
harping away over there from the Opposition benc hes; let us look at what they left us.
14 Feb 2012 Address in Reply 327
From 2004 to 2008 Labour increased Governme nt spending by more than 50 percent—
50 percent increases in core Government spe nding. That would be fine if things were
going well in the real sector—

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: We got rid of all the consultants that National employed.

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: —but over that same period, Mr s King, that party presided
over a recession in the productive sector well ahead of  the rest of the world. While
Labour kept spending, our productive sector—the people in this country who earn stuff,
make stuff, grow stuff, and sell st uff—was going backwards, and the Labour
Government did not care. It just kept spe nding. It did not understa nd that it is the
productive sector in this country that creates jobs. You do not create jobs and you do not
create better opportunities by Government sp ending; you create them  by setting up the
conditions in which business can thrive, in which investment will come into New
Zealand, and where entrepreneurs are prepared to put their own capital on the line.
That is the next part of what we need to do. We need to make sure our economy is
resilient, and we need to make sure it is productive and that it is competitive with the
world. You have heard my colleagues Sam Lo tu-Iiga and others talk about our 120-
point plan. That is a comprehensive docum ent recognising that the best thing the
Government can do—the best thing the Government can do—i s create an environment
in which business can thrive.
We are in the season of maiden speeches in the House, and it makes me think back to
my maiden statement. In that I talked at some length about the fact that we needed to
wake up to the fact that in this country bus iness is small to medi um enterprises, more
often than not. It is not the big, ugly corporates that the Gr een Party likes to attack at
every opportunity. Actually, more often than not, it is a mum and dad running their own
enterprise, struggling to employ a few staff; it is a dairy owner; it is someone working
out of his garage. It is small business. Thos e are the people who create jobs in this
country; those are the people we have to support.
We have to do that by doing a couple of things. We have  got to create the right
infrastructure. We have to get the roa d, rail, electricity, and, very importantly,
broadband networks in place to ensure that  they can conduct their business easily. We
have to ensure that we have got the sk ills coming through our education system to
support that business, and there is some tremendous work happening through my
colleague Minister Joyce’s portfolios in tertiary education and skills. There is some
tremendous work happening in the inform ation and communications technology space
around the entrepreneurs scheme to ensure that we are supporting our New Zealanders.
They are incredibly innovative, and we need  to ensure that those skills are harnessed,
nurtured, and retained in New Zealand. That is  what this strategy is designed to do: to
make New Zealand a place where young New Z ealanders coming up come out of our
system with the skills to l ead the world, and with every in centive to stay here in New
Zealand.
Obviously I have taken on the portfolio  of broadband and communications and
information technology, and in that space alone over the period to July of this year we
are going to see 58,000 premises, including  211 schools, connected to ultra-fast
broadband. The impact that is going to have on our education system, our health system,
and our way of doing business will be revolutiona ry. It is due to the investment of this
Government, which the Labour Party opposed, that we are going to see world-leading
connectivity for New Zealand households, New Zealand Government services, and New
Zealand consumers.
Better public services are a core part of what  we need to deliver. We have to have a
welfare system that incentivises people to ge t back to work, because that is the path out
of poverty. You can talk about poverty all you like;  the path out of poverty is to get
328 Address in Reply 14 Feb 2012
people back into work. You have to create th e jobs and you have to have a system that
incentivises and rewards them for getting back  into that system. We have to have a
world-leading education system, and my coll eague Minister Parata is doing excellent
work, building on the good work of Minister Tolley in that space. And we have to
ensure that the Public Service provides value for money.
I know that my time is coming to an end, and I do want to touch on the rebuilding of
Canterbury. The rebuilding of Canterbury is a signi ficant priority for this Government.
The people in my region have shown incredib le resilience over the past 18 months. We
are now up at more than 10,000 ear thquakes, and I want to pay tribute, in particular, to
the residents of suburbs like Parklands a nd those out east who, on 23 December, when
everyone else was settling back for Christmas, looking forward to hanging up their
briefcases and their suits, were once again ha ving to be out there digging out tonnes of
liquefaction from their homes. The way th at they get up time and time again, keep
going, and stay committed to their province is  absolutely heroic. I cannot speak too
highly of them, and this Government is going to walk with them every step of the way.
We are going to build a temporary rugby stadium to get th e Crusaders back there, and I
look forward to seeing every member of this House down there supporting the
Crusaders on 24 March.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE
items.text: Mr Assistant Speaker Tisch, may
I take the opportunity in this, my first,  contribution in the new Parliament to
congratulate you on your elevation to the Chair and to congratulate, through you,
Speaker Smith. May I also offer congratulat ions to the Govern ment on the election
results, as it begins its second and last term of this Government.
Can I acknowledge the member who has just  resumed her seat, the maiden opposite,
Amy Adams, who has become a Minister th rough reciting key lines, it appears. I would
like to deal with just three of them befo re commencing my materi al. The first one was
that you cannot spend it befo re you earn it—a fa ir enough point. They reckon their
Government has reduced debt. Well, as my co lleague Mr Goff interjected, quite rightly,
it was the previous Labour Government that reduced debt. But do not take our word for
it; look at Treasury’s number s: debt was 35 percent of GDP—35 percent of GDP—
when Labour took office in 1999, and 17 percent, in gross terms, in 2008. In net terms it
went down from 18 percent to zero, formi ng the first credit since Sir Julius Vogel
borrowed to build the railways. New Zeala nd’s Government books were in credit under
Labour. Where are they now? I ask the member whether she really wants to stand on a
record of debt reduction.
The second point was Government spendi ng, which was 29 percent of GDP, on
average, under the Labour Government. It started at 29 percent and ended on 30
percent. Guess what it is today: 33 percen t of GDP. It has gone up 2.5 percent under
National, not gone down. Every year the Gove rnment reduces the tax take because the
economy has fallen in a hole, and every year it promises restraint to get the books back
in order. National is chasing its tail. It is chasing its tail because we all know that when
in a recession, retrenchment and austerity prol ong it. It is time for a growth strategy. It
is time for jobs. It is time for getting New Zealand moving again.
There is one thing I agree with the memb er opposite on: I do wa nt to extend the
condolences, the sympathy, and the empathy of  members on this side to the people of
Canterbury. Ten thousand eart hquakes is an appalling thi ng to have lived through, and
we do, I think, offer solidarity in respect of  Canterbury. But I would say this: there is
$25 billion to be invested in rebuilding that wonderful city—and it was my home
province for many years too. But I tell you this : if we do not sort out the insurance
situation down there—where insurers will not insure new builds, new plants, new
homes, or new businesses—the recovery will not occur. I commend my colleague
14 Feb 2012 Address in Reply 329
Lianne Dalziel for leading the charge on the insurance fiasco. Where is the
Government? And more to the point, where are the Government’s books if Canterbury
continues to subside into a policy liquefaction?
The Address in Reply debate—for people li stening in or watc hing at home—is the
triennial free-for-all that goes on after the Governor-General gets  the privilege of
reading out the Prime Minister’s Speech from the Throne. I have a huge amount of
respect for His Excellency Lieutenant General The Rt Hon Sir Jerry Mateparae, the new
Governor-General, but I have to say I felt a tad sorry for him reading out, during his
first time in that chair, what has to go down in history as the smallest, the shortest, the
meanest, and the most vacuous Speech from the Throne that this Parliament has ever
had the misfortune to hear. There were no ideas—

items.speaker: Simon Bridges
items.text: Did you write it? Did you write it, David?

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE
items.text: —no new ideas. Sure as hell Paul Goldsmith did not
write it; it would have gone to 1,000 pages if it was from that member. I think John Key
must have written it on the bus on the way to the office.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: What bus? Do you mean the limo?

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE
items.text: Oh, the limo on the way to the office—good point. No,
he would not be taking a bus. It was rema rkable. Why was it so short? Shortness is
sometimes something to be admired, but not in the case of this Speech from the Throne,
because it was short on achievement. Gone was the aspiration. Gone were the sunny
uplands of the brighter future. Gone was the target of the first term of catching up with
Australia. It was a 30 percent wage gap when it started; it is close to 40 percent today. It
would be a joke if our young people were not leaving in droves, if  in 2011 we did not
have the highest net out migration of New Zeal anders in our history, and if more people
had not voted with their feet and told their children, their families, and their workmates
“I’ve been trying for years. I’m sick of it. I can’t do it any more. We’ve got to go.” They
have got to go because this Government has got no ideas.
There is a 120-point plan. If you have got 120 points of everything, let me tell you,
members opposite, it is not a plan; it is a laundr y list. It is not a plan; it is a laundry list.
There are no priorities and no performanc e measures. It has gi ven up on catching
Australia. There is no strategy. That is w hy. Do not ask the Labour Party; ask Business
New Zealand. Three-quarters of chief execu tive officers surveyed before the election
said National did not have a plan for th e economy. Three-quarters in Business New
Zealand—how would we put it—manured in their own nest by saying that the
Government had not got a clue on economic management, and they were right.
This Government has ballooned debt, just like the Republicans in the United States:
come in, preach balanced Budgets, blow out th e deficit, and then blame the Democrats.

items.speaker: It is the same thing here
items.text: preach free mark ets; implement sell, cut, and hope; and blow
out the deficit because tax revenue collapses. What happens? Very little—very little in
terms of growth and very little in terms of recovery.
Where did that leave the Governor-General? It reminded me of the American senator
who had rather annoyed his speech-writer. In  the opening page of his address to the

items.speaker: Senate it said
items.text: “In my speech I will grow the economy—”

items.speaker: Simon Bridges
items.text: This is as old as the hills, David.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE
items.text: “I will solve world hunger” —or child poverty, in the
case of Mr Bridges; he w ill worry about world hunger when  he grows up. And on page
2 it said as follows: “Now you’re on your  own, you bugger.”—“Now you’re on your
own, you bugger.” That is how His Excellency the Governor-General must have felt
when he got to page 4 of the Speech from the Throne and there was no plan. All he had
was the dismal results of a failed 3 ye ars, thousands of broken lives, and New
330 Address in Reply 14 Feb 2012
Zealanders who have rushed for the exit because they have given up hope in their own
country.
They say that Oppositions do not win elec tions; Governments lose them. Well, the
Government is on track to lose the next one , and Labour will be do ing its little bit to
help. We will be doing our bit to help in two ways. No. 1 is by holding the Government
to account. We will not put up with rubber nu mbers. Here is today’s latest rubber
number from the Ministry of Economic De velopment: how much does the Ministry of
Economic Development think tourism has given to the New Zealand economy in Rugby
World Cup year? The answer is $320 million, pl us or minus 20 percent, according to its
survey. Plus or minus 20 percent? The mi nistry has invested hundreds of millions of
dollars in the Rugby World C up, and it cannot get the figure on the tourism spend to
within 20 percent.
What is worse, figures out today from th e Ministry of Economic Development show
that the tourism spend was only 3 percent highe r than the previous year, lower than the
year before that, and lower than 2 years befo re that. In other words, the much-vaunted
Rugby World Cup—fun as it was; I loved it too—did absolutely nothing for our
economy. It did absolutely nothing for our econom y. If that is the Government’s idea of
an economic plan, it proves what the Opposi tion has been saying for the last 3 years:
they are platitudes in search of a plan—platit udes in search of a plan—and gimmicks in
search of a strategy.
Those ragtag members over there are here fo r one reason, and it is not a very secure
one. They are here on the co at-tails of John Key. Now, J ohn Key is currently setting a
record: a record reduction in personal poll ratings. He is down 9 percent in 2 weeks—

items.speaker: Hon Amy Adams
items.text: He’s still got a rath er large lead over y our leader. Who is your
leader?

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE
items.text: —down 9 percent. The parrot opposite has got a
problem. I feel sorry for the backbenchers in  the far rows of Mongo lia or Bulgaria or
whatever they call it up there in the back row. They are here because of Mr Key’s
personal popularity—personal popularity—and th ey will not be here long, because it
does not look like it is going to last to the next election. They will not be here long, so it
was nice to know you guys. Have fun back on the farm. Have fun back on the farm.

items.speaker: Hon CRAIG FOSS
items.text: And so says David—a Sermon on
the Mount, Mr Cunliffe. It is good to see you back in the House. I suggest that next time
you stand a little closer to the razor, though. A few things have changed over there in
the Labour Party, but some things do not chan ge whatsoever. I do note there were some
changes, although listening to the speeches, I do not know. I think some of them maybe
had been written in about Augus t last year. What did we see just yesterday? They have
changed leaders over in the Labour Party, and that is fine. Mr Shearer is now leading the
assembled masses over there, if you like. But I did see a picture of  him being led by a
poodle, in the paper or online somewhere, so that is not particul arly encouraging, I
think, for his leadership thus far.
First of all, though—I do digress, and I apologise to members—is the
acknowledgments of other members for the el ection results. Congrats and otherwise to
the National Party for its winning of the election—thank you—are taken on board. But I
return the compliments to those whom I contested in my electorate of Tukituki, who ran
a pretty good campaign and ke pt it clean. I think respect was gained for all parties
concerned. I also welcome new members to Parliament and welcome back returning
members. I am sure we will get to know some of the new members a bit more, and I
look forward to seeing you from time to time , particularly around the House. I, for one,
quite enjoy discussions outside of this Chamber, around committees and things like that.
14 Feb 2012 Address in Reply 331
November 26 does seem quite some time ago no w, but I would just like to point out
that if one looks at the map of the North Island, say, from Wairarapa all the way up to
somewhere near Auckland, one sees it is a nice shade of blue—Na tional Party blue. I
feel a little bit sorry for the Hon Parekura Horomia, who has quite a burden on his broad
shoulders to look after that whole part of  the country. But the people have spoken. The
people spoke on November 26, and they res oundingly rejected the policies that the
Labour Opposition put up to the public. They resoundingly rejected those policies, to
the tune of the lowest poll re sult, I think it is, for the Labour Party ever—27 percent, or
you could say 73 percent against. [Interruption] I do not know what the issue there with
that one is—27 percent.  Did I miss half a percent or something? I do not know; I will
give it to you. But it was 27 percent.
The people of New Zealand gave this G overnment a mandate. They gave this
Government the permission to continue working towards such a brighter future. They
gave us permission to continue to manage the country’s finances in such a better way, to
prudently manage every single taxpayer cent, every single dollar, so as to get the best
outcome possible, because we fully and hone stly acknowledge where that dollar comes
from in the first instance. As we all know, it comes from taxpayers in one way, shape,
or form.
As we saw, previous speakers were talki ng about structural issues in the economy.
Well, yes, we were in Government for the pr evious 3 years, but much of what we are
still trying to tidy up was set in train from about 2004 to 2007, when Government
spending and Government revenue doubled.

items.speaker: Kris Faafoi
items.text: This is the speech from last year.

items.speaker: Hon CRAIG FOSS
items.text: That is right, but I am responding to the other speeches that
were written last year.
New Zealand voted for the mixed-ownership model. Interestingly, all the rhetoric
aside, the former Labour finance spokesma n Mr Cunliffe—and, I think, the Hon Trevor
Mallard when he was commerce Minister or thereabouts—used terms along the lines
that their ambition was to unleash the power and potential of State-owned enterprises. A
speech Mr Cunliffe gave at Victoria Univer sity in November 2010, I think it was, used
that exact term. Funnily enough, I think it got taken out of some online versions, but
unleash—

items.speaker: Hon Amy Adams
items.text: What?

items.speaker: Hon CRAIG FOSS
items.text: Well, yes, I think that is wh at we may be doing. I cannot quite
understand why they are still  arguing about it now, having  ignored the mandate and
what New Zealand said. If I listened carefully to what Mr Parker said, essentially he
said the National Party’s victory at the election was some kind of statistical error—

items.speaker: Hon Amy Adams
items.text: An aberration.

items.speaker: Hon CRAIG FOSS
items.text: —an aberration, because there has only been one other one-
term Government, the one where unfortunately the Hon Mr Norman Kirk passed away.
I actually fully encourage memb ers opposite to continue in th at vein, because if I recall
the rhetoric before the election, apparently  it was about policies—I do remember that
bit. If it was about policies, and Labour put its policies out th ere, National put our
policies out there to the public, and only 27 percent or so of the public voted for
Labour’s policies, think it through a little bi t. Remember the old GST off fruit and
veges? Perhaps Labour members have thrown that out, to be fair; I do not know about
that. I will be interested to hear. Remember not paying PAYE on your first $5K? I do
not know whether they have thrown that one out. I would be intere sted to hear. They
have changed leader, they have changed some  of the front bench around, to be fair, and
good luck to them all. I am looking forward to what they have to say in that space.
332 Address in Reply 14 Feb 2012
I would also particularly like to acknowle dge, in my new role as Minister of
Commerce, that I do intend to work as closel y as I can with Mr Cosgrove, who is the
new commerce spokesman over there, continuing the heavy regulatory reform work that
the Hon Simon Power started, of  necessity, in the last 3 ye ars. But I fully acknowledge
that it was assisted generall y, in a bipartisan way, across the House, and, hopefully, we
can continue down that track. I look forwar d to working with hi m quite closely, where
and when possible. I am sure there will be policy differences, but on the whole I suspect
we are all heading to the same place as far as that regulation and legislation coming up
is concerned.
I noted before the mixed-ownership model,  and I noted what Mr Cunliffe and Mr
Mallard had said previousl y. I recall that the history of the new Leader of the
Opposition—I think it came up when he was th e candidate for Mt Albert 2 or 3 years
ago—includes writing a paper proposing that defence forces were contracted out. I think
it was to Sandline International or something like that. I do not re ally mind—I have not
read the paper—but I was just thinking about this the other day. I do not really mind,
but I am just quite interested to hear—i f it was good enough for that member to write a
paper or thesis about that and propose it, fair enough—if he has changed his mind, how
he reconciles that with his current positio n on the mixed-ownership model as we try to
unleash the potential of New Zealand, and therefore the Crown’s balance sheet, to try to
realise our awesome future.
New Zealanders see on TV every night what  is going on in Europe . We see what is
happening in southern Europe, across Greece,  across Spain, etc. I do note that the
previous Labour Party leader in one of hi s speeches essentially announced that the
global financial crisis was over. He may ha ve changed his mind, to be fair. What is
going on over in Europe is a threat to this country—regar dless of the reason, for the
moment. It is indebted to the tune of $180 billion. We are reliant on the world’s capital
markets to fund our aspirations. Regardless of the policy stuff around that, actually, it is
right that New Zealanders and this Government  are prudent and very cautious to try to
avoid down here what we see is going on up there. If we do not, unemployment will
indeed go through the roof if the Government fi nances are out of control—if that in fact
happens. Interest rates will go through the r oof, inflation will go through the roof, and
the whole thing will start to collapse.
Little old New Zealand, which is doing its best to try to punch  above our exporting
weight around the world, actually has to do so well, even so much better, I think, than
many people realise, just to tread  water as we try to realise our expectations, as we start
to grow our exports, particularly to As ia. Again I freely acknowledge the generally
bipartisan nature of free-trade agreements, which have been ratified by different parties
and Ministers of Trade and Prime Minister s over the years—absolutely—and that is
great. You know, when we exit New Zealand we generally speak as one, and most
members understand how necessary that is to  help pay for our aspirations. I heard a
speaker say this quite recently. It is simp ly this: “New Zeala nders, I think they
understand that if we want more, better schools,  if we want more, be tter health, if we
want those things that we expect of an OECD develope d country in 2012, do you know
how we do it? We simply have to export more, grow more.”
SU’A WILLIAM SIO (Labour—M āngere): Thank you for the opportunity to
speak. That last speaker had difficulty believing what he was saying about the mandate.
That was an unbelievable gesture, because he  said that National has a mandate from
New Zealanders to sell off State assets  when he knows full well it has got only 59
members in a 121-member House. National is going to rely on Mr Banks, who is a
National Party member masquerading as an AC T Party member; it is going to rely on
Peter Dunne; and it is going to rely on the M āori Party, which by all accounts is not
14 Feb 2012 Address in Reply 333
going to be part of that Government. How can  it have a mandate with 59 members in a
121-member House when over a million peopl e did not vote—a million people did not
vote? National needs to be worried. It does not have the mandate—none, whatsoever—
from the public of New Zealand. It does not have the mandate, at all, to sell off the
assets that it intends to sell.
Mr Assistant Speaker Tisch, I want to  congratulate you and welcome you to your
role. I look forward, no doubt in the not too distant future, perhaps, to recognising and
congratulating you when you are wearing the full regalia of the office of Speaker of the
House. I also want to acknowledge and we lcome all the other new members who are
here, and I particularly acknowledge also Asenati Lole-Taylor.
We have heard from that side of the House—from the Government. We have been
promised a brighter future, more jobs, and higher incomes. Only last week, the
household labour force survey for the final quarter of last year was released, and it is not
a brighter future. Last Friday, for many wo rkers and for many small businesses, it was
not a brighter future. This is what the Government has said in the speech that it has
given us, and it has been repeated by many of  its members, but I want to say what the
community is saying. Those members are worki ng on the basis that they can fool some
of the people some of the time or all of the people some of the time, but we are going to
work on the basis that, in the next 3 years, they cannot fool all of  the people all of the
time.
When they say that they are going to provide  a brighter future, I would ask that they
go out and talk to workers in Manukau and talk to small businesses up and down this
country and ask them how they are feeling about what they are experiencing at the
moment. Last Friday I met with workers fr om Criterion, an East Tamaki manufacturing
company that has gone into receivership. One hundred and eighty workers are affected.
Some of those, after 20 or 30 years working in  the same job, have lost their jobs. There
are no jobs out there.  Yes, this Government promised 170,000 jobs over 4 years. If it is
to be on track, it has got to create 36,000. So  far we can count only about 10,000, so it
has not done it. That is due to  the struggles and the battle s of small businesses, which
are the backbone of this coun try. These people who lost j obs last Friday through no
fault of their own—do they feel that they have got a brighter  future? The answer is no.
There is no brighter future for many of these families, particularly those with
schoolchildren and teenagers whom they have got to support.
There are no jobs out there, but that is what we have been promised. There is no
plan, yet the Government attempts to make out as if it ha s got a plan. When you look at
the 120 points that the Government keeps th rowing out, none of th at makes sense to
ordinary people—hard-working workers, and small businesses that are struggling to pay
their bills in the face of a rising cost of living and in the face of uncertainty in the future.
Those who have lost jobs are having to st ruggle, because when they get re-employed,
for the lucky few, they are having to be paid lower wages than they were paid before.
We have got to hold this G overnment to accoun t. If it is going to be making those
promises, then we—yourself, every member of  this Opposition side—have got to make
sure that it honours those words, because wh en you consider that over a million people
did not vote in this election, you have got to as k yourself why that is. Just because
National is in the Government seats does not m ean that it is trusted. Just because it is
holding the offices of power does not mean that the people ac cept what it is going to do
for this country.
I say that we have all just heard a lot of hogwash from this Government. National
made promises that just do not turn out to be the reality for many, many families the
length and breadth of New Zealand. The wo rld has changed, but National’s answers
have not. It still thinks that  by sitting on its hands, the economic forces that are there
334 Address in Reply 14 Feb 2012
will simply create the jobs that it is promis ing it will create. Sitting on your hands is not
going to do it. It has got to come up with a comprehensive plan that all of us can follow,
that all of us can see, and that  all of us can make a contribu tion in. It is just not enough
for it to simply say these jobs are going to appear out of thin air.
It is just not acceptable when it says that it will sell off the assets and all will be well.
That is not prosperity. Selling off our Stat e assets, the assets that members of our
country own—the elderly, and those who have contributed significantly over many,
many years. Those assets belong to the New Zealand public, and if the Government
took the time to read the many, many polls th at have been made available, it would
know that just because it has a seat in power , it does not mean that it has the right to
flog off those assets. That is right.
Over 113,000 New Zealanders have left our  shores for Australia. Over 113,000 New
Zealanders have left our shores to go over to  Australia. Why is that? They have given
up under this Government. They have given up hope for a brighter future. For them,
going across the Ditch to Australia provides a brighter and a more confident future for
their families than hanging around here with Mr Key at the helm of power.
[Interruption] Those members do not like hearing th at, but it was they who said that
they would reduce the number of New Zeal anders going across the Ditch to Australia—
113,000, all under their particular watch.
The Government has said to us that it is focused on the young people of New
Zealand, particularly M āori and Pacific. We have not seen any of that. There is 41
percent unemployment among young people aged 15 to 19—not in education,
employment, or training—all under Mr Key’s watch, all under the National
Government’s watch. Close to 65,000 people ag ed 15 to 24 are not in education and are
not in employment or training. The Govern ment thinks that by allowing these young
people not to be in educati on or training, or by sweeping them under the carpet, all is
going to be well. It is was ting our young people. It is was ting the potential of this
country. It is wasting the potential of our communities—people who want a brighter
future, who want to be able to work, who want to earn higher incomes, who want to
have their children get an education, and who want to get into a house of their own.
But so far all that we have heard from this Government are empty promises that
things are going to ge t better—empty promises that it wi ll be brighter round the corner.
It has been in power for the last 3, going on 4, years and all that I have heard, all that
my community has heard, are empty promises—empty promises. So we will hold the
Government to account. We will hold it to account in the next  3 years. I move that we
support the amendment that my colleague David Shearer, the leader of the Labour
Party, has moved: “and the National-led Government will sell New Zealand’s assets
against the will of the public; the Government has no ideas to create jobs or a clean and
innovative New Zealand; that the Government  is widening the gap between the very
rich and the rest and therefore this H ouse has no confidence in the National-led
government.”
New Zealanders are battling to stay afloat, New Zealanders are battling to make ends
meet, and all we get are empty promises. I say to you that the people of M āngere are
sick and tired of empty promises from Mr Key and the National Government.

items.speaker: GARETH HUGHES
items.text: Kia ora, Mr Deputy Speaker. Ng ā mihi nui ki a
koutou. Kia ora. I would like to greet all me mbers in the Chamber, congratulate all
those successful members, and commiserate  and acknowledge all those unsuccessful
members. I would like to acknowledge you, Mr  Deputy Speaker, in your returning role,
and I guess it is fair to acknowledge the Government. Good on you for forming a
Government. I think that this side of the House would have preferred it differently, but I
would like to acknowledge that you did have  the numbers. What I would like to touch
14 Feb 2012 Address in Reply 335
on is what your plan is for this next 3 years.  I am happy to take a cal l in this Address in
Reply debate responding to John Key and the Speech from the Throne.
I want to touch on what the Prime Minist er touched on, which is the four key
priorities: trying to get the Government’s books  into surplus, trying to get a competitive
economy, trying to reform the Public Service, and trying to rebuild Christchurch. I want
to look at what they mean for this country, and why this Government is asking the right
questions but is providing the wrong answers to those four priority points—surplus, the
economy, the Public Service, and Christchur ch. I want to ask the Government why,
when there are 120 points in th e plan, it still does not make the grade. I want to ask the
Government where the vision is with al l those 120 points. I want to show the
Government benches that we do have options available. We do have options. If we keep
our assets Kiwi, if we invest in our valuab le “clean, green” brand, and if we invest in a
compassionate economy, we can build a ri cher New Zealand—a New Zealand for
everyone.
So, firstly, let us look at the first Governme nt priority: trying to get the Government
books back into surplus by 2014-15. It might surprise some of the members, but the
Greens support it in this aspect. You know, we support sustainability when it comes to
the environment and we support fiscal and en vironmental sustainability as well. It is
clear that the country has got a debt problem. We have  got a gross Government debt of
around 33 percent to 36 percent of GDP and you only have to  look at Europe—what is
happening in Portugal and Ireland, and the ri ots on the streets in Greece—and you see
that we are on an unsustainable track. So we are asking the right question, which is
about Government debt, but we have co me up with the wrong answers. John Key’s
speech talked about announcing only $800 m illion of new Government spending, cuts
to the public sector, further cuts to the Government, and departments like the
Department of Conservation getting gutted, ye t what we are seeing is more wasteful
spending being announced by the Government.
Take the motorways. We have got $19 billion being borrowed by the Government to
pour on these motorways, with negative be nefit-cost ratios. We have got the
Government subsidising risky deep-sea oil ventures with $25 million - plus and direct
subsidies to foreign offshore drillers. We have seen the new irrigation fund. What we
are seeing is this Government cherry-picking: picking the winners in our economy. We
are seeing motorways for truckies, we are se eing special deals for Warner Bros, we are
seeing more pokies for Skycity, we are seeing the Government picking the winner when
it comes to the economy, but it is the taxpayer picking up the tab. We see fiscal austerity
as the watchword, but the Government is se lectively borrowing billions to back these
supposed winners, which are going to have huge  impacts for our economy and country.
When there are 120 points, and there is no point when it comes to revenue, you have got
to ask some serious questions. Raising revenue has to be part of th e question if we are
trying to return the Government books into surplus.
The Government said yes to more obscene bonuses. We saw the Government say yes
to more tax cuts for the super-rich, but we saw the Government saying no to capital
gains tax, we saw the Government say no to the temporary earthquake levy, and we saw
the Government say no to the small irri gation levy, which would have helped our
farmers and our waterways. We were the only  party in the last election to go to the
public with a plan to actually pay off debt  faster. The Green Party went to the public
with a plan to pay off $6 billion in debt ove r the next 3 years. But what we see from the
Government benches is members playing po litics, looking out for their mates, and
taking our economy down the wrong road.
When it comes to the competitive economy prio rity of the Government, this again is
another area where we agree with the Govern ment. To help the sustainability of our
336 Address in Reply 14 Feb 2012
economy and our environment we need to be reducing debt, and to do that we need a
competitive economy. But again what we see is the wrong answers given to the right
question. The 120-point plan can  be summarised in four word s; I think they would be
“drill it, mine it”.
Oil is the biggest strategic risk to our national economy. It is 16 percent of our
imports. That is the largest single share of our national imports. We are seeing wealth
directly flow offshore. Every US$1 rise in  the price of oil wipes $40 billion to $60
billion off our GDP. It is the key area in the Ministry of Economic Development energy
outlook analysis of the country, so if oil is the problem, wh y is drilling more of it the
answer? The pathway to prosperity is not dr illing new, risky oil wells in deep, hostile
environment. It does not stack up when New Zealand sells itself far too cheaply. We see
hardly any royalties, hardly any taxes, hardly any jobs for Kiwis, we see the profits flow
offshore, yet it is the taxpayer who is picking up the tab when it becomes a mess.
We see the Government with its insurance liability say: “Sure, you are liable, but you
need only $30 million in insurance.” We see the Government quite happy to see New
Zealanders, who love their ma rine environment, pay 100 pe rcent of the environmental
costs, yet for only 5 percent of the valu e of the oil. What we saw with the Rena tragedy
off the Bay of Plenty was that the country is not prepared to deal with a moderate spill,
let alone a risky, deep-sea oi l well blowout. The only way to  achieve oil exports, which
is what the Government wants to achieve —net oil exports, as in its briefing for the
incoming Minister of Energy and Resource s—is to encourage risky deep-sea oil
drilling, more hydraulic fractur ing, or fracking, and digging up the lignite, the lowest-
grade coal in the country.
When it comes to the deep-sea wells that the Government plans to dig all over the
offshore environment in New Zealand, there is simply no way to plug a well blowout.
What we saw in the Gulf of Mexico, even wi th all of those rigs in the environment,
were 40,000 people ready to respond, but they  still could not plug the well for weeks
and weeks. I do not know how the Government thinks it is going to plug a well with its
new legislation, the Exclusive Economic Z one and Continental Shelf (Environmental
Effects) Bill. Yet where it is planning to be allowing these permits for these deep-sea oil
rigs is between what is known as the “roaring forties” and the “furious fifties” off the
Raukūmara Basin, one of the most seismically active parts of the country. And when it
comes to the bill supposedly giving Kiwis and taxpayers protection from these risky
deep-sea oil wells, the “EEZ Bill”, it is really  more of an “E-zee Drilling Bill”, for the
way it simply facilitates more risky deep-sea oil drilling.
The second part of the plan relies on fr acking—more fracking across our country.
Fracking, or hydraulic fracturing, is drilling ve rtical and horizontal wells, letting off
explosives, and then using drilling fluids, wh ich are proprietary, secret, and often very
toxic, to extract oil and gas. What we know from fracking overseas is that it pollutes the
groundwater, it pollutes the air, there are significant health worries, and then we also
know there is growing evidence, including from prestigious UK and American scientific
bodies, of its links with earthquakes. So  I do not know why the Government is
embarking on this risky and very controvers ial fracking practice. It is no wonder that
New South Wales, Quebec, France, and many states in America have put moratoriums
on it. And that is what this Government s hould be doing: if it wants to look out for the
taxpayer, if it wants to look out for Kiwi s, it should encourage the Parliamentary
Commissioner for the Environment to be doing some more research into the risks, and,
until then, put in an immediate moratorium.
Now the nexus of the Government’s so-cal led economic development plans of “drill
it and mine it”, is its “sell it” approach. Wh en it comes to the State-owned asset Solid
Energy, one of the State-owned assets on the books, it is its plan to be bringing in
14 Feb 2012 Address in Reply 337
billions of dollars of capital to dig up the lignite. The lignite coal—[ Interruption]—I
could not hear the interjections, but I am  sure they were not any good anyway. But
anyway, when it comes to the lignite, we are going to see the taxpayer pick up the bill—
hundreds of millions, maybe up to a billion dollars, the Parliamentary Commissioner for
the Environment reports—for subsidising it through the emissions trading scheme. This
is the forefront where we should be using our  expertise, investing in innovation like in
efficient wood pellet products, other wood pr oducts, and biofuels, for which, again, the
Government has not announced an extension of  the grant. This is where we should be
planting our effort and our focus to get innovation for prosperity for Kiwis.
Like selling the State assets, which the G overnment wants to flog off, it is simple
madness. These are assets returning a divide nd of 18.5 percent to pa y off debt of only 5
percent. It does not make any sense. It has no mandate. There is massive opposition in
the country. Yet on the flip side there is a massive opportunity cost as well. We could be
using these assets to drive our prosperity, to drive our innovation. We have got world-
leading expertise in renewable electricity generation already. If we, using our State-
owned assets to drive export growth, could capture only 1 percent of that $800 billion
industry, this could bring $800 million per annum into the country and 67,000 jobs.
So, in summary, I ask where the vision is—“drill it, mine it” is not enough to lift
Kiwis’ living standards. Slashing the publ ic sector is not enough to lift 200,000 Kiwi
kids out of poverty. The wasteful spending on the motorways, and subsidising polluters,
is not enough to protect our wonderful e nvironment and our valuable “clean, green”
brand. And the Green Party will be supporting the motion that this House has no
confidence in the National Government.

items.speaker: KATRINA SHANKS
items.text: It is my pleasure to ta ke a call this afternoon. I
would like to congratulate you, Mr Deputy Speaker, and the ot her presiding officers on
being re-elected in this Parliament. I would like to begin my address this afternoon by
talking about three very  inspirational groups. We have h eard a lot of negative talk in
this House this afternoon, and I just want to  talk about these three groups I have met in
the last couple of weeks.
The first one I want to ta lk about is Maria Johnson. Ma ria Johnson is the founder of
the Little Schools programme in Wellingt on. She is an entrepreneur, she won the Her
Business award in Wellington at the end of last year, and she is absolutely passionate
about early childhood education. In fact, she is so passionate that she is in the process of
breaking through into China and the markets ove r there. She is tota lly aspirational for
business, and business women in particular, in New Zealand.
I would like to talk about the sanofi cyclists. The sanofi cyclists are a group of world-
class cyclists who suffer from type 1 diabet es. They are elite athletes who can prove to
and inspire other diabetes sufferers around th e world that they can go out and live their
lives to the full. They were recently in New Zealand competing, and they became first
or second, I believe, in the races they ran around Palmerston North.
The third group is the Johnsonville and Newla nds volunteer fire brigade. Like these
volunteers and all other voluntee rs in New Zealand, they give  day after day, week after
week, year after year  to their communities. They ar e the backbone of our community
and our country. I went to their awards cere mony, and it was great to be part of that.
Annette King was present as well, it was good to see. It is always good to celebrate
people who go out and make a difference in New Zealand.
These three groups of people represent Kiwi ingenuity, Kiwi spirit, and the Kiwi way
of life. We have heard in this House from the last couple of speakers from Labour about
failures, about how badly the country is going, and how there is no hope for the country.

items.speaker: Kris Faafoi
items.text: What happened to the positivity?
