items.speaker: KATRINA SHANKS
items.text: Well, actually, you are absolutely wrong. Su’a William Sio
just sat down, and he had said “I’ve just been around my businesses, and I can tell you”.
Well, I just went to Maria J ohnson’s business yesterday, and I can tell you we have got
some wonderful entrepreneur s out there doing some great work. Not often do we hear
from the Labour members about solutions—sol utions to the probl ems that face New
Zealand, solutions to our challenges—and about any innovation or inspiration at all.
Well, lucky this National Government has a solution. We have a pl an, and it lies in
the spirit and the ambition of entrepreneurs like Maria Johnson. The role models of our
cyclists, and all those who work hard for our communities—

items.speaker: Iain Lees-Galloway
items.text: The plan, the plan, I want to hear about the plan.

items.speaker: KATRINA SHANKS
items.text: National is committed to building a brighter future. It is so
good to hear, actually, the Opposition talking about  the brighter future that we have. I
am going to look in Su’a William Sio’s Hansard, because I believe he talked about the
brighter future, most probably, 10 times in hi s 10 minutes. It is great  to see he believes
in a brighter future for New Zealand, wh ere New Zealanders have opportunity, where
they are going to have jobs, where we are going to have higher incomes, where we are
going to have better public services. When I ta lk about better public services, what do I
talk about? I talk about more elective surgery, I talk about ensuring that our M āori and
Pacific Island children have access to ear ly childhood education—actually, that we
provide early childhood education that they want to access.
We are going to ensure that we have high targets, like the 95 percent target for the
immunisation of our children before they get to school, like rheu matic fever—reducing
that, instead of it increasing under the Labour Government—

items.speaker: Iain Lees-Galloway
items.text: How?

items.speaker: KATRINA SHANKS
items.text: How? Oh my goodness, you know exactly how we are going
to do it, because we have got our 120-point  action plan. It is funny—Clare Curran is
now sitting in the back there, and last week Clare Curran said to us “You have no plan,
no plan at all.” And we said we have got  the 120-point economic action plan, and Clare
Curran goes “What 120-point actio n plan?”. Well, actually, it is on the internet—
www.national.org.nz—and anybody can go and have a look at it . It is a very
comprehensive plan, and it takes us through the next 3 years.
Unlike the Labour Party, which has no plan, no  vision, no aspiration at all, we have
four main priorities over the next 4 years. The first is responsibly managing the
Government’s finances. The others are building a more competitive and productive
economy, delivering better public services, and, of course, rebuilding Canterbury.

items.speaker: Iain Lees-Galloway
items.text: How?

items.speaker: KATRINA SHANKS
items.text: OK, so how are we going to do it? A great question—I am
pleased you asked. What we are not going to  do is, we are not going to borrow more
money, like Labour would have done if it had got into Government, because we are all
sitting back and watching Europe and seei ng all those countries  that are heavily
indebted, and knowing that we cannot borrow any more money. In fact, I believe that in
the election Labour campaigned on borrowing b illions of dollars more money. We are
not going to do that; we know we are not going to do that . We are thinking of other
ways of raising capital, and one of those is through our mixed-ownership model.
But we alone as a Government cannot reduce the debt of the country. People have to
take responsibility for reducing their own personal debt, as well. We know that the tax
switch was significant in ensuring that New Z ealanders got to find a different way to
look at how they are getting their money a nd what they are going to do with it. We
know that before the tax switch, for every dollar that was earne d, $1.10 was spent, and
after the tax switch, for every dollar that was earned, 99c was spent. So we know that
New Zealanders are changing the way they  are saving and spending their money. In
14 Feb 2012 Address in Reply 339
fact, in 2008 personal loans were $13.25 billion. Now, pe rsonal loans are $12.5 billion.
That is a significant decrease for New Zeal anders in how they are spending and saving
their money.
This Government is committed to returni ng to surpluses in 2014-15. We are looking
at $300 million in surpluses in our forecasts. We know that we have to be financially
responsible—fiscally responsible—to ensure that we keep the pressure off interest rates,
because we know that one of the biggest pres sures on households is interest rates. We
need to keep those low so mortgage repa yments stay low. Also, we have to be
responsible for our exporters, to ensure that our exchange rate is stable and as beneficial
to them as it possibly can be. But we know the only way we are going to grow our
economy is through our exports: being producti ve, and being a competitive exporter in
overseas markets. We know that we need free-trade agreements, and successive
Governments have worked towards that. We know that our biggest trading partners are
Australia and China, and they have to be ou r biggest trading partners because they are
the growing partners. We cannot afford to go back to our traditional partners, which are
not growing. If we want to grow, we need  to ensure that we hitch our wagon to the
economies that are growing as well.
I am excited about the future for our families, our businesses, and our organisations
in New Zealand. I am excited that Maria has the opportunity one day to expand her
business into China, because of National’s co mmitment to business. I am excited about
the future of sanofi cyclists and about how they inspire others in  New Zealand, and in
their communities, to overcome adversity day after day. I am proud that so many people
in New Zealand are willing to put their hands up to help each other, to help their
communities. I am excited about this Government having its second term, and that we
can deliver the brighter future that we pr omised. We believe in opportunity, personal
freedom, and the ambition to succeed. Thank you.

items.speaker: CLARE CURRAN
items.text: Let us have a bit of a look at that
plan, because when I heard the news yester day that John Key’s Government was going
to take us to a brave new world within the public sector, my  ears pricked up with
interest. Could it be that this Governme nt would use its purch asing power and its
considerable influence and resources to driv e technological change in the public sector
in a way that would lead to  innovation, job growth, a nd resurgence in our private
sector? Could it be that it would invest in th e skills required to ensure that we have a
highly skilled technological workforce, and that the pathways fr om school into that
workforce were being considered and were bei ng seen as a priority, so that kids coming
out of school could get into high tech jobs ? Would it ensure that the growing digital
divide in this country, and the closing of that digital divide, would be seen as a priority?
No, sadly.
After looking a bit more closely at what the Prime Minister actually said, it is all
about slashing—slashing budgets—and using technology as a cover, not to drive job
growth or innovation but rather to cut jobs and make fr ont-line services automated, and
maybe even send them offshore. Labour is all for efficiencies: making our public
services better, improving New Zealanders ’ access to services  using technology, and
data sharing among Government agencies. Th ere is no question about that. But Labour
is also about a productive, high tech, i nnovative economy—a clean, green, high tech
economy. An innovation society is what we want for New Zealand.
Unfortunately, with this Government—a nd this is a tragedy—the technology
argument is being used as an excuse for serv ices to be diminished, and if the driving
reason for doing it is to cut budgets and to cut staff, then you have got to wonder what
on earth the thinking is. Delivering core serv ices through a call centre, maybe not even
in this country—or, even worse, via an au tomated service—is not  a public service.
340 Address in Reply 14 Feb 2012
Duncan Garner has written about this toda y, describing it as Treasury-speak from the
1980s. That is not future talk; that is talk very much from the past.
Then there is the spectre of user-pays. He re we have the same old story about cuts
and diminished services. That is what underlines the Government’s 120-point plan. I see
that John Key is not going to be pressed on how many jobs are going to be cut, but I ask
him how he thinks New Zeala nders are going to receive a hi gher quality of service for
their complex issues if they cannot even speak  to a person. I see that  he is reported as
saying that people will be able to use their smartphones to apply for passports and other
things, rather than having to wait in lines in offices. Well, there are two things. Firstly,
many people do not even have smartphones. Th ey cannot afford them, and they are not
likely to be able to afford them if they  do not have a job. Secondly, just how many
services will be taken off the front line? I bet it is more than just applying for passports.
Technology is critically important to this country’s future, and innovation is critically
important to this country’s future, but so is direct contact. Technology should be about
bringing people and their Government closer together, not taking them further apart and
then making them pay for it. That is why we pay taxes. As anyone knows, if you take
away the personal contact between people a nd an organisation, then  the organisation
suffers as much as the customer. You cannot  trust an organisation you cannot talk to,
where you cannot talk to an actual person wh en you need to. Taking the people out of
Public Service will affect the service.
New Zealand should become an innovati on society—an innovation society in a
country that uses innovation successfully to create jobs and to create exports. It does not
use technology as a means to slash them and create even more inequality. This
Government has no plan to grow the economy. It is short-term, dumb thinking, just as is
its agenda to sell assets. New Zealanders do not want their assets sold.
This fits with some of the other agenda s of this Government, which are equally
disturbing but are definitely deliberate. The first is that our public broadcasting sector is
being reduced to a shell—a shadow. We need  a strong public media that is independent
of any Government—any Government—and that  provides critical analysis, discussion,
and debate in our country. We should be pr oud of our public broa dcasters. We should
hold our public broadcasting service up as an example of a truly functioning democracy
just like most of our fellow OECD countries. It should be part of the fabric of our
democracy. Instead, what has the Government done? It has frozen Radio New Zealand’s
funding. It will not be able to provide its current services under its current funding
model. It has stripped Television New Zealan d (TVNZ) of its charter. It has made it
become fully commercial. It has axed fundi ng to TVNZ 7, which is  our digital public
TV station and which punches enormously above its weight.
This has happened at the same time as co sy and dubious relations hips are emerging
between the Government and its corporate media mates. There was a $43 million soft
loan to MediaWorks so it could pay its TV licences. There is a refusal to consider or
discuss the glaring need—the glaring nee d—for some regulation in the broadcasting
sector, which is happening everywhere else  except New Zealand. Why? Because that
would affect its mate Sky television, which dominates the pay television market. It is
now doing deals with TVNZ to put even mo re content behind the pay wall, meaning
that great tracts of TV will not, and cannot, be seen, because people cannot afford the
subscription.
Meanwhile—and most disturbing—this is al l shrouded by the growing scandal of
political interference. There is clear evidence emerging of overt political interference by
this Government in our media to promote its own agenda. You have heard my colleague
Grant Robertson, today in question time, que stion the Prime Minister about his free
hour on Radio Live. The Prime Minister became strangely silent today on the extent to
14 Feb 2012 Address in Reply 341
which he was directly involved in determinin g the content of what he described as an
election-free zone, but which could be described as a free hit.
I know that many people are grappling with the extent of these issues out there in our
community, and more and more people are starting to speak out about them. Many
people are asking how this sort of thing can  be happening in New Zealand. Why is the
Government doing it? It does not have a pl an, and it does not want public scrutiny of
where it is failing. And it is happening. It is happening in our country, and more and
more people are waking up to that. We s hould be fighting agains t any perception of
Government interference in broadcasting. Th is Government does not seem to give a
toss. Broadcasting programming matters shoul d be the responsibility of NZ On Air;
they are not the business of Government Mini sters, Prime Ministers, or anyone attached
to a political party. In any ot her country, where the Prime Mini ster’s electorate chair is
involved in programming, where the Government gives soft loans to broadcasters, and
where the Prime Minister gets a free hit on air time, this would rightfully be regarded as
corrupt, and I agree with that sentiment.
Just before the election a programme was screened on TV3 called Inside Child
Poverty. It was controversial. It provided an evidence base for an issue that we all know
is very important and concerning for our country right now. Too many children are
living in poverty. Yes, it invited debate an d discussion, but it was a good thing to have
that discussion out there. But in January we  discovered that the Prime Minister’s man
did not like it and had complained to the boa rd chair and the chief executive officer
before that programme—

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Before?

items.speaker: CLARE CURRAN
items.text: —before that programme was ev en aired. Now we have that
man, the Prime Minister’s own electorate ch air, on the board of NZ On Air, deeply
involved in making decisions about funding and the content of programmes that are
promoting the Government’s own agenda—Wh ānau Ora; the Government’s own
agenda—and is scrambling around inside TV3 and NZ On Air to cover its back.
How could this happen in our country? Is NZ On Air not charged to be independent
and fearlessly protective of pub lic broadcasting values that are independent of politics?
Is NZ On Air funding propaganda? How can some one so close to the Prime Minister be
allowed to be involved in these decisions? The new broadcasting Mi nister, Craig Foss,
has the extremely difficult job of reassuri ng the public that the Government has
credibility—

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER

items.speaker: SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: Congratulations, Mr Deputy Speaker,
on your well-deserved elevati on to the position you hold in this Parliament, which I
know you will serve with grace and dignity. I have  to say, in talking about the speech I
have just heard from Clare Curran, that ma ybe it is just me but there is a deep and
twisted irony in what she is saying about broadcasting. On the one hand she talks about
freedom and the need to let freedom reign within the broadcasting world, but on the
other she is straight in attacking the Sky TVs—the ones who are doing well in this area.
Ultimately—and I am pretty sure I am right in terms of the policies Labour espoused on
broadcasting before the last election—it co mes down to the same old, same old from
that party, and that is more regulation, more State regulation, and, ultimately, more
State control, with the State controlling br oadcasting. And if she wants to know about a
State inappropriately deciding what is on television, all we need to do is go down the
road that Clare Curran wants us to go down, which she espoused and which was
roundly rejected at the last election.
You see, in National, we believe in freedom , and we want to see people out there in
the free marketplace of ideas talking about these things and not being bullied down
342 Address in Reply 14 Feb 2012
because their idea does not fit with someone’s view. I want to give you a quotation I
read in this morning’s New Zealand Herald from Greek finance Minister Evangelos

items.speaker: Venizelos. He said
items.text: “Our coun try has an acute issue of su rvival. The question is not
whether some salaries and pensions will be curtailed, but whether we will be able to pay
even these reduced wages and pensions. When you have to choose between bad and
worse, you will pick what is bad to avoid wh at is worse.” I am no economist, but I chair
the Finance and Expenditure Committee; I am  literate in these matters. But, ultimately,
what happened in Greece is pretty simple. For way too long it spent more than it earned.
I think that New Zealanders r oundly rejected that sort of approach, which we saw from
the Labour Party opposite in the election campa ign. You see, Labour wants to take this
country down that route. Now, Phil Goff, in campaigning at the last election made—I
think at last count Amy Adams was saying it was $15 billion more in spending promises
than National; I thought it was more like $20 b illion. But what I do know is that it is a
whole lot of money that Labour—

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: It was just made up.

items.speaker: SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: Well, it was made up; I agre e with Annette King. That is
exactly what it was. It was made up by Phil Goff. He was shown up in the debates for
making it up, because he did not know where his figures came from, and he just kept on
promising. Actually, just as we have seen in Greece, it does not work, and it does not
work here either. So we are determined to  be fiscally conserva tive and to get our
spending and our debt down in this country  and to return to surplus in 2014-15. When
National talks this way, many of the memb ers on the other side—and David Cunliffe
committed this crime, if I can put it this way—say: “Oh, but we got debt down.” Well,
let me explain something to the Labour Party. There is a fundamental difference
between spending and debt—right? They are diffe rent concepts. And yes, that is right.
In the best economy the world has probably ever seen, it is true that Michael Cullen was
able to return surpluses, ar guably, I would say, by taxing mo re than he needed to. But
he was able to return big surpluses. Bu t how did he do that? Well, from 2005 we know
that he spent like a drunke n sailor. Every day, day in, day out, he was spending much
more than he needed to do, a nd he was not spending it on productive stuff, on the kinds
of things Clare Curran harped on about be fore—innovation this, innovation that. No, he
put it into the non-productive economy. And why did he do that? Well, a cynic might
say he did that to buy elections. But, fort unately, New Zealanders woke up. They knew
it was a hopeless set of policie s that Labour was selling. Th ey did not want the “Greek-
onomics” - styled stuff that Labour was putting in place.
I was talking to a top economist just last  week. He said to me that doing a good job
by the economy comes down to two things. You can dress it up in all sorts of ways and
you can talk about 15 things, but it comes dow n to two things. Firstly, it comes down to
spending less and having less debt. They ar e different things, but related. Secondly, it
comes down to building a more competitive and productive economy. And that is
precisely what National wants to do. He also  said this to me on the competitive and
productive economy: “Actually, it doesn’t come down to one  big thing; it comes down
to lots and lots of little things done right, over time, in crementally. That is how you
make a difference in an economy.” [ Interruption] I hear Rajen Prasad, and I know that
on that side of the House, Labour, and probabl y the Greens as well, says: “Actually, it
does come down to two or three things. Y ou can just have some big bang. You know,
the innovation economy, or the green economy,  and we just do all these magic little
things.” Well, that is exactly what it is; it is the magic theory of economics. It is the idea
that the Government can just magic up indus tries, and suddenly, hey presto, we are
billionaires. Well, let me tell the Opposition that that is actually not how the real
economy works.
14 Feb 2012 Address in Reply 343

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: How are you going to magic the 170,000 jobs?

items.speaker: SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: There is no magic on this side of the House, Annette King, or
Kris Faafoi. What there is, is lots of things —a 120-point plan that adds up over time to
making a step change in this economy. I know; I understand; Labour does not like it.
Labour members are good people. They are we ll-meaning people, but they are wrong
fundamentally on the economics. [ Interruption] Well, I am being generous. I wanted to
be generous. They do have the magic wand theory of economics. As I say, just dream
up an industry. For Clare Curran it is innovati on, and for the Green Party it is a green
economy. Actually, we just want to build  a more productive and competitive economy,
and we do that by reforming the economy day in and day out, with lots of things.
Labour says there is no plan—well, here it  is. They can get it on www.national.org.nz. I
will go through some of these things: connect  58,000 premises to ultra-fast broadband,
including 221 schools.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: How?

items.speaker: SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: How? Well, we put them in the ground, Annette. They dig
them up and it works kind of well. Also, ther e is changing ACC to allow choice in the
work account, reduce business costs, and prom ote growth. We will pass legislation to
implement the start-out wage to ensure our  young people are not locked out of the job
market. It is all of these things, 120 things , that make a substantial difference to the
economy and do mean that we can deliver a brighter future for this country.
I also have to say that there is something else that is needed to deliver a brighter
future. It is basically attitudinal; it is not being a misery guts like some of the members
opposite are when they stand up—“Woe is me!”, and all this and that . Not that I have
done it often, but when you have been to South-east Asia to the so-called tiger
economies and you read their newspapers, you see that they focus on “can do”, on what
can be done, on how a road can be built. They  do not, as Steven Joyce pointed out in
what I thought was a stellar column in the New Zealand Herald, focus on all the
“can’ts”, all the things you cannot do. They do  not say: “There is this problem, and
that.” They do not shut off things here, there, and everywhere. Their papers are
relentlessly positive. They talk about economic  growth, the things they are doing, the
broadband plans, and this and that, and we coul d do with a dose of that attitude and that
optimism, because there is room for optim ism. When we look around the world, at
Europe and its issues, at America, which is doing better than it was but has its issues,
and we look at where we are next to th e Asian economies—and I include Australia in
that, which is arguably the richest per capit a country in the world right now—there is
much room for optimism in New Zealand, b ecause we have a great spirit, we are
optimistic, and we have a wonderful Government leading us at this time of trial.

items.speaker: Dr RAJEN PRASAD
items.text: The first thing I want to say to the member who
has just sat down is that clea rly he is not an economist. Because he chairs the Finance
and Expenditure Committee he might like to think that he is an economist, but he is not.
He believes only the two things that the friend of his, the economist, said were
important—only those two things. I say to that  member there are many more things that
a responsible Government has to address, and it cannot be just those two things.
That is the problem with the Speech from th e Throne. This society has, as a right, to
look at the set-piece speech from the Gove rnment about its strategic intent—its
statement of its aspirations—and to find a place for itself within this statement. This is a
statement for all New Zealanders, and one that we all should be able to look confidently
at to see how the Government intends to advance our interests—everybody’s interests.
So it is a fair test of this particular statement to see how it addresses the needs of all
New Zealanders and how it reflects their point of view.
344 Address in Reply 14 Feb 2012
In the Speech from the Throne the Government states that its driving goal is to build
a more competitive economy with less debt, more jobs, and higher incomes. We should
hold those three things in our minds. That was the goal of the G overnment throughout
the last 3 years, and here it is restated in  a slightly different form, but it is the same
statement. Over the past 3 years we have not seen less debt; in f act, debt has ballooned
under this particular Government. No matte r how it tries to explain it, and no matter
what reasons it finds, the fact is that the debt under this Government has mushroomed.
It has borrowed like there is no tomorrow. Ther e is not any less debt  and there will not
be for some time.
We have not seen more full-time jobs; fu ll-time jobs are down. No matter how the
Government tries to package that fact, the fact is that full-time jobs are down. The
number of hours worked is down, and 100,000 people need more hours to make ends
meet. Maybe the Government does not care th at some people are job-weak, in the sense
that they do not have the hours. They work less time, they do not have enough money,
and they live, in a sense, suboptimal lives. We have already been told in this debate that
83,000 people are not in education, work, or tr aining. How could that be a judgment of
the aspirations and performance of that Government over the last 3 years?
As for higher incomes, that applies only to those at the very top of the income scale.
Ordinary people have not seen any meaningful  increase under the stewardship of this
Government, and the programme it has outlined in this document will not do it for them,
either. Tax cuts notwithstanding—that ga ve advantages to one side. So by the
Government’s own statements—less debt, more jobs, higher incomes—it has failed.
This was a Government that promised it would make the boat go faster; it borrowed
that from the America’s Cup challenge. However,  what it intends to do is actually sell
the boat. That ain’t going to make it go fa ster. The Government knows that it does not
have wide support for its asset sales programme , and yet it intends to persist. It has no
mandate. That has been well established, and just because it won an election that does
not mean it has a mandate for this one policy.
There are two points about the Government’s asset sales programmes that need to be
made. The first is to ask when a Government  takes the views of th e public into account
in setting such a major policy goal. Does th e lack of wide support for the asset sales,
currently reflected in surveys and opinion polls, demonstrate to the Government that the
level of support for such a ra dical policy is just not ther e? The Government knows it is
just not there. It trie s to say it has a mandate, but it does not. Clearly, the support is not
there and it has no mandate. If  it wants to test that, th en perhaps it should have a
referendum and test that out, and we know that the majority would not support it.
The second point is that there is no agreemen t that selling State a ssets that currently
produce a good rate of return for the Government is a no-br ainer. It is a no-brainer,
selling those? Not many people see the logic of this policy, exp ect perhaps those who
would benefit directly from it. Many mo re will pay, through higher prices for
electricity. Many ordinary New Zealand families cannot afford it at the moment, but the
Government does not care for this particul ar group. The policy is entirely driven by
ideology. This is the belief that the State ha s no business owning stra tegic assets for all
New Zealanders. The Government will driv e this ideology, no matter what, because
only its supporters are likely to benefit. Why does the Government not govern for all
New Zealanders? Certainly, it is not there for the average citizen, and this does not
benefit them. The same applies to the privatisation of accident compensation, in a sense,
or opening up those accounts. Charter school s are the same sort of stuff. It is
ideologically driven, and the facts are not there.
Clearly this Government does not have a plan to meet its  own goals of less debt,
more jobs, and higher incomes. When challenge d about this last November, it hurriedly
14 Feb 2012 Address in Reply 345
put together a 120-point plan in the last days of the election campaign. That seemed like
a desperate act at the time, but somehow it was promoted as a new idea. I have had a
look at the 120-point plan, which many speak ers opposite have spoke n to, and see that
only 21 percent of the 120 are new proposals. The rest have already been completed or
are under way, and many of them are the ragtag group of ideas that the Government
promoted over the last 3 year s. It has put them together , and now it is a plan. This
confirms that there are few ideas; selling State assets does not constitute a real plan for
growth and progress towards a smart, clean, clever country.
This country has already been judged as one of the most unequal in the OECD. This
is a terrible indictment, but where in this statement is there a real commitment to change
that, a real commitment to m ove much faster to make this  a more equal society? There
is a whole raft of anti-wor ker legislation, which reduces their incomes. How does that
create a fairer society? How does that create a more equal society? There is nothing in
this plan that addresses our low-wage economy. In fact, the Government policy is
designed to make that even more difficult.  I wonder how members of the Government
go to bed comfortably at night, knowing there are many others out there living lives of
quiet desperation, who have not been fed well that night, and whose children are
probably hungry and not looking forward to th e next day. Yet this statement is the
Government’s plan to address that. Those who are hungry and poor cannot wait.
One of the changing aspects of New Zealand’s society is its culture and ethnic
diversification. There are almost half a m illion people who identify as an ethnic group
other than Pākehā, Māori, or Pasifika. They play a crit ical role in New Zealand society
and, given the social capital they represent, they are well placed to make a difference—a
real difference—to this country ’s growth and well-being. Bu t there is no reference to
them in this particular document, at all.  These people are faceless, and you would have
thought that in the strategi c statement from the Govern ment to guide its 3-year
programme there would be a reflection on at least the diversificat ion of New Zealand
society, and what new ideas this Government  had that might address them much more
directly.
This country has to invest much greater t hought than it has to da te in harvesting the
potential of the ethnic sector. This is the new New Zealand, particularly in Auckland,
but in other cities as well. Given this, one would have thought that there would be some
reference to their interests in this plan. So far we have become familiar with ethnic
celebrations and ethnic elements or culture , like food and entertainment, but their
interest in New Zealand is much greater than  that. There has to be a much deeper level
of engagement and involvement with the ethnic sector and with all New Zealand society
about our ethnic diversification. I thought, as this change is so important, that in this
strategic statement it would be addressed. Ther e has to be a greater  level of dialogue
with and regarding the ethnic sector, as well as with all New Zealanders.
We are all reasonably well info rmed about the plight of our  children in this country.
This document says very little about our mo st vulnerable. We know that there is a
correlation between abuse, neglect, and pove rty, yet this document is quite silent on
many of those factors. There is a belief that somehow the trickle-down will trickle down
to their interests as well.
In conclusion, this is a disappointing and bland Speech from the Throne. It will not
give comfort to the many or reward them, because their interests are not addressed.
Instead it will advantage only the few who are already advantaged. I guess New Zealand
will have to wait for a Labour Government t o, once again, lift all boats through a clean,
green, and clever programme. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL HEATLEY
items.text: I appreciate the
opportunity to once again lay out for New Zealand and for interested colleagues the
346 Address in Reply 14 Feb 2012
National-led Government’s plan for a brighter New Zealand, and what we are laying out
for the next 3 years. Our four main priorities , of course, are, first, responsibly managing
the Government’s finances. We have no partic ular interest in borrowing more and more
and more from overseas, such as other parties are peddling to the New Zealand public at
the moment in order to fulfil their election promises.
Secondly, we want to build a more competitive and productive economy. Part of that,
of course, is investment in very important  infrastructure, whether it is electricity
transmission and generation infras tructure, whether it is roading or rail, or whether it is
broadband or other forms of telecommuni cations, which is important for New
Zealanders, particularly in the provinces, to communicate w ith the rest of the country
and the world. All those areas of infrastructure investment are important to us.
Thirdly, we want to deliver a better, more  effective, and more responsive Public
Service so that New Zealanders can more  readily engage with Government and
Government departments and agencies righ t throughout the country. Lastly, of course,
is that all-important rebuilding of Christ church. Those are our goals over the next 3
years, ones that we will be measured on, and, fortunately, ones we have already made
considerable progress on.
In terms of building a more competitiv e and productive econom y, I have already
outlined that the importance of infrastructure is so very, very high. It does not matter
whether we communicate by rail and road, physically travelling to places; through
transport links delivering goods and services from one place to another; or in the virtual,
travelling through broadband or telecommuni cations. The point is that New Zealand,
being a long, narrow nation, needs to ensure  that our communications and transport
links are world class.
I was stunned, for instance, when we had a regi on that historically has been isolated
from the rest of New Zealand—I am talki ng about Northland. I am sure Southland, Mr
Deputy Speaker, where you are fr om, has never experienced th is, but Northland, in the
far reaches of the north of New Zealand, has historically—100 years ago—been isolated
from the capital and other parts of the country . I was stunned to se e the Leader of the
Opposition beating the drum for no more i nvestment on that State highway network
north of Auckland. He was beating the dr um saying that State Highway 1 from
Auckland to Whangarei should not be upgrade d. In fact, in a condescending manner he
called it the “Holiday Highway” and said that the Labour Pa rty would rather pull the $1
billion committed to that and spend it on ever ywhere else but Northland. It is very
disappointing for Northlanders—very disappointing for Northlanders.
For colleagues this will come as some surprise, because my colleagues on this side of
the House do not actually realise that the La bour Party leader at the moment ran for the
seat of Whangarei.

items.speaker: Hon Maurice Williamson
items.text: No.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL HEATLEY
items.text: No, you did not know that, did you?

items.speaker: Hon Amy Adams
items.text: No.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL HEATLEY
items.text: Many colleagues did not know. He ran for the seat of
Whangarei in 2002 as a proud Aucklander. The Labour Party usually sends Aucklanders
to Whangarei to stand. He came to Whangare i and actually said, back in 2002, that he
would stand up for Whangarei, would st and up for Northland, and wanted more
attention to be given to Wha ngarei and Northland. That is wh at the Labour Party leader
said in 2002. In this general election we found that he wanted to cut ties with Northland,
and did not want to invest more in that  highway, State Highway 1 to Whangarei.
Whangarei residents were aghast at the cha nge of fortunes—the turn, I guess, that the
Leader of the Opposition has made in that time.
14 Feb 2012 Address in Reply 347
So Labour Party members might want to c ontinue to call State Highway 1 north of
Auckland to Whangarei and Northland the “Holiday Highway”, and mock it, but,
actually, we will accept that. We are delighted  that Aucklanders want to come north.
We are pleased, actually, that it is a tourist destination. If  Aucklanders want to travel
north, pull out their credit cards, and spend money in Northland’s capital, Whangarei,
then we are absolutely delighted about that, but we want to see that sort of investment in
the north. We have seen decisions made on the Waterview Connection, and, of course,
on the Kōpū Bridge, and other important transport investment infrastructure right across
New Zealand, and we celebrate it. And there is much, much, much more to come.
Roads are not the only area where we are investing significant finances for the
benefit of economic growth. The electricity network across New Zealand is also looking
at a massive upgrade. People would have read in the last 2 weeks that there is going to
be a marginal increase in electricity prices  due to the investment in Transpower’s
network for the national grid right across New Zealand. I re call that when the National
Party was in Opposition, the Government of the day was talking about upgrading the
national grid. It was concerne d at that time that should there be power blackouts it
would be unfortunate if that occurred because Transpower’s grid throughout New
Zealand had somehow failed. I remember the Labour Party talking about that in the year
2000. In 2000 or 2001 they continued that  discussion, and I believe—and Maurice
Williamson will correct me on this—in 2002 the Labour Party did what it did best, and
the Government of that time, I think, formed an officials committee.

items.speaker: Hon Maurice Williamson
items.text: That’s right.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL HEATLEY
items.text: That is right. It discussed that for 12 months, and then was
it not in 2003 or 2004 th at it decided to get expert advice? I think some members called
for a select committee inquiry, so we had 5 years of Labour Gove rnment discussion
about whether we should, or whether we should not, upgrade the transmission lines
throughout the country. It probably issued  a discussion document—a discussion
document. I am not sure whether Labour surveyed, but, as was its habit when it
governed during that period—it did not ma tter whether it was building a road,
electricity generation, electricity transmissi on, broadband, rail, or whatever investment
it was—it simply did a number of things al l in a row. It would have an officials
committee, discussion documents, select comm ittee inquiries, expert  advice, and royal
commissions—anything but make a decision. It would do anything but make a decision
in case it isolated someone. Unfortunatel y, as is the case throughout the world, yes,
constituents like to be heard, like to be loved, and like to be agreed with, but, in the end,
if year on year you show no leadership and you show no decision-making prowess, they
will toss you out, and that is what has happened.
That is why we are saying, quite clearly—n ailing our colours to the wall—that we
are about responsibly managing the Governme nt’s finances and building a competitive
and productive economy. We will invest in roading, we will invest in electricity
generation and transmission, we will invest in broadband, and we will invest in all these
infrastructural opportunities. We will do that and make those decisions.
That, of course, leads me to the investme nt in housing. Members will know that the
previous Labour Government was very proud of increasing the number of State houses
in its stock. When we took over we made a very distinct and clear decision that we were
enthusiastic about having State houses that were fit for purpose, warm, dry, and livable,
as well as increasing their number. So we  decided that our i nvestment would be
upgrading the State housing stock and increas ing it—doing that t ogether—and that has
been a very wise decision, indeed.
The previous Government, interestingly enough, looked at the issue of State houses
being on quarter acre and ha lf acre sections and being,  sort of, 1940s and 1950s
348 Address in Reply 14 Feb 2012
houses—being old, cold, and mouldy pieces of infrastructure. It discussed for many,
many years doing something about that, but never actually did it. National has decided
that we will subdivide large sections, and we will demolish old, cold, and mouldy State
houses and build new, modern, insulated ones. We will make better use of those assets.
That is what we are doing. So although member s on that side of the House might have
increased the number of old, cold, and moul dy State houses, on this side of the House
we have decided that we need to invest in  the quality, not just the quantity, of housing.
That is what we are doing.
We are very proud of the goals that we ha ve outlined in our four main priorities:
responsibly managing the economy, building a more competitive and productive
economy, delivering better public services, and rebuilding Christchurch. That is what
we will be doing, that is what we will be m easured on, and we are pleased that that, in
fact, will be the bar we have set for ourselve s and for New Zealanders to judge us by in
3 years’ time.

items.speaker: Dr DAVID CLARK
items.text: Mr Speaker, I congratulate you
on your election. Support for your appointment  extended across the House. That is
testament to the success of your efforts during the first term of the current Government.
I have the honour of being the 12 th member of Parliament to represent the Dunedin
North electorate. The seat of Dunedin North has a proud history of strong representation
by the Labour Party, both in Opposition and around the Cabinet table. The individuals
who have held the seat have contributed to Labour holding it for 80 of the past 83 years.
My predecessor, the Hon Pete Hodgson, can  lay claim to a quarter of Dunedin
North’s history with a Labour Party MP—m ore if you count his involvement before
that. Pete pursued the integration of hone st, transparent, and accountable economic
policy with honest, transparent, and accountable environmental policy. He said so in his
maiden speech. The year was 1990, and he ar gued for a price on carbon. He sought to
make New Zealand “the first country in th e world to have an economy that is truly
sustainable”. Well, we are not a truly sust ainable economy yet. It  was fully 18 years
after Pete’s maiden speech that New Zealand finally legislated for a price on carbon. He
played an important part in shaping that ca rbon debate. Pete got stuff done. His animal
welfare private bill caused the Government to  rewrite animal welfare legislation. It
made New Zealand law amongst the best in the world. He did heavy lifting across 14
portfolios during 9 years in the Cabinet of the Clark Government. And he worked hard
locally too. In his constituen cy work Pete wore his poli tical colours lightly, and was
well-liked, as his sizable majorities atte st. As Pete makes good on his promise to
withdraw from political life, his talents and vigour are missed.
The electorate of Dunedin North includes the northern coastal settlements of Waitati,
Warrington, Karitane, and Waikouaiti. The so uthern boundary is formed by the Otago
harbour, while the bulk of the central city  and hill suburbs form the south-western
boundary. But what of its flavour? Well, Dunedin North is shaped by its Scottish
heritage. Many of its important educational institutions, including the University of
Otago, have Presbyterian roots. Manufacturi ng enterprises are important, especially
heavy engineering, and the electorate contai ns a port with a skilled workforce that
serves all of Otago. Dunedin North has mo re young people than any other electorate,
therefore the most who are single, the most on lowest annual incomes, and the highest
proportion employed in educati on and training. It also ha s the highest proportion of
people employed in the health care and social service sector.
Those who made my election to the House possible have placed trust in me to
represent this fine electora te. To them I extend my si ncere thanks. In 2011 Dunedin
North was the only general South Island seat  where Labour won both votes. That is a
credit to the hundreds of volunteers who helped out during the campaign and on
14 Feb 2012 Address in Reply 349
election day, and a tribute to the wisdom of the voters. To my wife , Katrina, I express
gratitude for the support provided during the transition from my previous role of service
at Selwyn College, to one that will surely a fford less reliable and frequent engagement
in duties properly the responsibility of a father and a husband. Although my previous
engagement in the parliamentary envir onment was short, it  was long enough to
engender real understanding of the correspondin g personal cost borne by wider families
of the members of this House.
Government will always be with us, and as citizens we must decide what kind of
Government we want. In my view Governments are elected to provide moral leadership,
not just to manage the economy to achieve th ings like market discipline and efficiency
gains. Markets make excellent servants, but terrible masters. Good regulation can
harness markets to support pe ople and their needs, rather  than the other way round. We
must take our destiny into our own hands and shape the eco nomy to benefit all of New
Zealand. In recent decades those benefits have been shared too unequally.
Politicians are elected to a life of public se rvice; the service they  are elected to is
leadership. Leadership involves listening, discerning, assisting, and decision making.
Service should never be confused with servility. Politicians ought not to hide behind the
term “service”, awaiting a mandate of majority support on every issue and forgetting, or
perhaps never realising, that th e public have elected the poli ticians to do a job in good
faith on their behalf. Politicians do not exis t to rubber-stamp what the electorate has
already decided, but to articulate and share a vision of a better society.
I will describe the better society to which I aspire. It has similarities with what
founding members of the New Zealand Labour Party de scribed as an “applied
Christianity”. It is a society where accident  of birth does not dictate one’s station and
prospects. It is a society where every citizen  can get ahead by dint of hard work that
builds on their natural endowment. It is one where all have free and equal access to
high-quality education, a society where all ha ve the ability to develop their talents
sufficiently to ensure fulfilling and enriching lives. It is one in which choices are not
driven by fear but are afforded by opportuni ty, and in which everyone has access to
legal representation, regardless  of their means. The societ y that I wish to live in
recognises that prevention is better than cure . It has a health system with universal
access: a trip to hospital does not require in surance or a cheque book. I believe that
more careful attention needs to given to th e prophylactic benefits of public health, as
compared with the resources required to at tend to the illnesses of the dying and the
diseases of the “worried well”.
To support our objectives, our economy must  change and grow. We must recognise
our dependence upon the primary se ctor, and treasure and enha nce it. But we must also
diversify if we wish to be a prosperous na tion. As a small country far from markets, we
must make some strategic decisions about th e types of industries we wish to promote
and support. The OECD recognises that we e ducate our kids well. We must leverage
this learning for research, for innovati on, and for New Zealand’s commercial gain.
Dunedin is already a base for firms with  a strong technology component. Taylormade
Productions and Scott Technology are two of the most well-known, but there are other
weightless exporters locally, like Pocket smith, Trunk.ly, and 1000Minds. Squid gel,
DNA sequencing, and probiotics illustrate the potential to commercialise science
developed at Otago. We need more of this if we are going to prosper as a country.
I have written and rewritten this speech several times. Allotted more time, I would
assert the benefits of placing a happiness i ndex alongside our GDP metric as a way of
measuring our progress as a society. I would suggest that a society is best judged by
how it treats its most vulnerable citizen s. I would canvass the importance of New
Zealand retaining a strong and independent voice in the Pacific. I would extol the
350 Address in Reply 14 Feb 2012
benefits of universal provision of M āori language education, both to brain development
and to national identity. I would argue for appropriate financial instruments for the
management of fresh water. I would emphasise  the responsibility of current generations
to hand over the planet in better shape than we inherited it. I would describe how we
might reconsider financial transactions taxes,  gift and estate dutie s, and a capital gains
tax, in order to broaden our tax base. And I wo uld describe the nature of public services
supported by a progressive taxation system that would drive greater social mobility.
These topics are all close to my heart, but I wish to concentrate the burden of my speech
on one thing that is someth ing of a precondition to good progress—that is, greater
equality.
Sadly, New Zealand has rushed towards greater inequality over the last 30 years. The
truly wealthy have grabbed a disproportionately large slice of the economic growth pie,
at the expense of other New Zealanders. There is an urgent need to level an evermore
slanted playing field. We need a broad-ba sed and progressive taxation system that
preserves the Kiwi dream of a country where a little talent and much hard work provide
real opportunities to be tter one’s lot. My Christian upbr inging instilled in me a strong
sense of social justice. My theological education and my time as a Presbyterian minister
have cemented that. That some people have  many opportunities while others have few
just does not feel right. For me, this is a gut-l evel response rooted in firmly held values.
A growing body of literature  shows a correlation betw een societies with large
inequalities and poor health, l ongevity, and other social stat istics. A more equal society
means better quality of life.
Generating the conditions for a more equal society is the right thing to do, but it
increasingly seems that it is also the pragmatic thing to do. I believe that a fairer society
also makes economic sense, and here are f our reasons why. First, resources shared
across society mean that all people are tr ained and available to make their best
contribution to society. In Ne w Zealand more than one in five children is born into
poverty. These kids have to battle against th e odds. They are more likely to suffer from
diseases of poverty, less likely to succeed in the education system, and have higher
chances of ending up in our prisons. For our  country to get ahead, we need all our
children to realise their potential.
Greater equality is good for a second reas on. If we remunerate talent by valuing
professions that support the w hole of society, rather than  those that preserve the
interests of a wealthy few, we all benefit. Neurosurgeons and teachers give more to
society than great brains wast ed on exploiting distortions in poorly regulated financial
markets.
A third reason that greater equality ma kes pragmatic sense relates to public
investment. Infrastructure is an example— witness growth in China’s high-speed rail
network. It is 12 times bigger than it was in 2008, four times larger  than that in any
other country, and is still growi ng at an astonishing rate. It is hard to imagine this
happening in the USA today. Where a critical  mass of the truly wealthy exert undue
influence on the political process, investme nt in infrastructure, education, research,
health care, and other matters related to the common good dwindles, and we all suffer.
In any society with extremes of wealth and poverty, the truly wealthy cease to value
common assets. Able to buy what they desire, they have no need for them.
A fourth reason why more equal societies te nd to be more successful is that people
work harder when they know that the ru les of society are fair. When everybody who
does a fair day’s work can live well, and when  it is always possible for someone born in
a family of modest means to be successful in  their chosen field, they are more likely to
strive so to do. In New Zealand today the poverty of spirit that can result from birth into
14 Feb 2012 Address in Reply 351
deprivation often has more far-reaching social consequences than those symptoms
measured more immediately and with greater statistical ease.
A more equal society that shares the benefits of a Western economy across its
citizenry avoids unrealised potential, wasted talent, and a kind of selfish behaviour that
results from distorted incentives and despair in the face of unfairness. Not only are the
conditions for a fair society the right thing for Governments to busy themselves with but
also they appear to provide for a better quality of life and the conditions for economic
success. A more equal society is healthier, wealthier, and wise.

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: Tēnā koutou katoa. I acknowledge the first people
of this great country: the original stewards of lands and waters. I pay respects to those
who have gone before us: our ancestors a nd those who have passed through this House
and whose wisdom and achievements we inher it. Mr Speaker, I congratulate you on
your re-election to the role of Speaker. I knew you more than 20 years ago when I was a
student leader campaigning on tertiary education issues, and you were approachable and
generous with your time then. I know you ha ve established a reputation as a Speaker
who acts without fear or favour and with mu ch integrity, and I look forward to playing
my part in this House under your guidance.
It is a great honour and a privilege to be in this House, and to be here under the
Labour banner. This year marks the centenary  of one of the most bitter and violent
industrial disputes in New Zealand’s history: the Waihī miners’ strike. It is an important
part of the Labour story. A young Scottish union organiser was witness to that dispute
and saw how workers who wanted nothing more  than decent pay and a fair go were
intimidated, divided, and—after a striking mi ner was beaten to death by those opposed
to the strike—run out of town. Those dark ev ents led to that organiser and many others
realising that justice would be achieved only when working people reached beyond the
workplace for influence and had a direct say on the laws and policies they were subject
to. The union organiser was Peter Fraser, who later became a Labour Prime Minister.
He and others set about orga nising the first of the uni ty conferences in 1913, which
drew in progressive elements, brought toge ther a social democratic programme, and
eventually led to the formation of the New Zealand Labour Party in 1916.
I enter this House as a first-generation Ne w Zealander. That means two things. I am
born of a land that is steeped in natural beauty but also settled by our forebears under
our foundation document, the Tr eaty of Waitangi, which was conceived in a spirit of
peace, collaboration, and respect. And I accept my responsibility to give honour to that.
The second aspect is that I am closer—if only by birth—to the other strand of our
founding values: those brought here from a distant land; values that go back to the
Magna Carta; values of respect for people, of freedom, of constitutional government and
citizens’ rights, of the rejec tion of arbitrary power and “m ight is right”, and of due
process and fairness—and I pledge to honour these traditions too.
My parents settled in New Zealand 50 y ears ago this April. My father had a
background in the military services and retrai ned as a school teacher, eventually taking
a post at New Plymouth Girls’ High Sc hool. My mother had a background in
professional secretarial work. They arrived here with my eldest sister, and with my
eldest brother on the way, and settled in the brand-new subu rb of Marfell. By 1965 the
Little household had grown to five childre n. I was fourth—or fourth equal—arriving
with my twin sister, Valerie, that year.
I look back on a great Taranaki childhood. Ours was a home that was far from
wealthy, dependent as it was almost entirely on my father’s teacher’s salary, but what
we lacked in material wealth was made up with in the rich experiences the region had to
offer: the mighty Mount Taranaki—my ma unga—the many beaches with the pounding
west coast surf and black sand, the beautiful  parks and gardens, and an emerging arts
352 Address in Reply 14 Feb 2012
and cultural life. My brothers and sisters and I enjoyed a home filled with love, good
guidance, strong educational values, and supportive parents.
Ours was a political household too. Dad was a staunch member of the National Party,
but one of his life experiences set him apart. As part of his military career he served in
the Middle East after World War II. He obs erved how powerful Arab States tried to
exploit and intimidate the stateless Bedouin pe ople, and he saw the world turn its back
on the Palestinian people. The sense of injus tice my father felt affected him deeply, and
it was impossible not to be influenced by it. Dad was a prodigious writer of letters to the
editor. He railed at the TV whenever a po litical foe appeared, the fiercest reactions
being reserved, as I recall, for union leaders of the day. But there was much humour and
irreverence in our house. Above all, we were  told to think for ourselves and make our
own way. Mum would say to us: “To thine own self be true.”
I enjoyed a good education, and at New Plymouth Boys’ High School we were
inculcated with very strong va lues of self-discipline, resp ect, and courtesy. Around this
time Taranaki was beneficiary of the mu ch-derided Think Big economic programme,
but that programme was instrumental in  boosting the region’ s heavy engineering
industry. I remember in 1982 being fascin ated by the huge hea vy loads of process
modules that had been fabricated overseas be ing hauled from the port to the east of the
city. But it was with huge pride during last y ear’s election campaign that I stood with
thousands of New Plymouth residents to wa tch a giant module being hauled in the
opposite direction, from one of the city ’s leading and highly unionised heavy
engineering firms, Fitzroy Engineering, to th e port, to make its way to Australia. It
confirmed Taranaki’s strength as a world-class engineering centre.
New Plymouth is a great city with, I might add, a great mayor, and I enjoyed
campaigning there last year, although I remain  intrigued by a question I was asked at
one of the first meetings I held: what my position was on the merger of Air New
Zealand and NAC. I said that Labour wa s taking a “wait-and-see” approach. I
acknowledge the successful candidate and now  my parliamentary colleague Jonathan
Young and thank him for a clean and worthy fight.
In 1992 I started work in Auckland as a lawyer for the organisation that would
dominate my life for the next 19 years, the New Zealand Amalgamated Engineering,
Printing and Manufacturing Union. My work for the union brought me into contact with
many thousands of working people, hundreds of companies and important industries,
and many managers, good and bad. I started then with a reasonably clear view about the
world and society I lived in. I did not accept th e reductionist view of humanity that lay
at the heart of the neo-liberal Washingt on consensus, Friedmanite, Thatcherite,
Reaganite, and “whatever else - ite” style of public policy th at was inflicted on us. I am
not particularly religious, but my driving values are neatly encapsulated in the biblical
question in Mark 8:36: “What benefits the man that he gains the world and loses his
soul?”. My work for the union made this conviction stronger. My time at the union gave
me insights about the New Zealand economy; about how we create wealth; about how
we ensure those who help to cr eate wealth share fairly in it ; how we ensure we rise to
the greatest challenge we face today—the sa fe keeping of our environment—and how
we protect and care for our most vulnerabl e: our young, our elderly, and our sick. From
the time I started at the union I saw abus es of power, a growing intolerance of
difference, and the rise of a managerial cl ass that thought it knew everything. I saw the
frustration of skilled and experienced worker s who had much to offer management but
whose voice, even if it was h eard, was often ignored. I formed the view then that it was
not just enough to secure and enforce contra ctual rights and benefits, but that working
people needed to be—were entitled to be—i nvolved in all decisi ons bearing on their
working life. Thirty years of the neo-liberal  policy programme have been a disaster for
14 Feb 2012 Address in Reply 353
working New Zealanders. Unfortunately, no t even the welcome arrival of good-faith
laws and better collective barg aining rights in 2000 has b een enough to ameliorate the
damage that has been done.
In 1991, when the Employment Contracts Ac t brought radical change to workplace
relations, the promise was that no one would lose conditions without their agreement.
But workers did lose conditions. The promise of 1991 was that there would be freedom.
Workers were told they would have the fr eedom to choose. But when the choice made
by many workers to belong to a union was unacceptable to an employer, they would
find their choice challenged and undermin ed and obstructed. Many employers
welcomed workers having freedom of choice—providing the choice was the
employer’s. We were promised that the nation’ s wealth would rise on the back of new
flexibility and better opportuni ties for investment, and that the wealth would be shared
around through higher wages. None of this ha ppened. The opposite did. Working life in
New Zealand got harder. Median and averag e real wages have gone down. The gap in
earnings between New Zealand and Australia has grown. Inequality of income has now
become so great, it is an injustice keenly fe lt. And resentment is real and growing. New
Zealand workers now work some of the l ongest hours in the developed world. Too
many people just cannot get ahead.
And then there is the most insidious devel opment of all: contracting out. Whenever
managers are in retreat or just lack skill and competence and creativity, they contract
out. Contracting out is seldom good manage ment. It is usually the absence of
management. And so at Ports of Auckland we  should look sceptical ly at claims about
the need for contracting out. The peopl e of Auckland City should demand that
management do its job—fix the problems, usi ng their management skills. That is what
they are paid to do.
In training and skills formation we have  performed poorly. The numbers signing up
for apprenticeships have fallen, and comp letion rates have dropped. A new business
culture has emerged in New Zealand—a cu lture of dominance by management, and
increasing servility by workers. We have forgotten the social contract of business—that
through limited liability, investors will be protected from full liability for the
misfortunes or incompetence and wrongdoing of the company they own, and that
communities upon which business depends for pe ople and resources will be respected.
We have a culture in our commercial sector  that says bare legal compliance is OK.
Never mind whether it is right or wrong. And never mind the impact on people. The
ultimate product of years of a culture of management dominance, deregulation, poor
enforcement, and bare legal compliance is sure ly the tragedy at Pike River Coal. A year
before that dreadful event, the union appr oached management a bout collaborating over
health and safety. The occupa tional safety and health mana ger took this up with the
chief executive, and, as the royal commission has now heard, the reply was this: “The
‘union’ … does not come into any consider ation. Please do not use the union in the
same sentence as anything at Pike.”
In the last 30 years some in New Zealand have done very well. But many more today
struggle to survive. In our rush to gain the world we have left many behind and we are
losing our soul. We have a massive challenge ahead for New Zealand, and a new way is
essential. Against a background of growing poverty, of a rising threat to our standard of
living, the primary challenge today is to lift the nation’s income so we can afford our
future and enjoy a decent society. The challenge  is harder than ever before because our
planet, the only one we have got, is struggling to cope wi th the demands of a growing
world population. So we will not recover our standard of living by doing more of the
same. And if we do not make change, we are destined to a life of  continual cutting,
slashing, scrimping, and grinching. We will just get poorer.
354 Address in Reply 14 Feb 2012
My leader, David Shearer, set out his visi on for New Zealand at the very beginning
of this Parliament, just before Christmas. It  was about rejecting “business as usual”. It
was about seeing new opportunitie s and connecting with the re st of the world, offering
new products and services. I am excited to be working with David and all my Labour
colleagues to realise the vision of lifting the value of what  we do and what we produce,
by being smarter with technology and lifting our national income. Our future must
involve investment, not disinvestment, which is what State asset sales amounts to, and
investment in new activity and investment in  people. There must be local investment
and foreign investment.
Although our agricultural sector  is vital to our economy, and is something we lead
the world in, we will need to do more than ag riculture to secure our future. Our future
must be in making stuff. Manufacturing a nd fabrication involve more technology and
more skilled people, and, as a result, generate more w ealth. We have some great
businesses harnessing the latest in t echnology, making amazing products they are
selling around the world. We can do this stu ff. We need more of it. But our goal cannot
just be about gaining a bigger share of the world. We must look after our people and we
must look after our natural world. We must pr eserve our soul. At the heart of economic
change must be a different attitude to pe ople. We need managers to involve their
workforce, actively seek out knowledge from  the front line, and open up management
decision-making to hear what the workforce has to say.
In the project to save Ai r New Zealand engineering j obs in 2005, th e alternative
proposal that was ultimately accepted by management was developed by front-line
union members. The courageous men and women of Air New Zealand provided the
ideas. In the nation’s largest and most impor tant corporate, Fonterra, the unions and
management have been involved in a long-te rm project to improve productivity in the
maintenance function. The front-line unionise d maintenance engine ers have taken on
more decision-making responsibility, have less supervision, work fewer hours, are some
of the top-earning fitters in New Zealand, and the processing plant and equipment is
some of the world’s most reliable. In bot h cases, management had to surrender some
control and hear from the workforce about what would work practically. This
Government knows there is a better way.
Before concluding, I want to pay tribute to the people who have supported me and
brought me here. I acknowledge the member s, delegates, and officials of the
Engineering, Printing and Manufacturing Union—you are the heroes  of a generation
and you have taught me much; the New Zealand Council of the Labour Party—
president, Moira Coatsworth, and secretary, Chris Flatt; my fantastic campaign team
and supporters in New Plymouth, who worked so  hard last year and ensured we all had
a great time; to my family—my mother Ci cely, my brothers and sisters, Jennifer,
Leighton, Patrick, and Valerie, my half-sisters, Nicky and Fiona, half a world away, my
in-laws, all of whom have been so lovi ng and supportive, and my wife, Leigh, and son,
Cam, without whose love and support and fo rbearance I would not be the person I am.
Because it is Valentine’s Day, let me channe l Whitney Houston and say: “I will always
love you.” I am inspired by thes e words of John F Kennedy: “I  am certain that after the
dust of centuries has passed over our cities, we, too, wi ll be remembered not for
victories or defeats in battle or in politics, but for our contribution to the human spirit.” I
hope to leave here secure in the knowledge that we are a people gaining our fair share of
the world, preserving and protecting it, and with our individual and community soul
intact. Thank you.

items.speaker: Dr MEGAN WOODS
items.text: Mr Speaker, I join with my colleagues
in congratulating you on your re-election. Like my colleague, the last time we spoke, it
was in a less formal situation. It was th e 1990s, you were the Mini ster of Education, I
14 Feb 2012 Address in Reply 355
was a student, we were at the University  of Canterbury, there were megaphones, and it
was said you made your getaway through a window—I am sure you remember those
days well.
Tēnā koutou katoa. It is with gr eat honour that I rise to give  the first speech in this
House as the Labour member for Wigram. Maiden statements from members from
Wigram are rare—so rare, in fact, there has never previously been one. Wigram and its
precursor seats, Sydenham and Yaldhurst, ar e both steeped in history. The story of
Wigram and its representation is an important part of New Zealand’s social and political
history. I feel the shoes I ha ve to fill are truly huge. Syde nham has been the seat of
giants: Mabel Howard, Norman Kirk, and Jim Anderton. All thr ee have shown an
absolute commitment to social justice and equality.
And Wigram is a seat where constituen ts have high expectation—and, like David
Clark’s constituents, they are very wise—as they are already reminding me. One of the
most vivid memories of my campaign came on a hot October Saturday afternoon, doing
street corner meetings. Robert Watson, my  friend and campaign volunteer, and I were
flagging a little at street corner meeting 100 and something and about the sixth of that
particular day when we pulled up on a corner in Hoon Hay. An older gentleman came
striding down the road towards the small crow d that had gathered. His stride was ripe
with intent and his first comment showed he  meant business: “I am here to argue.”
“Good,” I replied, “that’s what it ’s all about.” This being hear tland red territory, lest he
be mistaken for someone of a different political hue, he was quick to inform me: “I am a
Labour man. I have been going to street corn er meetings in this electorate for donkey’s
years, first one was Mabel Howard in Church Square, and I want to get the measure of
you.” The meeting went on. The striding man was as good as his word. He argued with
me, he argued with the others present, and at  one point I am convinced he argued with
himself. But, meeting done, he came over to me, shook my hand, and informed me:
“You’ll do.”, and with this, he strode home.
But there is one predecessor I want to pa y special tribute to, and that is Jim
Anderton. Although I did not kno w it at the time, growi ng up in the 1980s in the
Sydenham electorate, I was witnessing the ev eryday reality of new-right reform. I had
friends whose parents lost thei r jobs at the Addington rail yards. I saw people lose their
homes, and I saw the local post  office disappear. Ordinary pe ople were stripped of their
jobs, their dignity, and their security. Bu t then there was the local MP, who stood
shoulder to shoulder with us, his constituen ts. For nearly three decades Jim Anderton
refused to accept that there was no alternativ e. Jim, as your successor, I thank you for
the high bar you have set in terms of politi cal courage and for standing up for what you
believe in and for the people you represented.
Maiden statements are a bit like a note to self about why you are here and what you
want to achieve. My note to self is simp le: I believe in the power of an active New
Zealand Government and State to make a real  difference in people’s lives, and that is
why I am here. I was selected to be Labou r’s candidate in Wigram on 19 September
2010—women’s suffrage day—only 2 weeks and 1 day after the first of Christchurch’s
devastating earthquakes. On 22 February that rebuilding task ahead of us became
mammoth. There are buildings, homes, roads,  sewage pipes, and businesses to be
rebuilt. Institutions with long histories now face uncertain futures. This is something we
all feel on a personal level. My former school, Catholic Cathedral College, a school that
once stood in the shadow of the mighty Cat holic Basilica, is now behind a crumbling
building and a pile of rubble. The University  of Canterbury, where I spent a decade of
my life, faces an uncertain fu ture with falling student numb ers. It is imperative that
broad, research-based excellence is retain ed. Engineering, commerc e, and science are
356 Address in Reply 14 Feb 2012
undoubtedly crucial to our rebuilding, but th e humanities and social sciences are
essential, too. We need critical thinkers now more than ever.
We have lost so much in our city, and I want to acknowledge the people whose lives
were lost and their families. We are all th inking of you. There is no doubt that people
are struggling with the devastation of the la st 17 months. The sense of loss is so much
more than the physical; we lost the locations  of so many of our memories—the school
steps we scaled with trepidation as 5-year-o lds, the homes we toiled to build and make
our own, the churches where we worshippe d and were married, and the list goes on.
This is hard enough, but there is an even bi gger job ahead of us, a nd that is rebuilding
hope—hope that we will have a vibrant and thriving city again; a city where people will
not be looking for the nearest exit to terra  firma; and, of course, a city where the
Crusaders will continue to win every game  they play. But some of that hope is
embedded in a tension as people search fo r the right answers. When 4,000 quake- and
battle-weary people gathered in the centre of our city earlier this month, collectively we
were demanding fairness, accountability, preser vation of our democratic rights, and our
right to participate in our future. These are the same sentiments and feelings that are
driving the amazing community and grassroot s responses we are seeing all over our
city. These values are the future and are the solid foundations on which we will rebuild
our city. These are also the very values that drive me politically, and these are the values
that have brought me to this House.
There is no rabble at the gate that n eeds quashing and silencing. This is not
something to be feared; it is quite the opposite. This is an engaged public, and this is
something I celebrate. An active and engaged Government must work with this public.
Controversially, in the wake of the 22 Fe bruary quakes, this House granted what
amounted to wartime powers to the Government to rebuild our city. I am here today to
remind those who wield those powers that with these powers comes great responsibility.
The Act granted the Government the rights and responsibility to be active—and active it
must be. It is an active State that will rebu ild Christchurch. If we think about moments
of greatness in our history—moments when we have taken a great leap forward as a
country—it has been an active State and a belief in the power of communities that has
delivered that reform, not individualism and a rampant free market.
In the 1870s Sir Julius Vogel had a vision and committed the colonial State to
investing in the infrastructu re essential for economic development. In the 1880s the
Liberals intervened, with the old-age pens ion scheme, industrial legislation, and the
genesis of our public housing scheme. Ne w Zealand was a progressive and world-
leading social laboratory. In the 1930s the first Labour Government committed the State
to creating constructive employment and a housing programme as a way out of the
Great Depression, and shaped our very present. Today, in the 21st century, I am proud to
stand here as a Labour member , an heir to those who have  had the courage to reform.
As in the past it is together, collectively, that we can solve the pressing issues we face as
a nation. Government needs to facilitate this and em power people and community.
“Look mum, no hands”, laissez-faire, tric kle-down economics based on individualism
has failed.
Christchurch may be a city currently on an active fault, but it is simply cannot be a
faulty city. We must believe that out of this destruction we have a unique opportunity to
create something special, and, once again, take  that great leap forw ard. But it will take
an active State that is willing to intervene. We have the opportunity to train a generation
of young people with the necessa ry skills to be active pa rticipants in  this work.
Currently we have 83,000 young people aged 15 to 24 who are not in any form of work,
training, or education. This is up 4,000 from last quarter. We cannot sit idly by and
watch this figure continue to climb. I finished high school in 1991, when youth
14 Feb 2012 Address in Reply 357
unemployment was at 20 percen t, so I know firsthand the fear of leaving school and
there being no jobs. We had two choices then : further study or go on the dole. I made a
decision to go to university—I was the first in  my family to go straight from school—
but the hopelessness felt by my friends who were looking for work is something I will
never forget.
