There is an alternative. By 2013, 36,000 a dditional workers will be required in
Christchurch. Bringing in sk illed trades professionals fr om overseas simply cannot be
our solution. We need to invest in our young people and let them lead the way. Such a
commitment is not a leap into the unknown; we have done this before on the scale that
is necessary now. Following World War II, New Zealand faced both a critical housing
shortage and the underemployment of young Māori. Labour Prime Minister Peter Fraser
showed the necessary vision to res ource trade training schemes for young M āori
workers. This scheme was the subject of my PhD thesis and I saw both the positive
opportunities this scheme provided individuals  and the benefit the nation received in
having a generation of skilled tradespeopl e—not to mention a stock of well-built
houses.
Real aspiration cannot come to mean policie s and measures that make life a little bit
more bearable for those on the lowest incomes. If we want to be aspirational for all New
Zealanders, if we are to raise wages, if we believe in the right of all New Zealanders to
get ahead, if we will not tolerate poverty, and if we believe in fairness, then we need a
commitment to an active State that believes it has an active role in creating a productive
economy. In my previous role at Plant and Food Research, I observed firsthand the real
difference science and innovation can make. We need more businesses to access and
utilise the exceptional knowledge that is bei ng created in our Crow n research institutes
and universities. And we need  a proper commitment to the fundamental research that
underpins this. To improve this we must  commit to adequately fund science and
innovation to create jobs and li ft wages. We must abandon the view that it is OK for
someone to toil for a wage that is insufficient to make ends meet. This needs to be
replaced with a belief that people have a right to be paid a decent wage for a decent
day’s work. We need to move beyond quibbli ng about a few cents’ rise in the minimum
wage and the constant questioning of wh ether the wages of the lowest paid are
affordable while ignoring the excesses of ma nagerial salaries. A living minimum wage
must be an immediate priority  and we must see it as just  that—a minimum. We must
have an environment where workers not only have the right but are encouraged to join
unions and bargain collectively, they have the right to have  a voice at work, and they
have the right to be protected from unfair or unsafe treatment at work. We need to
recognise that this does not mean that business is harder to do.
As a proud member of the Service and Food Workers Union and the New Zealand
Public Service Association, I believe that  decent wages and e ffective employment
relations will enable New Zealanders to lift productivity and to perform well. It is not
OK for me to stand in this House represen ting people who cannot afford to put food on
their tables. Last week I met with a constitu ent who is on a sickness  benefit. After his
rent and fixed expenses, he had $27 a week  left for food. He was hungry. Neither is it
OK that in my electorate there are homes th at last winter had bedrooms that were
monitored as being 9 degrees overnight, with 90 percent humidity. I have not come here
to stand idly by and watch this happen. It is  not tolerable that in the OECD’s recent
findings inequality has grown fa ster here than in most othe r countries. This is not an
OECD table that we can accept being in the to p half of. We need to reject the notion
that tough economic times necessarily mean gr eater inequality and injustice. Selling
publicly owned assets, cutt ing spending, low wages and benefits, and ravaging the
358 Address in Reply 14 Feb 2012
environment is neither a strategy for a hea lthy economy, nor a recipe for a healthy,
vibrant, and fair society.
Growing up in the Sydenham electorate, I learnt  that selling assets is not the answer,
no matter what the question. It just does not make sense. At tempting to shroud the sell-
off and the ideological commitment to privatisation under the rhetorical cloak of mixed-
ownership models does nothing to change the simple fact that our current Government
plans to sell off assets that have been bu ilt up by generations of New Zealanders. Let us
call this what it is—selling them is selling them.
No one comes to this House on their own, and like all new members there are many I
owe a huge debt of gratitude to for their support and encouragement. Firstly, to my
family, especially to my parents—to Go rdon and Maureen Woods and my sister
Melissa, thank you for your belief and your encouragement over many years. It is
humbling as a candidate to have so many peopl e give so generously  of their time and
skills. My campaign team and the many volunteers wrung th e towel during an
incredibly trying year in Christchurch, and for that I am incredibly grateful and proud of
what we achieved together. The experienced hands were joined by a fantastic Wigram
Young Labour team, who together created a creative and energetic team who did not
neglect the tried and true basics of campaigning.
In conclusion, it is with great pride that I stand in this House representing the people
of Wigram. I am a New Zealand historian by training who has worked in science and
innovation. I am a former community board member who believes in the power of
communities and the grassroots. I am a Christ church native who grew up in the ravages
of a user-pays world. Despite being glued to  the royal wedding in 1981, I believe in the
desirability and inevitability  of our country becoming a re public in my lifetime, and I
celebrate the diversity of modern New Zealand. I am here because I have a strong belief
in social justice. I am here because I believe  that there are always real alternatives in
working to ensure that hope, opportunity, and being all you can be are not accidents of
birth for the privileged few but the birthright of all New Zealanders.

items.speaker: RINO TIRIKATENE
items.text: Ka rere taku manu ki te T āhuhu-
o-te-Rangi topatopa ai, ko muritai tokerau āta rangaranga hei hiki i ōna parirau. Tau ana
ngā kanohi ki te pito o te Tiriti ki Waitangi ki roto o Ng āpuhi nui tonu, te kāinga o taku
whaea, te ūkaipō.
Tere tonu te haere tae noa ki ngā tai o te uru ki te P ā o ngā Ariki, ki te papa i tūria ai,
te temepara i kauhautia ai e Tahup ōtiki W īremu R ātana, te M āngai, te tangata n āna i
hāpai te Tiriti me te Paipera ki ōna ringa. Kor ōria, hareruia ki a Īhoa o ng ā mano,
Matua, Tama, Wairua Tapu me ngā ānahera pono—me te Māngai hei tautoko mai. Āe.
Whakawhiti atu i Te Ikaroa a M āui ki Te Wai Pounamu  makere noa ki ng ā maunga
hukahuka o te tonga. Tau ana te mata ki ng ā taonga i Arahura, ōku pānga tūpuna. Huri
noa ki Kaiapoi, ki Murihiku, te ure t ārewa. Piki rawa ki te tauihu o te waka, ka rongo te
ao, ka rongo te pō—tihei mauri ora!
E ngā iwi, e ngā reo, e ngā mana, e ngā mātāwaka, tēnā koutou katoa. E te Kaikōrero
o te Whare P āremata o Aotearoa, t ēnā koe. E rau rangatira m ā, e mihi tonu atu ki a
koutou e huihui mai nei tātou i tēnei wā. Nō reira, tēnā anō tātou katoa.
[My bird soars high to T āhuhu-o-te-Rangi, its wings uplifted by the northern sea
breeze. The eyes gaze upon the part of the Treaty founded at Waitangi among greater
Ngāpuhi, my mother’s home.
The flight continues quickly down to th e western tides, until it reaches R ātana, the
place where the temple was establ ished and where the Mouthpiece, Tahup ōtiki Wīremu
Rātana, the man, preached and held up the Tr eaty and the Bible in his hands. Glory,
hallelujah to God of the t housands, the Father, the Son, the Holy Spirit, the faithful
angels—and the Mouthpiece endorses. Yes, indeed.
14 Feb 2012 Address in Reply 359
My bird crosses over from the North Is land to the South Isl and to alight upon the
snow-covered mountains of the south. The eye gazes upon the treasures at Arahura, my
ancestral ties, and turns to look upon my paternal heritage at Kaiapoi and Murihiku.
Eventually it ascends to the prow of the canoe, where the day hears and the night
hears—behold I speak.
To the people, voices, authorities, and many races, greetings to you all. Greetings to
you, Mr Speaker of the House of Parl iament of New Zealand. I particularly
acknowledge you, the many leaders, as we gather here at this point in time. Greetings to
us all once again.]
Mr Speaker, I join with my colleagues in  congratulating you on your reappointment
in this 50th Parliament.
It is gratifying to be here as the member of Parliament for Te Tai Tonga, representing
the largest electorate in the country  and the many diverse iwi and M āori communities
within it. It goes from our  capital city, Te-Whanga-nui-a -Tara, or Wellington, to the
entire Te Waka-a-Māui, the entire South Island, and extending to the outlying islands of
Rakiura, or Stewart Is land, and Wharekauri R ēkohu, or the Chatham Islands. To the
people of Te Tai Tonga, thank you for your tautoko.
I wish to acknowledge my predece ssor, Rahui Katene of the M āori Party, and her
work and service to Te Tai Tonga during her term. I extend my heartfelt personal thanks
to the many helpers and volunteers in the Labour wh ānau across Te Tai Tonga for their
generous support, and, in par ticular, my small, dedicated team, many of whom are here
today. To my new caucus colleagues, I look forward to working with you all and
making my contribution as a paddl er on the Labour waka. To my tu ākana Parekura,
Shane, and Nanaia, thank you for your support,  mentoring, and encouragement. To all
other members of Parliament from a ll sides of this House, and all M āori members of
Parliament, I congratulate you all. My hope is that M āori will see the benefits of our
presence here.
Finally, to my family, my beau tiful children and extended wh ānau, thank you for
your unwavering love and belief in me. I dedicate this occasion of my maiden speech to
my late father, Te Rino Tirikātene.
Mr Speaker, 80 years ago, in th is room, maybe even in this chair, my grandfather Sir
Eruera Tirik ātene stood before this House as the MP for Southern Maori. Forty-five
years ago, in this room, maybe even in this chair, my aunt Whet ū Tirikātene-Sullivan
ONZ stood before this House as  the MP for Southe rn Maori. Today I stand before the
House as the MP for Te Tai Tonga.
At the time my grandfather rose to address the House for the first time, the M āori
population numbered a mere 82,000. We were at that time a ru ral people, still
recovering from the ravages of land sales a nd the scourge of introduced diseases. We
existed at the very margin of the country’s economy. What income we were able to earn
as unskilled labourers in the ag riculture and forestry indu stries was supplemented by
gardening and foraging. The land developmen t assistance programme introduced by Sir
Apirana Ngāta in the 1920s, which eventually gave rise to the M āori incorporations and
trusts of today, was in its infancy, and poverty was all pe rvasive, esp ecially among
those communities that had been left landless by confiscation and land sales.
Statutory recognition of the Treat y of Waitangi, the claims of Ng āi Tahu, Waikato,
and Taranaki, and poverty were my gr andfather’s main concerns. As a R ātana
Independent member of this House, he pr esented T W Ratana’s Treaty petition, and
took every opportunity to press for its adoption. He drew attention to M āori
unemployment, and to the need to remove  the discriminatory rates paid to M āori for
relief work, pensions, and family  allowances, and pressed for a M āori housing
programme. Unfortunately, the Treaty petiti on languished, and it w ould be another 33
360 Address in Reply 14 Feb 2012
years, in the time of the third Labour Gove rnment, before his effo rts in this area bore
fruit. But the issues of discriminatory treatment of M āori in the social assistance area
were addressed after the election of the first Labour Government, as were M āori
housing and education.
By the time that my aunt, Whet ū Tirikātene-Sullivan, entered Parliament, the M āori
population had grown to 201,000 M āori. Urbanisation had quickened in the intervening
years, reaching a peak in the 1950s and early 1960s, and 62 percent of the population
was now living and working in towns and ci ties. Lack of educational qualifications
meant most M āori were employed in unskilled or se mi-skilled jobs in factories and
freezing works, and on the wharves—industries that were sensitive to boom and bust.
Nevertheless, the incomes they received were considerably higher than what they might
have received had they remained “at home” in  rural areas, and th e overall standard of
living of Māori improved.
Urbanisation, however, was not without its downsides. On the one hand, many Māori
found it difficult to adjust, and social probl ems, now much more visible given the
proximity of M āori and P ākehā, began to emerge and grow; on the other, the retention
of Māori culture was being threatened. I understand that Norman Kirk used to refer to
urbanisation as a movement as significant to M āori as the Great Migration in terms of
distance and socio-cultural impact. And he  conceived of that impact from two
perspectives: from that of the people who had migrated to the towns and cities, and
were now in danger of losing their bearings  through loss of culture ; and from that of
their whānaunga left at home and still struggling w ith the legacies of colonial land laws
and practices. It was these issues—those aff licting urban migrants and those afflicting
the rural sections of their wh ānau—that my aunt, Mati u Rata, and the other M āori
Labour MPs sought to redress in the shaping and passage of the Treaty of Waitangi Act
1975. It was a watershed moment in the history of our people.
Fast forward to my time. In 2011 the M āori population was estimated to be 673,000.
The urban component at the time of the last census, 2006, was 84 percent. With
urbanisation has come deeper and deeper integration into New Zealand’s economy. In
2006 more than 78,000 M āori were employed as managers , professionals, technicians,
and trades workers, and, for the first time, workers in these occupation groups combined
outstripped the number working as plant and machinery operators and labourers. More
than 70,000 M āori held a qualification above Nati onal Certificate of Educational
Achievement level 3, and mo re than 45,000 received a personal income of $50,000 or
more. In terms of household income, more than one in every two M āori was living in a
household with a combined income of more than $50,000, and well over one in every
three in a household with a total income of $70,000 or more. What we are witnessing is
the steady growth of a Māori middle class.
On the collective front, we are witnessing the rise of the M āori economic
authorities—Māori land trusts and incorporations, a nd iwi authorities. It has been my
good fortune to have held positions that have  enabled me to work either alongside or
within some of these organisations, and I have found the experien ce exhilarating. I
began my professional career as a commer cial lawyer, but after a few years I
transitioned from the law, as I wanted to broaden my scope and become involved in the
emerging Māori business sector. It was through tr ade promotion work with Trade New
Zealand that I became involved with M āori businesses and M āori exporters—in
particular, working alongside them in trad e development and promotion. I then took up
a position with Ngāi Tahu to help in the expansion of its seafood business. All this work
has allowed me to become involved in M āori economic networ ks, such as the
Federation of M āori Authorities, and to develop great er awareness of the potential for
Māori to continue to improve on the contribution they are already making.
14 Feb 2012 Address in Reply 361
The rise of the M āori economic authorities is something that goes largely unnoticed
by New Zealanders. Not only are these organi sations contributing to national wealth;
they also contribute to the economies of their local regions. In some local body districts,
Māori authorities are already the largest single employer of la bour—and, I might add,
not just M āori labour. Many have reached out to Asia and the Pacific, and as they
continue to do so, that contribution will become even more significant. In the not too
distant future, I can see at least five of th ese authorities breaking the $1 billion mark in
their own right—something my forebears coul d not have dreamt of. And what is more,
sustainable development is not an option for these organisations sinc e the principles of
sustainability are already spel t out for them, either in M āori land law generally or in
their enabling legislation.

items.speaker: There is a saying
items.text: the more things change, the more they stay the same. The origin of
this saying is thought to be Frenc h, but I am pretty sure it is M āori. Life and prospects
for Māori are so much better than they were 80 years ago, but M āori know better than
anyone that much remains to be done. We are still overrepresented at the bottom of the
wealth pyramid. We will, on av erage, die sooner than our P ākehā mates. We will, more
so than our Pacific cousins, end up in pr ison, and, unlike any other group in Aotearoa
New Zealand, we now receive more in transfer  payments than we pay in tax. Too many
of us remain locked into a cycle of dependency and poverty.
The issue of M āori poverty is exacerbated by th e deficit approach to the
measurement of our progress, and the eagerness of the media to capitalise on M āori
failures and to ignore our successes. We have travelled a long way towards socio-
economic parity with P ākehā, and we have a fair way to travel yet. Our people are not
helped by being constantly framed as a probl em to be fixed, or by a growing climate of
opinion that positions inequality as a signal of market success rather than market failure;
that attributes underperformance to rocky economic conditions rather than the structural
settings of our economy; and that maintains it is too costly to change the present, even if
a change made now might save the future.
For me, M āori development, as M āori conceive of the idea, has always been about
enabling M āori to live the life that they want to live by extending the range of
opportunities and choices open to  them to do so. Mana M āori motuhake, a concept that
Pākehā have feared and some M āori have misconstrued, was the term that was used in
my grandfather’s day. It has little to do w ith secession but a lot to do with freedom.
Until very recently, for example, M āori had little or no c hoice about the type of
schooling they received or a bout how their health services  should be delivered. It was
the mainstream or nothing at all. Today some, but certainly not all, M āori have a choice
between k ōhanga reo and mainstream at the preschool level, kura kaupapa and
mainstream at the school level, wānanga and mainstream at the tertiary level, and M āori
or mainstream primary health care delivery.
I stand in awe of the succession of M āori MPs and of M āori leaders from outside of
this House who never lost sight of the goal, despite the hardships and frustrations that
must have been involved in challenging mindsets and wi nning majority support for
change. Incremental, ad hoc, and opportunistic  though these initiatives might appear to
be, there is no mistaking their direction. A lthough I might differ from them in outlook,
priorities, and experience, I nevertheless share with them a commitment to the
fundamental idea of Māori living the life they want to liv e, and, as well as ensuring that
the safety net is set at a high enough leve l, of working to ex tend the range of
opportunities and choices open to those among us who are falling by the wayside.
We are no longer as homogenous as we were in the past. Indeed, increasing diversity
and differentiation are the hallmarks of modern M āori society. It is this diversity—of
ethnic and iwi affiliation, of cultural proficiency, of attachments to the past, of the
362 Address in Reply 14 Feb 2012
composition of our households and families, of knowledge and skills, of occupations
and incomes, and of values, beliefs and opi nions—that we as members of this House
will be challenged by. It is not our place to tell our people how they should live their
lives or to marginalise those who do not fit a prescribed picture of what it is to be
Māori. As I see it, our job as elected represen tatives is to embrace th e diversity, to give
fair hearing to all interests, and to ensure that the range of views are voiced and weighed
fairly when it comes to decision making. This is my commitme nt I give to my
electorate, to M āori generally, and to my parliamentary colleagues. N ō reira, t ēnā
koutou, tēnā koutou, tēnā tātou katoa.
Waiata

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: In the last couple of minutes of time I have
remaining, it would be remiss of me not to re fer to the fantastic and wonderful speeches

But in regards to the Road User Charges Bill, before the adjournment last week I had

I just wanted to record in my last remain ing seconds that actually we have a fantastic

items.speaker: JULIE ANNE GENTER
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Deputy Speaker. T ēnā koutou e te
Whare. I am very pleased to take a call on the third reading of the Road User Charges
Bill, which the Green Party will be suppor ting. I did not have the privilege of
contributing to the development of this bill  myself, so I must acknowledge the work of
the Transport and Industrial Relations Comm ittee, the submitters and officials, the
members of this House who contributed dur ing the Committee stage, and, especially,
my eminently qualified colleague Gareth H ughes, who was intimately involved in the
scrutiny of the bill up until this point.
As Mr Hughes mentioned in his previous  speeches on this bi ll, we are happy to
support the bill because it begins to modernise and simplify the road-user charges
system. Road-user charges contributed about 37 percent of the National Land Transport
Fund last year, and that was about $1 billi on. The goal of this bill is to increase
14 Feb 2012 Road User Charges Bill 363
compliance, which is good; to simplify enfo rcement, which is also good; and to provide
an incentive for the efficient use of heavy vehicles. I note that by basing the charging on
the maximum permissible weight for a give n vehicle class, there is a very small
incentive to use a heavy vehicle to its fu ll capacity. Now, by optimising heavy vehicle
movements around the country, we can deliver the same amount of freight at a much
lower cost to business with better social  and environmental outcomes and at a lower
cost to the public purse. This is a win-win, and it is the ki nd of win-win that we could
achieve a lot more of with our transport policy and funding.
I believe there is a real role  for the Government to play in levelling the playing field
and providing an incentive for transport to occur in a more efficient and effective
manner. Although we support this bill, the Green Party sees it as a real lost opportunity
to encourage greater efficiency, especially energy efficiency. We are currently facing a
paradigm shift in transport. If New Zeala nd seizes this opportunity, we can spend less
money and have a transport system that delivers far better outcomes.
In 2008 there was a report to the New Zeal and Transport Agency  that identified a
number of transport market distortions that  have lead to an over-reliance on private
vehicles for the movement of people and of freight in this countr y. It was an entirely
understandable unintended consequence of G overnment policy and funding at all levels
of government—local government, central government, and regional government—that
has led to a transport system that is really not energy efficient and is incredibly overly
reliant on cars for personal transport and on trucks for freight. This  report identified a
number of changes to the road-user charges system, to the petrol tax system, and to
transport funding in general that would help  deliver a much more  efficient transport
system for New Zealand, and this is going to  be particularly important, as higher oil
prices are imminent.
What I would like to identify about this bill is that currently the road-user charges are
contributing 37 to 40 percent of our Nationa l Land Transport Fund, and that is about
equivalent to the amount of money that is planned to be spent by this Government each
year just on new motorways. Now, some may think that is fair, but in fact road-user
charges are intended to pay for maintenanc e and renewal of the existing network, and
should be used for transport solutions that  are going to enable goods and people to be
moved in the most cost-effective way possi ble. Is a new motorway or extending the
expressway north and south of Auckland the most efficient way to enable freight to
move on our roads? Evidently not. At peak  hour, only 1 percent of the traffic on the
roads in Auckland is heavy vehicles, so we could easily fr ee up the roads quite
significantly for freight and commercial ve hicles simply by shifting commuters on to
more cost-effective modes such as walking, cycling, buses, and trains. We do not have
to force people to do that; we just need to make the costs of transport more direct and
people will be able to weigh up those decisions for themselves. What the transport
modelling shows us is that people would choose to take  public transport, walk, and
cycle more if those options were delivered for them.
By continuing transport policy and land use pol icy that artificially subsidise private
vehicles, we are making the transport system more vulnerable to hi gh oil prices, which
we know are coming. So spending all the ro ad-user charges on a few motorways is a
stupid idea that will not actually be good fo r the freight industry, as households and
businesses have to spend more to get around at peak hour. That means they have less
money available to pay for goods in the do mestic economy. What does that result in?
Lower demand for goods that are transported by heavy vehicles for freight.
I note that despite all of these unintentional subsidies to road transport, the briefing to
the incoming Minister of Transport stated th at 45 percent of the products destined to
become exports are currently moved around Ne w Zealand by rail. The Green Party sees
364 Road User Charges Bill 14 Feb 2012
significant opportunities to grow the role of rail and sea freight, an d that is a perfectly
legitimate use of the National Land Transport Fund because it is actually going to
improve the situation for those who are curren tly in the freight i ndustry, whether they
are using trucks or other means.
In conclusion, the Green Party is happy to support this bill, but we feel it is a real lost
opportunity. It does not go far enough to changi ng the transport system in the way that
is necessary for New Zealand to meet the challenges of this century. Thank you.

items.speaker: JAMI-LEE ROSS
items.text: This is the first time  I have spoken in this
Chamber since the election, so can I take th e opportunity to congratulate, firstly, the
presiding officers, and especially yourself  on your elevation to Deputy Speaker, and I
would also like to congratul ate all members of the House on their re-election, or their
initial election if it is their first time.

items.speaker: Hon Nathan Guy
items.text: Great result in Botany.

items.speaker: JAMI-LEE ROSS
items.text: Thank you, and all that hard campaigning you did for me, Mr
Guy, was much appreciated; thank you. Can I sa y that I have enjoyed the contributions
from new members so far, but I am looking forward to the real stars of the class of 2011
taking their first stand in the House on Thursday.
It is good to see that the Road User Charge s Bill is finally here for its third reading.
Can I say thank you to the Ministers of Tran sport—firstly, the Hon Steven Joyce, and
the Hon Gerry Brownlee, now—for getting this bill this far in the House. It is a good
bill, and it is one that I hope a large num ber of members in th e Parliament will be
supporting. And credit where credit is due—I think it is worthwhile acknowledging that
the Labour Party actually initiated the road-use r charges review back  in, I think, 2008,
which ended up culminating in this bill, where we are seeing these quite significant
changes to the road-user charges system.
As has been pointed out by members in th is debate before it was adjourned last
week, and also by the new member Julie Anne Genter earlier, this is about making the
road-user charges system more simplified, it is about making it easier to understand, and
it is about making it easier for the Government to enforce. It is important that when you
have taxes in place, and when you have penalties for not paying those taxes, it is easy to
enforce the paying of those taxes, as well. I am pleased to see that just about every party
in the House, I understand, is supporting this bill. We heard from the Labour members
last week about their views on the bill. They  are supporting the bill , but they indicated
some areas of concern. I do not tend to agree with the areas of concern that the members
of the Labour Party were raising last week, and in a minute I will take a few moments to
outline why I do not think the views they are bringing to the House really have much
credibility.
This bill is about making it easier for busin ess. It is about ma king it easier for New
Zealanders to run their road transport usi ng the road-user charges system. The previous
system of nominated weights was incredibly complicated and it led to operators having
to estimate how heavy the vehicles were. There are inherent problems in that, and it also
meant that the authorities had to work out whether there were problems and try to work
out what the weight was after the fact. W ith this new system we have a road-user
charges regime where we will know what ever y vehicle’s gross wei ght is and what its
road-user charges will be. There is no estimating involved, and it is far simpler.
I was listening very intently to the Labour Party members last week. Darien Fenton
and Phil Twyford outlined some concerns.

items.speaker: Darien Fenton
items.text: “Dar-rien” Fenton.

items.speaker: JAMI-LEE ROSS
items.text: Darien Fenton; I am sorry, Da rien. Darien Fenton and Phil
Twyford outlined some concerns they had, and they were complaining that they did not
feel that their concerns were answered ade quately. I have done a bit of research this
14 Feb 2012 Road User Charges Bill 365
afternoon, and actually just about all the answ ers to their concerns are found within the
documents they were concerned about. We  heard from two Opposition members that
they did not feel as though there was very mu ch consultation on this bill. Well, I went
through to page 178 of 189 pages—and it is buried quite deep in the departmental report
but it is in there. This bill went through f our phases of consultation by the Ministry of
Transport before we got to the bill here. It had a consultation in September to November
2009. It had consultation in early 2010. It ha d another consultation a bit later in 2010,
and then in October and December 2010 it had further consultation. That is four

There was also the road-user charges revi ew that the Hon Annette King initiated
when she was the Minister of Transport.  That went through consultation with the
industry, and on top of that we had the Tran sport and Industrial Relations Committee
consultation. Now, that is six phases of cons ultation on the work that led up to this bill.
I do not think anyone can stand up in this House and say there has not been consultation
with the industry, when this issue has b een through six phases of consultation. There
will be further consultation on top of that wh en it comes to the setting of the charges
through regulations, which will probably be taking place later this year.
We also heard complaints that the Govern ment is doing this nasty thing called
regulations. What the Government will be doing is setting in place the charges through a
secondary phase of legislation. It is not possible to set the charges in this bill because
this bill, we are hoping, will stand for many years, and obviously the charges have to
change from time to time. I know Labour  members know about changing road-user
charges rates, as 2008 was quite a hectic time for them when it came to road-user
charges. But you simply cannot set those ch arges in the primary bill. It would be
ridiculous to try to do th at, so setting those charges th rough regulations is not an
unusual step. It is quite a logical ste p. But if you are aski ng yourself why the
Government is doing this through regul ations, and you are concerned that the
Government is using regulations, and if you are hearing that from the Labour members,
you would think that Labour members are somehow opposed to the use of regulations.
Well, I was a little bit busy this afternoon a nd I did a little bit mo re research. In the
last term of the Labour G overnment 1,263 regulations were  passed by the last Labour
Government. So I take offence a little bit when I hear Labour members standing up and
saying they do not like the use of regulations. In the last term of the Labour Government
it passed 1,263 regulations. So pl ease stop whacking us over the head about the use of
regulations. It is reasonable to set the charges through the use of regulation.
The third topic I want to discuss is about who are going to be winners and who are
going to be losers. We heard from Darien  Fenton and Phil Twyford about the Motor
Caravan Association. The Motor Caravan A ssociation raised some points. It is
concerned about what the char ges will be. I think it is wort hwhile pointing out that the
charges have not been set yet. They will be set later on. We are going through
consultation first, but the members raised th e plight of the Motor Caravan Association.
The association, in its submission, was under the impression that charges were going to
go up astronomically. It is important to remember that this change will be revenue-
neutral for the Government. There will be some people who get small increases, and
there will be people who get some small de creases, but there is no expectation that
overall revenue will increase. This is a bout changing the system, not increasing the
revenue.
The Motor Caravan Association, unfortuna tely, used some ol d figures in its
submission. It was using existing road-user ch arges figures, which just will not apply to
the new regime. It believes that its charges will be going up, and it gave an example of a
motor caravan that is 19,000 kilograms, or  19 tonnes—a type 5 motor vehicle. It
366 Road User Charges Bill 14 Feb 2012
believes that that charge will go up by 270 percent. I can quite understand that 270
percent sounds like a lot, but that is simp ly not the case. Again, I am looking at the
departmental report, and the answer was right there for the Labour members. The
Labour members did not quite see this, but th e departmental report itself outlines an
answer to the Motor Caravan Association. Ra ther than the road-user charge going up to
$451, as the association believed it would, it would actually go up to only about $246. It
is just an estimate at the moment, but $246 versus $451 is quite a difference and
nowhere near the increase that Labour memb ers were telling this House last week that
road-user charges would be going up by.
This is a good bill. This is a bill that will make it easier for the industry. It is a bill
that will make it easier for the Government, and it is a bill that will remove a whole lot
of complexity from the road-user charges system. I am glad the Labour members are
supporting it. I am glad other members in the House are supporting it, but I just had to
answer some of those concerns we heard from the Opposition. They are simply not
concerns that are relevant to this debate , because the research was not done, and the
answers were right there in the departmental  report. I look forward to this bill being
passed by the House tonight.

items.speaker: BRENDAN HORAN
items.text: I rise on behalf of New Zealand First to speak on
the Road User Charges Bill. It is very interesting that the honourable Jami-Lee Ross has
done a little bit of research. I would lik e to remind members that actions have
consequences, and the consequences of this bill could be far-reaching indeed for the
citizens of New Zealand. And I would remind members that consultation is one thing,
but listening and taking heed are entirely another.
This is New Zealand First’s first vote on the bill, and we oppose it. After careful
scrutiny and after considering items that are transported by di esel—everything from
people, public transport users,  and schoolchildren to inanim ate objects such as building
products, chemicals, and medicines; then we  have household rubbish and everything on
the supermarket shelf—New Zealand First also entered into discussions and listened to
affected and concerned parties within the industry, including road transport freight
owners, crane operators, trucking firms, larg e livestock-carrying fi rms, horse trainers,
individual truck owner-opera tors, and members and representatives of the Motor
Caravan Association. Now, without excep tion, everyone spoken to expressed grave
reservations on this bill in the areas of fairness and expense.
It is also a bill that, it is fair to say, many in the industry know very little about. It has
been stated that the purpose of the bill is to modernise and simplify the road-user
charges system, to eliminate the scope for error and fraud. Upon first inspection, despite
a failure to prove sy stematic fraud surrounding road-u ser charges, a rather heavy-
handed approach seems to have been followed in penalising everyone for the
unsubstantiated presumed fraudulent behaviour of a few.
There are other goals, and they are to  reduce administration complexity, reduce
compliance costs, and simplify enforcement. New Zealand First believes that the bill
has far-reaching implications that will have a negative impact within our New Zealand
society in terms of fairness, affordab ility, safety, and even environmental
considerations. Let us first consider fairness. The honourable members Shane Jones and
Phil Twyford both expressed th eir reservations with regard to the effects on small
businesses and motorhome owners, and one should respect their experience.
We ask whether it is fair for small trucking operators such as furniture movers, who
transport large, bulky items such as mattresses, pillows, and sofas—and they are not
necessarily heavy objects. Pray tell how will they be able to operate profitably when
they will be charged every day for heavier loads than they will probably ever carry? Is it
fair to skip operators, who drop off an empty skip to most building sites in New
14 Feb 2012 Road User Charges Bill 367
Zealand, return empty to their yard, and then drive empty to collect a full skip? Surely,
we can find a better, more equitable way than  to charge full-load prices on every trip.
These increases will undoubtedly trickle down to the end-user and add to building costs
in the New Zealand housing industry.
New Zealand First has concerns for the 22,000 motorhome owners registered with
the Motor Caravan Associati on. In talks with them they  question the fairness of
suddenly having their road-use r charges increased—mostly doubled, and in some cases
trebled—because of new band widths and maximum permissible on-road weight
charges, when their weight is constant and in most cases considerably less than their
maximum chassis weight. There are other considerations amongst motorhome owners in
their contribution to internal tourism. This can be seen in the many rallies that the Motor
Caravan Association holds th roughout New Zealand every w eekend in our cities and
small towns, adding to the economies of those areas. Many mo torhome owners are
pensioners, and dramatic incr eases will affect their di scretionary spend and also
potentially affect the resale of their motorhomes. So Ne w Zealand First cannot, in good
conscience, do a Pontius Pilate here and have these clear failings in  the bill left to the
Minister of Transport to sort out.
There are similar obstacles in this bill for those in the racing industry, where we have
horse trucks continually load ing and offloading animals and their frustration with the
administration. We have buses, refrigerat or units, and many others. There are many
truckies who have invested considerable sums  to purchase B train units to enable them
to compete within the current, sense-making fr amework of the current legislation. What
about them? These multi-wheeled vehicles are safer because more axles distribute the
load, meaning safer driving. If this bill is passed, these operators will need full loads
both ways to compete, and in some cases to stay in business. This  bill could very well
be the catalyst that leads to every truck on the road carrying maximum loads, leading to
worse wear and tear on our highways and obvious  safety issues. It also has the potential
to lead to more smaller trucks on the road s, again travelling with maximum weights,
and the challenges that I have expressed that that brings.
So although this bill started with the very best of intentions, there are many holes
that—pardon the pun—you could drive a truck through, provided you could afford the
road charges. To date, I have highlighted the injustice of this bill, and in the same vein I
would ask the parties to cons ider the social ramifications  that drill right down from
exporters and importers to the average man and woman on the street, with the flow-on
cost effect. Large or small goods—even a hum ble can of peas—travel by truck at least
10 times from seed until they reach a supe rmarket shelf. Now, obviously, the cost is
going to go to the end-user , and with affordability st retched one wonders how the
average Kiwi mum and dad will be able to afford to buy those asset shares that we hear
so much about from this National-led Government.
There are also environmental concerns. At a time when we are trying to encourage
people into public transport, how can we intr oduce a cost increase to public transport
and school buses? New Zealand First is not he re just to oppose; we suggest a more
equitable system of levying that is not one of one-size-fits-all. Th e solution may be to
look at charges at the pump. There is a simple  formula here, and that is diesel is fuel,
fuel is proportional to horse power, and horsepower is directly proportional to weight.
So the more weight you pull, the more fuel  you need. By addre ssing the issue at the
pumps, we would cut compliance costs and do away with administrative complexity and
any requirement for legal enforcement.
There could also be concessions for e nvironmentally friendly engines. The new
diesel engines are more environmentally friendly than ever before, and surely we should
be encouraging innovation and creativity. Now, one  of the flaws of this system is that
368 Road User Charges Bill 14 Feb 2012
the fishing and shipping industries do not use the roads, but surely it is a path that could
do with investigation and robust discussion. So on behalf of all of those in New Zealand
who have expressed their conc erns about this bill, New Zealand First opposes it for the
above reasons. Thank you.

items.speaker: Dr JACKIE BLUE
items.text: I am pleased to be speaking to the third reading of
the Road User Charges Bill. I sat on the Tr ansport and Industrial Relations Committee
in the last term of Parliament, and wh at a good committee it was, chaired by David
Bennett and continuing to be chaired by David Bennett. We heard many submissions on
this bill. I would like to congratulate Steven Joyce, the previous Minister of Transport. I
think he made a significant contribution in th e transport area, and certainly he has made
safer journeys for New Zealanders over his te rm. I would like to take the opportunity to
congratulate the officials and submitters on this bill, and to wish the new committee,
which I am no longer on, well on its future deliberations and business in the future.
This bill has been amended to ensure that  it is enduring because, quite frankly, the
current system is outdated. It is really last  century and it was well  and truly overdue for
an overhaul. This bill will modernise the road-user charges system. It will reduce
compliance costs for operators, eliminate the scope for error and fraud in the purchase
of road-user charges licences, and si mplify enforcement and administration
requirements. It is very important. We must have a fair system, a balanced system, and a
well-managed system. This is what this law will do. The road-user charges—or RUC—
system was established in 1978. It is a long time ago, and this review is very timely. All
the revenue from the road-user charges system goes to the National Land Transport
Fund, and the fund is used mainly for road  construction and maintenance, along with
other activities benefiting road users.
The bill is a result of the recommendations of the Independent Review of the New
Zealand Road User Charging System, and it brings about the most significant reform of
road-user charges since it was introduced—i t is a very significant reform. Diesel
vehicles are very popular in New Zealand—di esel is cheaper than petrol—and more
economical to run. Fuel consumption tests generally give results between 20 percent
and 30 percent better for a diesel-engine ca r compared with the same model with a
petrol engine. But also you have got to know that up to 36 percent of diesel is used off-
road, such as on farms; in manufacturing, industrial, and commerc ial ventures; and on
boats.
But back to this bill. This bill is about bringing the road-user charges system into the
21st century, from 1978 to 2012. This bill  addresses the conc ern about road-user
charges evasion, which is conservatively estim ated to be $30 million per year, which is
not an insignificant sum. This  bill will remove the evas ion opportunities and encourage
timely payment, making a fairer system for all.
The main provisions of the bill are, first of  all, a change in th e definition of vehicle
weight. Currently, road-user charges are base d on the distance travelled and the weight
carried. The system is complicated, and it ha s been open to error.  An operator has to
guess the actual gross weight to be carried, and it can be difficult for an operator to
predict in advance the actual weight to be carri ed. It is also very difficult, of course, to
recover the charges owing after the fact. The bill changes the definition of vehicle
weight to a fixed road-user charge, so that operators do not have to guess in advance,
and so that Government authorities do no t have to deal w ith recovering money
afterwards. Inevitably this will result in lower administrative costs for the industry and
the Government, and, of course, it will m ean that fewer road-user charges are lost
through evasion, so it is a win-win.
There are a number of other provisions. Ot hers are removal of a time licence system
and modernisation of the list of vehicles exempted from road-user charges. There is also
14 Feb 2012 Road User Charges Bill 369
an improvement to the regulatory framewor k for electronic management systems, and
this really shows how far we have come from 1978 through to 2012. Really, back in
1977 when the Road User Charges Act came into power, we did not have electronic
systems and we did not have the internet. N one of this would have been dreamt of all
that time ago. So, really, we have brought the system into the 21st century, and it means
much more efficiency and much more fairne ss. It means that road-user charges can be
purchased electronically, and that a distance licence can be displayed electronically on
an on-board unit situated in the vehicle. And, of course, the distance travelled by the
vehicle is measured electronically. It is all done electronically, something which no one,
and certainly not our parents, would have thought of back in 1977. Quite frankly, the
Road User Charges Bill of 1977 never would have dreamt of such a possibility, that in
2012 we would be going to such a modern system.
Another provision in the bill is that it is a fairer, simpler, and less costly structure in
relation to offences—penalties —particularly for light vehicles. I cannot emphasise the
fact that, really, a fixed road -user charges weight means that the distance-based evasion
will be the main focus of compliance management, and will, obviously, save money and
save time.
Really, this bill, I cannot stress enough, is about bringing road-user charges into the
21st century. It is about reducing compliance cost s for transport operators, and,
ultimately, reducing transport costs for our businesses and exporters. These changes will
make it easier and fairer to all those who pay road-user charges, and that has to be good.
Changing the definition of licence weights, removing the confusing time licence system,
and simplifying the list of exempted vehicles will all reduce compliance costs for
businesses, simplify the administrative pr ocesses for industry and Government, and
save a lot of time and frustration and conf usion at times. The New Zealand Transport
Agency will also be able to  take greater advantage of mo dern internet technology in
administering road-user charges payment channels.
This bill addresses concerns about the ev asion, which I mentioned before, which has
been estimated to be up to $30 million a year , which is a very big sum of money, and
that will be addressed in this bill with the different provisions that we have talked about.
Really, people who are using road-user char ges honestly have been subsidising people
who have been evading the system and w ho have not been paying their road-user
charges as they should be. This bill will  remove a number of evasion opportunities,
encourage timely payment, and make the system fairer for all. I commend this bill to the
House.

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: Labour supports the Road User
Charges Bill, with some reservations. But befo re I get on to that, I did listen with some
interest to Jami-Lee Ross’ c ontribution. Mr Ross, that was the first time I have heard
you speak, actually, and I thought you made some very interes ting points, particularly
about transport overall, and the importance of transport on the economic and social
well-being of New Zealand. That is why we on this side of the House have always
supported a balanced transport policy. We do no t believe that transport has to be about
just tarmac and road building. We believe, and we have for a long time, that it is not
also only about cycling and walking, but it is  actually about utilising all the modes of
transport, including road transport, sea tran sport, air, and rail, for the best economic
benefit of this country.
So when we were in Government we set out to have a fair funding system for
roading and transport in New Zealand, and it  was a Labour Governme nt that brought in
hypothecation of all funding for roading, which included road-user charges, excise duty,
and registration into a National Land Tr ansport Fund—something the previous
Government had refused to do for many, many years—which enables us now to have a
370 Road User Charges Bill 14 Feb 2012
much fairer approach to funding transport in New Zealand. But if anyone should know
about a road-user charges system, and getting a fairer road-user charges system in place,
it probably should be a former Minister of  Transport who actually confronted many
truckies in 2008 when, in fact, I increased th e road-user charges for truckies in this
country. So I have been very interested in the progress of this bill.
The former Minister of Transport, Steven Joyce, called this bill a “fairer road-user
charges system for everybody” bill, but I w ondered why there were people who were
upset about it if that was the case. It seemed  to me there was a fair amount of spin over
substance in Mr Joyce’s comments in that respect.
In July 2008, as the Minister of Transport, I increased road-user charges—the second
increase they had had since 1989. So in 19 years road-user charges went up twice—2
years in a row—and I put them up. That was for vehicles over 6 tonnes. And what
happened? The truck operators took to the road  in protest. So I said: “What I want is a
fairer system, one where all the road-user ope rators paid their fair share and they got
their fair share.” But they went to protest over two i ssues. One was the amount of
increase that was going to be charged to them. In fact, it was an extra $32 a year for a
small diesel car with an average mileage, and for a typical 5-tonne truck—

items.speaker: Michael Woodhouse
items.text: They weren’t small diesel cars in the Octagon protesting.

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: Just listen and you might learn something, Mr Woodhouse.
For a typical 5-tonne truck it was $53 a year, and for a 23-tonne truck, which is capable
of carrying quite a lot of freight, it was $198 a year, the reason being that diesel is not
subject to any taxation apart from less than half a cent per litre, compared with 42.524c
a litre for a car. So I wanted a balanced and fair system.
The second reason they protested at that time was that they did not get enough notice
there was going to be an increase. The year before I had given 3 da ys’ notice that there
was going to be an increase in road-user charges. What happened? Many operators went
out and pre-purchased road-user charges at  the old rate, costing the Government $17
million. So there was a protest.
I set up a working party in conjunction with  the industry to look at the formula we
could have for setting road-user charges for heavy vehicles, a nd to put in place
legislation to address the notice issue. We put on to that committee three people with
expertise and knowledge, and they were to report back in March 2009. We are almost in
March 2012, and we have legislation finally  going through this House that is going to,
in two respects—and particularly in one pa rticular effect—have a big impact on a high
percentage of trucking firms. But what exactly that impact is going to be is, at this stage,
still secret. Nobody knows what the figures are; they have not been divulged.
The question I am wanting to ask is whethe r the truck operators will protest again,
because they will have a reason to this time.  Rather than come up with a system that
addresses the notice period, under this bill the charges will be set by regul ation by the
Minister without public debate. No final numbers will be known before this bill
becomes law. The actual charges will be set at a later date. It is seen to be a pretty
complicated process, and it could have legal challenges and lead to cost and delay.
One of the submissions to the Transport a nd Industrial Relations Committee pointed
out that clause 79 provides for 42 days’ notification of regulations specifying the
changes, but there is no process for consultatio n, so I cannot see that there has been any
improvement on the issues that were raised in 2008 and what is happening in this bill.
You see, the Road Transport Forum demanded consultation, and that is what I thought
was going to happen in this bill. I cannot see in it how this is occurring.
Perhaps I could remind the members what wa s said at the time when I, in fact,
increased road-user charges, and what the National Party sa id about it. It  said it was
sneaky to raise road-user charges without warning, but that is what is going to happen in
14 Feb 2012 Road User Charges Bill 371
this legislation. It said it would pile huge  costs on people, but people are not going to
know what those increases are go ing to be. Bill English went so far as to say that we
changed things in the dead of night, that we had promised to consult on it, and that there
should have been consultation. Where in this bill now, and when it is passed, is there
going to be consultation before road-user charges are increased?
That was the basis of the protest in 2008, so it will be interesting to see whether Tony
Friedlander comes out of retirement and asks  the truckies to once again protest, now
against a National Government. After all, Tony Friedlander was a former National Party
member of Parliament. I wonder whether he has the same strength of feeling against
what is happening now, as against what happened when we were in Government.
The second major issue that has been prot ested against is the change moving from
nominated weight to gross we ights for calculating road-use r charges. Well, what does
all that mean? To the people listening out ther e it does not mean an awful lot, but at
present, road-user charges are based on dist ance travelled and weight carried, and the
carrier has to estimate in advance the actual gross weight to be carried. For example—
and I have never forgotten this example, whic h was told to me by F onterra way back in
the time when I was Minister of Transport— Fonterra’s trucks can carry 50 tonnes of
milk. It is actually allowed to carry only 44 to nnes, so it does not fill  its trucks to their
full weight. But it is actually going to be charged for carrying a 50-tonne weight. That is
what its maximum allowable weight would be. So Fonterra has opposed  this bill. It has
said that it fails to do what it has said it was going to do.
Operators will now be deemed to be carrying the maximum permissible load on the
road at all times, and that is going to put a huge hike on the smaller operators. Now, I
know it suits some of the bigger operators. They are the members of the Road Transport
Forum. Some of them were very good at avoi ding road-user charges. But it is not going
to help many of the smaller truck operato rs. One operator said there would be an
additional average cost of $18,000 per vehi cle for him, totalling an extra $137,000 per
year.
So I am saying there should be a protest about these changes by this Government, if
people were really concerned about changes th at have been made in the past and are
wanting a fairer system. Also, how it can be—as is much claimed by this
Government—a fiscally neutral change, when those who carry lighter loads are going to
be disadvantaged? I think that the Government missed a very good opportunity to make
it fairer.

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: That would have been a very short meeting.
14 Feb 2012 Road User Charges Bill 373

items.speaker: MELISSA LEE
items.text: Sorry? Where are you a member for, sir? This particular bill aims

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: A win is a win, according to Melissa Lee.

items.text: how would she know? How would she know after her

David Shearer wakes up every morning and he thanks God for Melissa Lee. He is

I want to know from Melissa Lee, though, about road-user charges. How many of

points. I do not think anyone could name th e 120 points. Nobody has got any idea what
they are. I have not heard National name one, but apparently the Road User Charges
Bill is one of them. This is what is going to contribute to our massive economic
transformation under the second term of a Na tional Government! And things are going
to get so much better now that the truc kies have to pay more for carting empty

Charges Bill, which we are debating in the House tonight.
And I have to say, I agree with some of the drivers of the m ilk tankers—the people

agree with the New Zealand Motor Caravan Association, wh ich is concerned about the
374 Road User Charges Bill 14 Feb 2012

I also have a question for the Government . In the week that John Key has been
talking about modernising public  services and having a tech nological solution to make
public services more responsible, why are we  not seeing evidence of  that in the Road
User Charges Bill? Because, actually, by thei r very definition, road-user charges are

items.text: Elegant solution.

items.text: That would be an elegant soluti on, to quote the Prime Minister’s

items.speaker: GARETH HUGHES
items.text: Kia ora, Mr Deputy Speaker. Ng ā mihi nui ki a
koutou. Kia ora. It is good to ta ke a call on the Road User Ch arges Bill. I have a pretty
hard act to follow. We have had comedy hour  from Melissa Lee and then Chris Hipkins
in the House. I would like to acknowledge  you, Mr Deputy Speak er, and all the new
members. I would like to acknowledge the new Minister of Transport, Gerry Brownlee.
I called the last Minister of Transport the “C olossus of Roads”, but I will not say what
we will be calling the new Minister of Transport.
This country is facing a debt crisis, an une mployment crisis, and a climate crisis, and
what do we hear from the Government? We hear  “Drill it, mine it, sell it.”, and about
the Road User Charges Bill. I mean, at a time when we have got so many important
issues facing our country, th is bill really does define “t inkering around the edges”. The
Greens will be supporting this bill, howev er, because there are some marginal
environmental and economic benefits accruing from it. I am surprised that New Zealand
First is not supporting the bill. I think that had New Zealand First been here through the
select committee process, it might have taken a different approach. We are glad to be
supporting this bill, but in the end this is the story of missed opportunities.
14 Feb 2012 Road User Charges Bill 375
Annette King asked a very powerful quest ion, which was whether we are going to
see protests when the regulations are formed  and the new road-user charges increase. I
say I doubt it. I doubt it because we know that the road lobby is the single biggest donor
to the National Party. We know that the G overnment is borrowing $19 billion to pour
into motorways benefitting truckies. This Government has made decisions, from the
juggernaut heavy trucks through to delaying the petrol and fuel excise and road-user
charge rises accruing from rising international oil prices. If the trucking industry has a
best mate, it is definitely the National Party. So I do not think we will be seeing protests
from the trucking industry like we saw under Annette King’s watch, but when it comes
to the regulations around small cars—those 200  small, light diesels—I think we might,
in fact, see protests from those small, effi cient diesels around the country, because what
they are going to see is th eir road-user charges increas ing. By how much, we do not
know, because that is entirely up  to the new Minister of Tr ansport to decide. What the
officials in the Transport and Industrial Relations Committee advised us is that the
charges are going to be increasing.
What we saw was essentially like a wealth swap, with those heaviest trucks giving
the most to the National Party, I guess. Thos e trucks will be paying the least amount of
road-user charges. But it is those small, light , efficient diesels that  will be paying the
most. They might be paying around $32 extra over 15,000 kilometres. That is not a
huge amount. What we are seei ng is that wealth transfer. The smallest and the most
efficient vehicles are the ones we should be en couraging in order to conserve our oil, to
protect our balance of trade, to enhance our economy, to reduce our emissions, and to
protect our environment. We should be enc ouraging those vehicles, but they are the
ones subsidising—and I do use the word “sub sidising”—those heavy trucks that the
Government wants to protect so much.
We do support the bill for the reasons that it is going to be simpler and it is hopefully
going to make a dent in that $120 million, that massive administration cost, which
comes from the road-user char ges. We support this switch to the maximum weight, and
this is where our support really comes from . When you have the trucks charged on their
maximum weight, what we want to see is these trucks being used as efficiently, as fully,
as possible, so that we do not see what we have at the moment, which is trucks with
numerous axles—because of past flaws in  the road-user charges regime—being carted
around the country empty, because that is the way the road-user charges prioritise it.
We are glad the bill maintains the electri c car subsidies. I gu ess we know all these
issues—the balance of trade problems, th e massive 16 percent oil imports, all the
problems facing our country—but the Governme nt has got only 40 electric cars on our
roads. In the end, this is a missed opportunit y. The Road User Charges Act is older than
I am. We are the only country in the world with a road-user charges scheme. We could
have actually embraced innovation. We h ear about technology, about information
technologies this Government is so-called embracing, but when it comes to embracing
new technology on this bill—when we could be using electronic monitoring or real-time
charging—we are instead going away from a smart approach to a dumb approach. We
are going to an averaging model that is not going to send those incentives. It is a
massive missed opportunity. We are not probabl y going to see an opportunity to reform
this in our generation, in a decade. It is a massive mi ssed opportunity. But we will be
supporting it for the reasons I outlined. Thank you.
