were not given notice, because the Minister  of Transport at the time, Mrs King, the
previous year had given the industry 3 days’ notice, and, horror of horrors, the trucking
industry and the people who needed to purch ase road-user charges, or RUCs, did the
rational thing: they went out and they purchased $30 million of charges.
Well, I see no harm in that. I am from that age where we, as children, listened around
the radio to the Budget being presented in the 1970s by the Rt Hon Sir Robert Muldoon,
who was also Minister of Finance. It was about the smokes and the petrol, was it not? It
was done on a Thursday night, I think, in those days. I can tell you that by the time he
got to the amount of excise that was going to be applied to fags, people were going
straight down to the supermarket. We did not  have many supermarkets in those days; it
was the dairies and the service stations that filled up.
But here is what happens when road-user charges are paid in that way. The Crown
has $30 million more in the bank, earning interest—money that it would not have got.
So, yes, there is an offsetting implication to the fact that because the prices are going to
go up people buy early. That is the normal, ra tional thing that people do. But the thing
that got people most upset was the fact that  they had been told that one thing would
happen, and another thing happened.
I want to elaborate on that point, because  of the criticisms that Mrs King made,
completely irrationally, about the lack of a notice period in this bill. Well, she clearly
has not read it. She was not on the select committee. Her colleagues Ms Fenton and the
14 Feb 2012 Road User Charges Bill 377
others on the Transport and Industrial Re lations Committee last year could have
enlightened her, but did not. So I will point out clause 79, which provides that
regulations made to specify rates of road-user charges co me into force 42 days after
they are gazetted. So the inference—well, it was not inferred; it was absolutely
unchallenged; it was stated—tha t this Government is not gi ving road users plenty of
notice of changes to the road-user charges is simply not true.
Nor, I have to say, is the continued wa iling and gnashing of teeth from members on
the other side at the concerns of the Motor Caravan Association. Indeed, the association
did come to the committee and express very serious concerns about the implications of
the changes in the road-user charges calcul ation for its members.  Its concerns were
completely wrongly placed. The officials of th e Ministry of Transport worked with the
Motor Caravan Association to alleviate th ose concerns, and, largely, they have gone
away, except that the people listening to th e debate in the Committee and in the third
reading tonight will be completely confused. Well, I want to give them the assurance
that the 270-something percent increases that the association says are going to come are
not accurate, because the baseline is going to be recalibrated once the move from
nominated weight to gross weight is brought in. That in itsel f is going to be much more
administratively efficient. The amount of paperwork done in order for truck companies
to record their actual nominated weight, a nd then to have it checked and policed on the
side of the road, is incredibly administrati vely inefficient, and a gross weight system
will be satisfactory to all but people who carry feathers or Pink Batts regularly in their
trucks, because they go out full and they come  back empty. If they are never close to
their gross weights, maybe there will be an issue, but it is around the margins. The
Ministry of Transport has work ed very carefully with the i ndustry to ensure that those
changes affect as few people as possible.
So with those words it is my pleasure to commend this bill to the House. It is a good
bill. It will improve road-user charges collection in this country.
A party vote was called for on the question, That the Road User Charges Bill be now
read a third time.
Ayes 113
New Zealand National 59; New Zeal and Labour 34; Green Party 14; M āori Party
3; ACT New Zealand 1; Mana 1; United Future 1.
Noes 8
New Zealand First 8.
Bill read a third time.

sections.heading: National Animal Identification And Tracing Bill

items.text: Third Reading

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CARTER
items.text: I move, That the
National Animal Identification and Tracing Bill be now read a third time. Agriculture is
a key industry driving our econom y. We must maintain our reputation as world leaders
in the production of top quality animal pr oducts. The Crown and industry have started
to work together since 2004 to ensure that we have the quality information we need
about livestock. In that regard, I would like to acknowledge and pay tribute to the earlier
work of Ian Corney, who chaired the initial working-group. His absolute commitment is
one of the reasons that this legislation is before the House tonight.
The National Animal Identification and Tracing (NAIT) scheme will support the
electronic recording of locations, the people in  charge of animals, and the movement of
animals between properties, along with ot her attributes. With NAIT we can give
378 National Animal Identification and Tracing Bill 14 Feb 2012
assurances to domestic consumers and our tr ade partners that the product is healthy and
disease-free. We can manage a disease more effectively and rapidly reopen markets if
they are closed. Furthermore, the NAIT scheme  allows for other information to be held
in conjunction with mandatory data and ca n further support improved productivity and
on-farm management.
The National Animal Identification and Tracing Bill sets out the legal framework for
the collection of information on livestock, and their location and movement history
throughout their lifetime. It also outlines  the governance arrangements and powers for
the NAIT organisation that will manage  the NAIT scheme. NAIT needs to be
mandatory to be effective. The bill will support the introduction of the NAIT scheme,
scheduled for July 2012 for cattle and March 2013 for deer.
It was agreed early on in the NAIT scheme’s development that the Government and
the industry would share its co sts as well as its benefits . The Government funded the
building of the database and is to fund a continuing contri bution of 35 percent of the
system’s operational costs. The livestock industry groups have provided financial
support during the scheme’s development and will do so once the bill has passed.
During the bill’s passage th rough the House I have spoke n about the history of the
project and how we got to this point. Ini tially, there was a substantial battle with
Federated Farmers, which were difficult,  and that led to unnecessary scepticism
amongst many farmers. Thankfully, with the new leadership of Federated Farmers,
realism now prevails. With the establishment of NAIT, farmers now have the ability to
manage stock at the level of an individual animal rather than as a herd. Farmers are able
to invest in automated systems to weigh and draft animals according to the criteria that
farmers themselves set, rather than having to assess an animal’s condition by eye.
Modern farming systems are able to provide labour savings and more accurate
responses to market demand. I also expect  the NAIT organisati on to respond to the
demands from its levy-paying farmers. Once the NAIT scheme is well settled and
functioning, the NAIT organisation and th e Animal Health Board will begin to
consolidate their governance and functions. I look forward to the efficiencies and cost
savings that will result at the level of both individual levy-paying farmers and the
livestock industries themselves.
I am pleased that most of the parties repr esented in this House have recognised the
importance of this bill and of the NAIT sche me. I tonight acknowledge the work of the
previous Labour Government in devel oping the NAIT scheme, and Labour’s ongoing
support for the NAIT legislation. I also ac knowledge the long-term commitment and
dedication to a successful NAIT scheme by a ll the industry parties that have been
involved in NAIT Ltd itself, which is now in charge of delivering the scheme. I
commend the National Animal Identification and Tracing Bill to the House.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: Can I just start my speech by
acknowledging the role of the Minister for Primary Industr ies in shepherding this
legislation through. It is true to—

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: “Shepherding”!

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: You liked that, Mr Cosgr ove? Yes, shepherding. I will
come back to sheep in a minute, actually, as  Mr Cosgrove often encourages me to do.
But I do want to acknowledge the Minister for his leadership on this issue. As he noted
in his speech, this was something that bega n under the previous Labour Government. In
particular, on the day that the member fo r Wigram, Megan Woods, gave her maiden
speech, it is worth noting that Jim Anderton had a significant role in the development of
the National Animal Identification and Trac ing system. Mr Anderton saw, as others
involved in the agricultural sector did, that a system of  national identification and
tracing that was consistent and was not the piecemeal system that we had, would allow
14 Feb 2012 National Animal Identification and Tracing Bill 379
New Zealand to both avoid significant problems and costs, and also embrace
opportunities. Those significant costs have b een noted throughout th is debate. The fact
that a major foot-and-mouth outbreak in New Zealand could cost this country in the
region of $10 billion makes the cost of actually  implementing a system like this pale in
comparison, and it is quite clear from the various times in New Zealand that we have
had foot-and-mouth scares just what impact that would have on our exports. So the idea
of an identification and tracing system stopping that, or at least significantly limiting the
impact of that, is something that all New Z ealanders and the agricu ltural sector should
be pleased about.
But also it is the opportunity that this provi des that I think is one of the things that
causes me to be really pleas ed to be supporting this Natio nal Animal Identification and
Tracing Bill tonight in the House, and that is  the opportunity to be able to sell into
markets across the world that are demanding more and more that they understand the
origins of the produce that is being purchase d. What this system allows us to do—to be
able to trace, as the Minister has just said, to the individual animal; in this case, cattle
and deer—actually allows people to have confidence about the sustainability of the New
Zealand farming system. People can understand exactly where produce comes from.
Members will be familiar with the Icebre aker brand. This is something that
Icebreaker has done magnificently well. Being able to provide Baacodes that people can
scan that can link back to exactly where th e wool for an Icebreaker product has come
from is hugely significant, selling into ma rkets that are worried about sustainability
concerns and that want to know that the product that they are buying comes from an
ethical farm, comes from a sustainable farm. This applies to produce, as well. In the
Committee stage of the debate I mentioned a project I have had a little bit to do with
called Paddock to Plate—and Paddock to Plate—

items.speaker: Hon Ruth Dyson
items.text: Horrible name.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: I still quite like it.

items.speaker: Colin King
items.text: Pasture to plate.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: —but Paddock to Plate was a project that was about
ensuring that the people who were really significant to the New Zealand economy—the
supermarket buyers in the UK—would be able to say with certainty: “This is where this
produce has come from. This is what we know  about it.” I actually think you could take
that further than just being able to identify and trace the cattle. What about knowing
more about the land, the pasture—for Mr King’s benefit—that was involved in the
production of these goods. There is technology av ailable now that can tell us about the
soil content, that can tell us about the way that grass is grown. Let us actually provide to
consumers internationally the full picture of how New Zealand is creating a more
sustainable farming process.

items.speaker: Jonathan Young
items.text: The soil.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: The soil—indeed, absolutely. This is exactly the kind of
thing that consumers internationally are looking for. So that is why I regard this bill as a
very good bill, because what it does is provide  opportunity for New Zealand to be able
to take advantage of those markets where peopl e are interested in ensuring that they are
purchasing sustainable products.
There is some concern on this side of  the House around the question of who is
developing this technology. There is huge oppor tunity in this traceability technology,
and Sirtrack, which was one of the organisations that was helping to develop this, came
out of Landcare Research and has been sold off. Now that is, in some ways, a good
thing for the people who developed the technolo gy, but really we do have to ensure that
we keep companies like that going inside New Zealand and to make sure that those
companies that are developing that technology are supported and understood.
380 National Animal Identification and Tracing Bill 14 Feb 2012
It is true to say that this bill has had widespread support across the House, as the
Minister noted. I understand that  in the earlier readings the only party to vote against it
was the ACT Party. It was the only party. I have no idea why—[ Interruption] It is lack
of freedom for livestock, Mr Cosgrove, that is the issue here—one law for all. It was
discussed earlier in the Comm ittee stage whether or not this would move beyond cattle
and deer to sheep. That is the obvious ne xt step and I know that the Minister has
discussed that and said that it is a possibility. But it is true to say that there was
reluctance from some in the farming sector to adopt this. It is unusual for the Minister in
charge of this bill to be one to be pushing compulsion so hard. He is not a man who
usually likes to support the idea of compulsion, but in this case the Minister has seen the
wisdom of the fact that we need a co mprehensive system. If there is not a
comprehensive system, then we undermine the opportunities that I mentioned before,
and we undermine our ability to fend off accusa tions if there is something like a foot-
and-mouth outbreak. As the Minister sai d, the farming community, the Federated
Farmers, did eventually come on board with this. I am sure Mr Anderton worked very
hard on that in the initial stages and it wa s obviously carried on by the current Minister
as well.
The fact that we have these systems in plac e now in New Zealand al so brings us into
line with a number of our other key trading pa rtners. We look at Australia, where cattle
are already using eartags from a traceability system. They are also looking, in Australia,
at the lifetime tracing of sheep. So clearly New Zealand needs to continue to advance
into that market—

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: Careful!

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: Mr Cosgrove is an expert on the lifetime tracing of sheep,
so he too will be able to contribute to the wisdom of following Australia in that
particular area. I do think that it is important. This is about market advantage as much as
anything for New Zealand, and if other countr ies such as Australia  are going into this
area, then we too need to do that when it comes to sheep.
So it is with great pleasure that I support this bill. I do not thi nk that it would be—
[Interruption] Perhaps some people would see it, Mr Cunliffe, as being unusual that the
member for Wellington Central is taking such an interest in this rural issue. But the fact
is this is about the New Zealand economy. This is about the strength of the New
Zealand economy. It is about applying tec hnological solutions that  are developed in
New Zealand to be able to establish our sustainability overseas.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Clean, green, clever!

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: It is about a clean, green, and clever New Zealand—that is
right, Mr Cunliffe—and that is why I am very pleased to be  able to suppor t it. I look
forward to the Government extending the pr ocess out further beyond dairy and cattle to
sheep, to create a fully comprehensive system of traceability from the paddock to the
plate and to make sure that New Zealand actua lly can sell into those overseas markets,
and to be able to say proudly that we are a fully sustainable country and being able to
prove that.

items.speaker: SHANE ARDERN
items.text: I do not know where to
start after that speech. I am suitably impre ssed, I think I should say for a start. You
know, the member for Wellington Central either  has Jim Anderton’s speech notes or he
has been talking to the Hon Damien O’Connor—or maybe he has had some advice from
Clayton Cosgrove. But I have to say that  was a remarkably good speech from the new
deputy leader of the Labour Party on this topic, so I congratulate him on it.
The issues canvassed so far are absolutely ri ght. I think that Mr Robertson said that
foot-and-mouth could cost New Zealand $10 bill ion; the last estimate I saw on that was
that, potentially, it could cost $25 billion per year—not one off; per year. That would
14 Feb 2012 National Animal Identification and Tracing Bill 381
devastate the New Zealand economy if it were  to happen at its worst possible impact.
To be able to trace animals in the event of a biosecurity incursion, regardless of what
the incursion may be, is an essential part  of having integrity in the system around
biosecurity. This National Animal Identifica tion and Tracing Bill is the first step, I
guess you can say, in moving forward into the 21 st century technology in regard to
doing that.
The issues that were canvassed in th e Primary Production Committee and through
the submission process, both in  terms of the consultation pa per that was put together
first of all to form the bill and then the pr ocess as the select committee went through its
work, are the issues of retent ion rates in sheep, in particul ar. That is the reason why the
Government at this point has chosen not to have lambs or sheep included in the national
identification regulations. So that issue has to be resolved, and I think technology in
time will find an answer to that. In fact, some work has gone on in the US in recent
years around implants. Now everyone throws their hands up in the air when you use the
term “implant”, but, basically, it is using the same kind of technology that has been used
in New Zealand for registration of dogs, but in a way that it can be inserted with
integrity so that the device itself retains its reliability and also so it does not become a
problem in further processing of the carcass of an animal, which is quite a challenge.
That is something that has been worked on. I think it will be overcome in time, and
when it is overcome, then, of course, the problem with retention rates of tagging devices
in sheep will be overcome and the cost then will be reduced substantially. So I think that
is probably where we need to start cranking up the research.
I notice that the Animal Health Board itsel f is likely to be the group—the instrument
if you like, the team of peopl e—that will drive a lot of that work, and, potentially, may
be the owner and controller of the database in conjunction, of course, and in partnership
with the Government, because the integrity of that database is equally as important as
anything else that goes with this whole keep ing of traceability, so that the integrity of
the system is maintained.
It is absolutely essential, if we are goi ng to be a First World exporter of high quality
protein products, particularly from animal production, that we have traceability that will
stand up to the scrutiny of th e international markets. When  you look at what  is driving
growth in—particularly—high quality production ar eas, it is that tr aceability that the
member for Wellington Central spoke of. He us ed the example of the Icebreaker brand,
and that is a very good example. But there are many others. If you look at some of the
products that come out of our dairy i ndustry, now going into nutraceuticals and
pharmaceuticals, clearly the integrity or safety  of that product is essential. Well, the
same will apply with meat products and other animal products that are produced on our
New Zealand farms as we speak. So having a solid, robust database, using the best
technology, and using the best measurement sy stems—that is, how you scan or read
high numbers of cattle, or sheep, as the case may be, in a timely and cost-effective
way—is something that this system and this bill is enabling of.
As we watch that develop, I suspect we will see quite a bit of development around
the different types of measurement systems and measuring devices. There was a lot of
debate at the time of the select committee hearings on this—around the use of high
frequency versus low frequenc y devices. The robustness of those devices was the thing
in question. I guess the biggest challenge for the select committee was to make sure that
the bill was able to adapt to whatever de vice the market and the farming users decided
to use and not to try to second-guess what woul d be the best. It woul d appear to us that
having the ability to be able to measure la rge numbers of animals in a simple way—and
if you can just imagine for a moment, Mr Assistant Speaker Tisch, and I know you may
have some experience with this yourself—being able to measure a whole flock of sheep
382 National Animal Identification and Tracing Bill 14 Feb 2012
or yard of cattle with a device that is ab le to scan that area within a reasonable
proximity, what a wonderful piece of technology that would be, to be able to know how
many you had in the yard, for a start, to know  each individual animal by number, and to
know what the ages and various groups and sector groups of those animals were. Think
about then being able to feed that informa tion into a drafting system like the Protrack
system, designed by Livestock Improvement  Corporation, which I know you have a
close family association with, Mr Assistant Speaker. That would be a wonderful ability
for farming so that you could actually draf t animals as you wished by entering the data
into a computer in a centralised place. Just imagine how that would simplify the
handling of large dairy herds, or large flocks of sheep, or cattle, for that matter. So those
things will develop.
As that happens, what you will see is the commercial drivers for such a system will
overtake the anxiety that some  farmers have now about cost , because there will be a
financial benefit to them for doing it. Those were the big debating points that Federated
Farmers raised in the early stages of the discussion, and what they could see was just yet
another cost being imposed on the farming sect or without any real justification for that
cost. So I think we have moved past that  point now to where the advantages are
overwhelming and most farmers who have b een watching this debate and watching the
technology develop are now much more receptiv e to it than they were perhaps 5 years
ago.
The other major issue, of course, is when  we are signing up to international trade
agreements, to be able to go into those negotiations with a high degree of certainty that
what we are about to sign up to will be able to be delivered with traceability back to
individual farms, individual animals, with  the safety standards in place. Recently,
remember the melamine scare in China, which had the whole of the dairy industry
shaking in its boots for a moment. We, of cour se, in New Zealand ar e able to say that
this product comes from this production system, it is safe, it is reli able, and it will not
suffer the same fate as that did. It is with those types of issues in mind that it is my
pleasure to support this bill through the third reading. Thank you.
Hon DAMIEN O’CONNOR (Labou r—West Coast - Tasman) : It is with great
pleasure that I welcome the third reading of the National Animal Identification and
Tracing Bill back into the House. It is abou t time, I have to say. It started in 2004. My
colleague the Hon Jim Sutton was actually in ch arge of the original development of this
concept, but it is right that the Hon Jim Anderton actually found the $10 million that the
Government was going to contribute to the im plementation of this scheme, and then it
was rejected by Federated Farmers. I have to say that was an outrageous abuse of a
position by someone who ended up being an  ACT candidate—that is, Don Nicolson—
who just campaigned against this for cheap political reasons, in my view.
Although there were some issues around th e radio frequency and some of the
technology, the bottom line was that in 2004 we knew full well that we needed to have
in place, very quickly, a proper system of  traceability. We had been alerted to the
inadequacies of our traceability systems through the foot-and-mouth scare on Waiheke
Island. That gave us a hell of  a fright, and we thought we had better do something. We
pride ourselves on being a very smart, Firs t World producer of f ood, but the reality is
that the countries that have these systems in place include Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay,
South Korea, and Canada, and we are just catching up. So it is about time it was passed
through the House. As I said, we welcome that.
Can I just say that I would like to tha nk my colleague Grant Robertson for his
speech. As acknowledged, it was a very good speech from the member for Auckland
Central—

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Wellington.
14 Feb 2012 National Animal Identification and Tracing Bill 383
Hon DAMIEN O’CONNOR: Wellington Central, sorry. I challenge National to put
up their member from Auckland Central to see whether she knows as much about it. We
hear lots of gibes and accusations from Na tional about the depth of knowledge of rural
issues in the Labour Party. Well, that spe ech just goes to show that we do have
widespread understanding of the dependence of both urban and rural New Zealand on
one another. It was an excellent speech and I will be calli ng on his knowledge and
support as we move forward in Government to put in place some wonderful policies.
I think many of the points have been covere d. This has been a long process. We do
claim to be a producer of high quality, safe, and—now—traceable food. That is, we will
know where the food comes from. There are some examples of excellence within
industries in this country, be they meat or dairy, where we know which cow, basically,
contributed to which bit of bu tter or cheese. In meat there are fewer examples, but none
the less some of excellence in that area. Most of those exporters get a premium for their
product, and we want more and more of that as this country moves forward.
I had a discussion tonight with some colleagues on whether we are still the producers
of commodity products or whether we are moving up the value chain. Well, we do want
to move up the value chain, and each step re quires a huge amount of investment. This is
a relatively small investment to move us qui te a way up and compete with at least the
countries that I named before, because if we do not, we simply will not be able to sell to
them.
One of the big issues, and it is still one of the contentious things going on at the
moment, is the management of the database. I must mention this. There was some fear
in the minds of some farmers, driven by misinformation from Federated Farmers for the
most part, that this database was going to be used to calculate methane emissions and
charge farmers, etc., etc. It was just outra geous, quite frankly, and, as I say, was driven
by a person who ultimately became an ACT candidate. That speaks for itself. But the
database is important. We currently ha ve two good databases—the Animal Health
Board has one, and the Livestock Improveme nt Corporation has another for dairy—and
they operate pretty well. The question was whether we should merge those databases or
create a new one, and I think that there was concern from officials and from farmers that
a new database would cost a whole lot of  money and maybe was unnecessary. In the
end, that is what was decided, and as long as people in NAIT Ltd and developing this do
a good job, hopefully we will end up with one  good database that can be used by other
sectors.
Hopefully, we can add in sheep, and although sheep farmers might get spooked about
that, at the value of their ewes now, getting up close to between $150 and $200—

items.speaker: John Hayes
items.text: $300 in the Wairarapa.
Hon DAMIEN O’CONNOR : Three hundred dollars? Any more? More on three,
three, three—going four, four, no? I would suggest that in fact good quality sheep, good
quality livestock—cows, deer—w ill be worth a lot of money. If we put our protein in
the higher value brackets in the supermarkets  around the world, then we will want to
know where those animals are, their genetics, whom they are traded to, and whom they
are sold to. It will become part and parcel of normal livestock and farm management in
this country—that is, full traceability of all our animals. We might even end up with all
the dogs being microchipped, but anyway, that is another deba te. My colleague in front
of me will chuckle on that one, but I am sure we will get to the point where every
animal on a farm will have to be microchi pped. We will have to know exactly where
they are so we can prove that any disease or any possible infection can be signed off and
we can tell our customers what they are getting when they buy that protein and they pay
more for it.
384 National Animal Identification and Tracing Bill 14 Feb 2012
I am not going to speak for too long. I wa s disappointed when farmers turned their
backs on the $10 million offered by the Labour G overnment at that time. The cost of
implementation now has been estimated by o fficials going forward, but the benefit has
been calculated at close to $40 million—I think $38 million—per year. I think that
would be a fair estimate. The rough annual cost is $6 million; it will cost $15.7 million
to set up. Labour in power offered $10 million. I am not sure that that is the amount that
the current National Government is going to give, but, none the less, it is committed to
implementing it and that is great.
Before I sign off, I say that the Primary Production Committee had a look at the issue
of high and low frequency. We wanted to ensure that we were futureproofing whatever
system was put in place and that we we re not imposing an unnecessary cost or
duplication of costs on either the farmers, the saleyards, the meat processors, or anyone.
The jury is still out, I have to say, so we ha ve left the door open. I think it will be a low
frequency system implemented first, moving to a high frequency one; we are told the
high frequency tag can hold more data and can be read at a greater distance.
In terms of the things that Mr Arde rn was talking about—knowing how many
animals are in your herd, where they are going, and to what part of your farm—many
farmers, in fact, now expect to know that. It is part of  normal management systems.
They are the most efficient farmers. They are at the forefront of technology, and this
will enable all farmers to potentially reach that high level of management. I must say
and put on the record that w ith such technology, I am sure we will be able through
satellite management to have fenceless farming systems, where animals will be
encouraged to graze one part of a farm today and then another part tomorrow. There
will be proactive management and stimulation through satellites. It all seems rather far-
fetched, but I would suggest th at within 10 years we will be  looking at those kinds of
systems. If we are not, then we will be falling behind other countries.
In conclusion, Labour supports this legislation. We initiated it in 2004, we offered to
pay for it in 2008, and we welcome its passage through the House. This is a big step for
New Zealand agriculture, and it will give a ssurance to the customers who buy our food
in the future—initially beef and venison, but moving forward, hopefully, and taking in
the others—that we know where the animals came from, we know wh at they ate, and
that consumption will be absolutely safe.

items.speaker: KEVIN HAGUE
items.text: It is a pleasure to take a call in this third reading of the
National Animal Identification and Tracing Bill. The Green Party has supported this bill
at every stage moving through the House. It was covered by my portfolio in the last
Parliament. It is now within Steffan Browni ng’s portfolio, but he is  unable to be here
tonight. Other speakers in this debate have  canvassed many of the advantages of the
National Animal Identification and Tracing (NAI T) system, and I just want to run very
briefly through those that we see, because some of those are the same that others see
and others are some different ones.
I guess the first one I want to highlight, and I do not think anyone has mentioned this
tonight, is the usefulness of this system in  the event that we encounter a food-borne
human disease. I am thinking of someth ing like bovine spongifo rm encephalopathy—
mad cow disease—and other pr ion diseases that are spr ead through meat, and where
traceability of meat and meat products plays an  incredibly useful role in best promoting
human health.
Others have mentioned a couple of the anim al health issues. One example that has
been mentioned tonight is foot-and-mouth dise ase. I think of what might happen in that
disastrous biosecurity situa tion. Some colleagues may not like me mentioning this, but
let us say that one of those palm kernel shipments comes in  from a country where foot-
and-mouth disease is endemic, and the bacteria  is found in the soil that comes with that
14 Feb 2012 National Animal Identification and Tracing Bill 385
palm kernel, and we face an outbreak in this  country. Actually being able to trace the
animals that may have been affected by an out break is going to be incredibly important
for our economy, as well as for, dare I say it, the animals themselves.
The other important use in relation to anim al-borne illness that occurs to me is
around control of stock movement. In this country, as we try to get the cap on TB in our
animal herd, actually having a tool that assists us with bette r control of stock
movement—and NAIT will provid e that—has to be a real ly helpful weapon in the
armoury. So some really important benefits  there. My colleague Damien O’Connor has
spoken about some of the innovation and stock improvement, for example, that this new
technology will facilitate. I think you will find that his musing is not far from the mark.
I agree with him that actual ly that is the kind of tec hnological improvement we will
need to make to keep adding value to our  products to continue  to have an export
agricultural economy.
Traceability—and other members have spoken about this—is important as one of
those value-add components to our agri cultural economy. Si mply exporting raw
commodities is no longer the way our economy needs to go. The future for agriculture
in New Zealand is around adding value to those products and, again, NAIT is one of the
fundamental tools for achieving that.
Someone has mentioned Icebreaker. I am a great cyclist and tramper, and I decided
long ago never to walk into the hills without being clad in Icebreaker. Indeed, that is the
choice that many people, both in  this country and around the world, have made. It is a
great example, a great illustration, of the kind of economic value that is associated with
traceability. Certainly, there is  an international movement of consumers along the lines
of that Paddock to Plate initiative that Gr ant Robertson spoke a bout earlier in this
debate. They want to know where their food comes from, a nd they are prep ared to pay
more to know that. That is the future for our  food export industries. So it is part of our
way of creating a higher quality export sector by adding value.
On the flipside, we have raised a number of concerns at different points in this
debate. These are not concerns that cause us tonight to reverse our position and to
oppose the bill. We support the bill. We believe the positive attributes outweigh the
concerns. But I just think in this third readi ng it is appropriate to recap some of those
issues that we were concerned about. The fi rst one of those was the lack of consultation
with the organics sector in the development of this bill. We believe that that was a
significant gap, and we hope that in the development of future legislation we will not
see that kind of gap. I draw the House’s attent ion to the fact that the organics sector is
already a part of our agricultural sector that  has considerable experience in the business
of adding value and in targeting those cons umers who have a very great concern about
where their food comes from, how the animal s were raised, and what the conditions
were like on that farm. So involvement of th e organics sector should have been a really
important thing that was done in preparing this bill.
The second issue that I want to raise, which we have raised previously in debates on
the bill, is around th e governance group. To our way of  thinking, it has yet to be
satisfactorily explained why the original intention of a Crown company or a Crown
entity was abandoned and replaced with the gov ernance group that now appears in this
bill before us. We do not see a rationale th at would justify that change, and we do not
believe that that has been satisfactorily advanced in the debate in this House. So that is a
concern for us. It is more than something that is an academic or abstruse kind of
concern, because the nature of the entity changes its responsibil ities. So a Crown
company or a Crown entity, for example, w ould have obligations under the Official
Information Act, which this governance group may well not end up having. The Animal
Health Board is a great exampl e of where the model that is  used for the governance of
386 National Animal Identification and Tracing Bill 14 Feb 2012
an operation can change that. In the c onsideration by the Local Government and
Environment Committee of the performance of  the Animal Health Board in the last
Parliament, one of the major concerns that was raised by submitters was around the
opacity of the Animal Health Board and the difficulty that one had actually getting
information out of that organisation. It is a needless problem, and it is one that we could
have avoided in this case.
Our related concern is that in this entity that  is not really an arm of the State we have
also chosen to vest quite considerable sear ch, seizure, and related powers, and we have
an abiding concern that the ex tent of those powers outweighs  the nature of the problem
that those powers are created for. We think that is a real problem . We have signalled
that we will be watching the performance of this Act in practice to see whether
problems arise, and we will bring them back to this House if they do.
Finally, I want to just mention the very big feature we see in this bill—that is,
providing value for our export industries by providing consumers overseas with
information about where their food comes from. It is about time New Zealand
consumers had that same right. It is time for mandatory and comprehensive labelling of
food in New Zealand. Thank you.

items.speaker: COLIN KING
items.text: It is fair to say that the bill as it stands has
been well canvassed during its third reading. Bu t I would just like to make one or two
points before I sit down again. One concerns the complexities that we are facing as we
implement this very worthy bill, the Nationa l Animal Identification and Tracing Bill.
One has to stop and think about the million or so cattle that are on lifestyle blocks and
are going to have to come into this system. Th at starts to illustrate the complexity. We
can start talking about sheep, and already st ud breeders are doing it with their high
frequency identification systems. But we ha ve just got to be mindful that it is
appropriate that the introduction of the Nati onal Identification and Tracing Bill deals
with cattle and deer—effectively cattle on 1 July 2012, and then deer on 1 March 2013.
It is appropriate to give a bit of flavour with regard to the difference between the low
frequency and high frequency transponders. The low frequency can  be read only at
about 1 metre, and that is where that debate crept in with regard to the high frequency,
where it was possible to read the animal’s tags out in the middle of a paddock about 200
to 300 metres away. There is still a wee way to go before we actually see innovation
around this area.
I would imagine that we certainly do need to keep a very close eye on what the rest
of the world is doing, because we do sell to the 5 percent of the world that have the
incomes to choose what they eat and are prepar ed to pay for it. So it is very important
that we protect New Zealand’s food safety r ecord and its credentials. They are at the
platinum level, and that is something we cannot take for grante d. There is, no doubt, a
lot of potential within the National Animal  Identification and Tracing system and the
farming technologies that will be applied in the future, and I know that our farmers and
our community of New Zealand are very quick in the uptake of modern technologies.
That having been said, this legislation is important. There is a view out in the
farming community—or there was a view for a while—that if it was this good or that
good, why is the industry not driving it? One has to think a wee bit long and hard to
answer that question, but the answer is that there are a lot of people in the meat industry
whose main financial drivers are not the m eat. You have only to look at the dairy
industry. There are hundreds of thousands of tonnes of beef going through to the market
that come off dairy farms, and their main driver and their whol e breeding systems are
geared around milk production and butterfat production—milksolids. So to give it the
integrity and credibility that it needs fr om an international point of view, it was
important that we draw up this legislation.
14 Feb 2012 National Animal Identification and Tracing Bill 387
We have overcome those obstacles. I do not find anything overly offensive in
farmers being concerned about costs being heaped upon them. They have to run very,
very challenging operations in challenging eco nomic times, and it is good to see that
although this legislation is to be implemente d, it is during a time when farmers are able
to see a bit of light at the e nd of the tunnel. This is very  good legislation. It has been
well handled by the Primary Production Committee members on both sides of the
House, and it is high time that  it quickly passes into law. It is a pleasure to support this
bill.

items.speaker: RICHARD PROSSER
items.text: As others have done, I would like to
congratulate some of the other new members of the House whose fine maiden speeches
we were able to enjoy today. I am encouraged by the intellect and sincerity displayed by
those members, and I am looking forward to working with them over the term of this
Parliament.
I am pleased to speak to the House on this important piece of legislation, the
National Animal Identification and Tracing Bi ll. I rise on behalf of the New Zealand
First Party. We are opposed to the passage of th is bill in its present form. We have not
had previous input into the c onstruction of this bill, or th e debate subsequent to its
introduction, due to our party’s unplanned sabbatical from the House, which, I am
pleased to say, is now, thankfully, completed for all eternity.
New Zealand First understands and fully s upports the importance of the agricultural
sector to New Zealand’s economy and way of life, and we apprecia te how critical the
success of this industry is in terms of our exports and international reputation. It is
indeed testament to that reputation that we as a nation have been able to maintain access
to both our traditional and expa nding markets over the past 8- year gestation of this bill
in spite of our not having such a system of  record as this bill proposes, and which many
of our trading partners have adopted themse lves or are in the process of developing.
Amongst them are Australia, the United Ki ngdom, Canada, the United States of
America, South Korea, Japan, Argentina, an d many of the member States of Europe—
the European Union. All agricultural nations li ve with the risk of animal disease and
epidemic, and their faith in our existing syst ems of inspection and assurance thus far is,
I am sure, appreciated by the Government and industry alike.
As a trading nation, New Zealand must take all practicable steps to protect its borders
and export base from unwanted threats, and to be a responsible in ternational citizen by
ensuring that such threats do not leave our shor es. It is true that the march of time and
technology makes it likely that consumers and regulatory authorities alike in our crucial
overseas markets may come to demand that  even known suppliers with impeccable
track records, such as New Z ealand, choose to bring themselv es into line with what is
more and more becoming accepted as internatio nal best practice in terms of safeguards
and accountability in record-keeping. It is worthy of note, however, we believe, that the
aforementioned countries have had incidences of foot-and-mouth disease, whereas New
Zealand, by good management, effective bios ecurity, and the grace of God, remains
thus far free of it.
It is a reality that  the maturing of what were gr ound-breaking technologies even a
few years ago means that what may have b een an arguably prohibitive cost when this
bill was first proposed has become, for the sections of the industry initially intended to
be covered by it at least, a far more financially acceptable proposition. Indeed, the
utilisation and further enha ncement of the iden tification technologi es in question by
New Zealand will certainly contribute to the increasing accessibility of those systems,
quite possibly to the point where their employment in other sectors of the industry, such
as sheep, is able to be made financially viab le. It remains a pity, as other members have
noted, that the disposal to overseas interests of New Zeal and’s own leading supplier in
388 National Animal Identification and Tracing Bill 14 Feb 2012
this field means that this country will not be in a position to profit directly from any
such expansion.
New Zealand First supports the promoti on of measures that enhance the ongoing
success and stability of our most important  industries. However,  we would ask, in
addition, whether New Zealand consumers are al so to be afforded the reassurance of
traceability, as Mr Grant Robe rtson referred to earlier, from paddock to plate. We hold
some concern that certain meat products ar e currently imported into New Zealand from
nations whose systems of recording and accoun tability fall far short of those that we
employ even today, and that in itself is wit hout the benefits of the technology heralded
as being the great advantage that this bill will supposedly afford both ourselves and our
overseas consumers.
But it is of concern to the New Zealand First Party that too great a reliance may come
to be placed on this new technology at th e expense of existing systems of record-
keeping, which are proven and which have se rved and continue to serve New Zealand
well. Some aspects of the radio frequency identification chips in  question, as other
members have alluded to, are still in their infancy or developmental stages. Some may
have crossover or interference issues with other high fre quency radio equipment, which
is increasingly being utilised in farming today. We are concerned that a system based on
radio frequency identification eartags will provide no tangible improvement in
traceability over and above that provided by existing numbered plastic eartags, once the
animal has reached the stage in the proces sing chain where the head is removed from
the body.
However, the use of radio frequency id entification tags does open doors to the
possibility both of counterfeiting once our  product reaches certa in less trustworthy
foreign markets and of the theft and rechipping of  stock. It is possible, in fact, that what
appears on the surface to be a more high-t ech and therefore safer and more secure
system may indeed prove to be less so in both regards, particularly when the human
propensity for placing great trust in advan ced technology is taken into account. I am
reminded, indeed, of the response of a well -known criminal gang to the introduction of
vehicle identification number plates some years ago, in an attempt to prevent the resale
of stolen cars. The motorcycle enthusiast s club in question availed themselves, in
reasonably short order, of a supply of bl ank plates complete with an impressing
machine, the combination of which allowed th em to continue thei r business with little
interruption. In many cases the cleverer the intended system of security, the easier and
ultimately more persuasive are the means found to circumvent it by those with nefarious
intent.
New Zealand First does not support this bill , for several reasons. In addition to the
aforementioned, we do not wish to s ee our farmers and consumers unfairly
disadvantaged by any financial or complianc e burdens placed upon them in the absence
of a similar required standard being applie d to comparable imported foodstuffs. In the
light of the inherent weaknesses of the tec hnology as it is propose d, and the inevitable
decline of the present system as it is progre ssively replaced, we s ee the direction of the
bill with regard to the mandatory adopti on of the National Animal Identification and
Tracing system as being precipitate. It is our view that this may be one occasion where
the market should be able to speak, in th at demand from foreign buyers, rather than
dictates from our own Government, should be  the driving force leading the adoption of
this technology.
We are concerned that the introduction of microchips for deer and cattle may be
beset by some of the same shortfalls that have been the experience of the introduction of
microchips for dogs. It promises a great deal with little in the way of proven benefits,
comes at a measurable cost with no guara ntee of improved return, and carries the
14 Feb 2012 National Animal Identification and Tracing Bill 389
potential to weaken the existing system, which even the bill’s authors agree will have to
continue in parallel with the new methodology until such time as the application of
radio frequency identification technology can  be made economically viable for sheep
and other stock animals outside of the two species initially speci fied. We would very
much not like to see the implementation of a policy and a technology that seek and
promise to reduce costs and improve performa nce but that in their application achieve
entirely the opposite result. We oppose the pass age of this bill in its present form and
urge members from all sides of the House to do the same. Thank you.

items.speaker: JONATHAN YOUNG
items.text: I would like to just draw,
perhaps, a backdrop behind this National Animal Identification and Tracing Bill of
events that happened, as we will remember, some time ago, particularly in the United
Kingdom, where the outbreak of bovine spong iform encephalopathy, or what is called
mad cow disease, created such a furore amongst the industry there, where 180,000 cattle
were infected and 4.4 million head of cattle were slaughtered during the eradication
programme, which is something that I th ink is a horrific thought to farmers and
agriculturists here in New Zealand. The National Animal Identification and Tracing Bill
will enable the establishment of a tracing sy stem that will control and prevent animal
disease and product contamination. This is an investment in current and modern
technology that is goin g to protect an industry that is  contributing over half of our
annual export volume to the rest of the world.
The global consumption of meat since 1961—and  this is one of the major areas that
this legislation will touch on—has tripled, and it  does continue to increase rapidly. It is
fuelled by rising living standa rds in nations such as India and China. As consumer
incomes rise, there is the tendency to buy more protein. We understand that; we know
that is why our exports and our commoditie s in this country have seen such a
tremendous lift in recent years. Indeed, people who live in developed countries consume
four times as much meat as those in developing countries. You would be interested to
know that since 1961 average consumption has risen from 56 kilograms to 89 kilograms
per person per year in India, and from 89 to 124 kilograms per person in the US,
according to the Food and Agriculture Organization. In 1961 the Chinese consumed
only 4 kilograms of meat pe r person per year, but that figure has reached over 55
kilograms and is still rising. So we see an international demand driv ing growth in this
particular area in this particular industry.
It is incredibly important that mana gement around disease prevention is hugely
enhanced. We understand that nations that New Zealand competes with are progressing
in these particular areas, and current animal-tracing schemes here in New Zealand are
falling behind the systems used by our trad ing partners. We live in a time of global
opportunity in this particular area, and it bodes well for us that we provide adequate
information for responding to biosecurity risk s and incursions, so we do not place our
market access at risk. The Food and Agricultu re Organization reports that import bans
on meat produced in disease-afflicted countri es in early 2004, for example, affected
approximately a third of global meat exports, or 6 million tonnes. This is the sort of
thing that happens when disease or dis eases can affect animals. From 2002 to 2006,
alternating disease outbreaks and recoveries resulted in rapid shortages, and increases in
exportable meat supplies led to considerable fluctuations in international prices.
The National Animal Identification and Tracing (NAIT) system is a very reliable, up-
to-date information system on individual animal locations and movements. It is going to
enable New Zealand to respond quickly in the event of a biosecurity  threat, such as a
disease outbreak, or a food safety threat, such as residues being found in animal-derived
food products. Such a quick response will help limit the spread and reduce the economic
impact of such an event. This is incredibly  important in order to protect not just the
390 National Animal Identification and Tracing Bill 14 Feb 2012
economic well-being but also the social we ll-being of our country . These things are
incredibly important. National wants to grow  the economy in order to deliver greater
prosperity, security, and opportunity to all New Zealanders. We want to deliver—and
are delivering—longer-lasting solutions for our  biosecurity and primary sector, to boost
productivity and to protect those exports. We are very proud of the history of supporting
our primary sector and our rural communities.
The NAIT system would enable rapid and ac curate tracking of animals from birth to
death for live export. I recall speaking to a manager of one of our food processing
factories in Taranaki, and he stated that if it came across a biosecurity threat, it would
instantly be able to identify not only the an imal but where it came from and the animals
that were associated with it that came from the same locality. That would enable it to
very, very quickly isolate that biosecurity th reat. That not only prot ects all of the farms
or the animals that live in proximity to that situation, but it also stops unnecessary
wastage because of doubt about where that bios ecurity threat may have spread to. So it
protects our economic base. Also, with this so rt of technology that is proven, it gives a
degree of confidence to our markets, so th ey can continue to purchase our products
knowing that we have a very strong system in place.
The NAIT scheme is a partnership that started before 2004—we understand that, and
we have heard that this evening—between  industry and the Crown, recognising the
public interest and the private good of identif ying and tracing animals. Industry across
the board is highly supportive of this bill . The NAIT scheme brings the New Zealand
primary sector up to speed with those of mo st other agricultural producing nations that
already have in place such schemes. It is effectively an insurance policy to support New
Zealand’s uniquely high livestock health st atus and biosecurity in frastructure, and can
enable other attributes of livestock to be recorded to improve productivity and on-farm
management. This is, I believe, a tremendous step forward that will enable our primary
sector to have great confidence as it forg es ahead and continues to have a dominant
place in the world market.

items.speaker: Hon RUTH DYSON
items.text: I begin the pleasurable task of
speaking on the third reading of the National Animal Identification and Tracing Bill by
acknowledging the Minister for Primary Industr ies, the Hon David Carter. I want to
express a little bit of disappointment in  the House, though, having commended the Hon
David Carter. He is exempted from this frustration.
During the Committee stage of the debate —you, Mr Assistant Speaker Tisch, were
actually present in the Chair at the time, I recall—I mentioned to the Committee that
David Carter and I had stood ag ainst each other in every el ection, bar one, since 1993,
and I thought that may have been a recor d. I thought it was wort hy of note. You know,
if it is in the Guinness Book of Records we would both like to share that glory. I said to
members of the Committee that, actually, I co uld not be bothered re searching the issue.
David Carter indicated the same lack of intere st in researching it. We just want to take
the credit. I asked some other members to take the time to do the work for us. You
know, not one single member has come back a nd said that David Carter and I hold the
record in the New Zealand system for standing  against each other. So we will just have
to leave that at the moment as an unanswered question.
In addition to that, though, the Hon David Carter did acknowledge former Ministers
of Agriculture. That is not often done in this House, a nd I think it was a good way to
start the new parliamentary term, particularly by acknowledging the Hon Jim Anderton,
who put a huge amount of effort into the initial stages of this work, as did his
predecessor, the Hon Jim Sutton, as well. The bill was, as we have heard, around in
ideas stage only in 2004. It we nt through a lot of consultati on. We had at that time an
ACT takeover of Federated Farmers. Don Nicolson—oh, the Hon John Banks is awake!
14 Feb 2012 National Animal Identification and Tracing Bill 391
You just have to say “ACT” and the eyes light up. That is good; he has remembered he
is an ACT member of Parliament at the moment. One of your colleagues, Mr Banks—
Don Nicolson—was running Federated Farmers at  the time. When he heard about this
scheme to track animals, he went ballistic. It was like a declaration of war on farmers
throughout New Zealand, and that raging continued until he became an ACT candidate.
Fortunately for Federated Farmers, he move d out of that position, and fortunately for
the good of the country, he did not get electe d to sit alongside Mr Banks in Parliament.
But there was huge opposition at that stage; nevertheless, the bill continued.
David Carter picked it up, it was referred to a select committee and, from my reading
of the Primary Production Committee report, very rigorous consideration was given to
this bill. I want to note particularly the ch airman of the select committee, Shane Ardern,
who has spoken earlier in this debate. My reco llection of reading the report is that four
members of that select committee who in my view—even though I was not on it, but
from reading the report—worked quite hard on the detail of this legislation are no
longer in the House, either through their own choice or the choice of the voters in their
electorates. So I want to acknowledge  my two parliament ary colleagues from
Christchurch Brendon Burns and Jim Andert on, also my colleague Ashraf Choudhary,
and National Party MP Sandra Goudie. They we re on this select committee at the time;
they are not here in Parliament any more . Obviously, they cannot  contribute in the
debate, and I think their work should be at least noted.
We have looked at the content of the bill in  some detail, but the area that I think we
have not looked to enough is th e future potential of this le gislation, not just across deer
and cattle, which it will currently cover, but  across a much broader area: positioning
New Zealand to be at the cutting edge and leading in what consumers actually want. I
think it was Jonathan Young, who just resume d his seat, who mentioned this fact as
well. I think more could be made of it. It  is really important for the New Zealand
economy that we are seen not to be followi ng other countries—as we unfortunately are
in this particular tracking process—but actually leading a response to what consumers
want, because they are the people who are going  to make us successful or not. If we are
not providing product in a way that consumers want and look to in the future—if we are
not what they seek—we will have much harsher competition than we already have.
What consumers want to know is where the product comes from. They want to know
that it is safe, they want to know, if we are talking about meat , that it has been raised in
a way that meets their ethical standards, a nd they want to know that it has not been
raised in a way that causes huge damage to the envir onment. That point, I think, we
miss out on quite substantially. We already do it in other ar eas. We do it in respect of
apples. If you buy an apple overseas, eat it, and say “I think this apple is contaminated. I
think it might have some residual spray on it.”,  you can take that apple in, get it tested
for the residual spray, and our New Zealand marketers can trace the apple back, not just
to New Zealand, but actually to  the very row of the orchard that that apple came from.
That can give overseas consumers huge confidence in the safety of our product, and that
is the sort of marketing that we could use for the National Animal Identification and
Tracking system, and apply it to what consumers will want now and in the future.
My colleague Grant Robertson talked about a project that he worked on with the Hon
Simon Upton some years ago at a very  pleasant university in Dunedin, Otago
University, doing what I think was a partic ularly tastelessly named project called
Paddock to Plate—but as a vege tarian, I would see that as a little bit tasteless. But
actually it was very, very substantial and good work that Grant Robertson and Simon
Upton did, and again it was looking at the traceability of various products, and how that
could be used to give consumers both with in New Zealand but also overseas a higher
392 National Animal Identification and Tracing Bill 14 Feb 2012
level of confidence in the ethical standa rds, the safety, the security, and the
environmental standards of the product that they were eating.
We can do the same with Icebreaker. Icebreaker can tell you where the wool came
from for any garment that you purchase from it, and it says that is a huge marketing tool
for overseas customers. And we know, tragically, that Fonterra is very well aware of the
importance of being able to trace the source of its milk and milk products, due to the
disastrous situation that we had in China not very many years ago. So this is a model
that is initially set up to provide just basic safety standards.
We know how important this industry is to us. If we do have—and heaven forbid that
we ever do have—an outbreak of foot-and-m outh disease or any other sort of disease
within this farming area, we will want to  know as quickly as possible where each
animal has been, and any of these traceability elements are, of course, important to that.
But from my perspective, this is much more important in looking at future opportunities
and the needs of consumers.
Members of the House will recall last year or the year before a programme on
television that has been quite harshly re viewed since its initial outburst into the
conversation, particularly in the social medi a. It snuck filming equipment in to a pig
farm and exposed some of what we would cal l the more unethical practices in farming
pigs. What every single consumer—according to reports, anyway, but jolly near every
single consumer—of pork after that programme asked their butcher or their supermarket
was “How are these pigs raised? Are they ra ised like in that dreadful programme on
television?”. So even in the New Zealand context—where we are very familiar with our
own farms, we know the high standards that are kept on most farms, and we are familiar
with farming, even if we are city-based people—having that familiarity raised an
important ethical issue, and people started saying “Where did this come from?”.
In conclusion, I am a little surprised at the contribution from Richard Prosser. I want
to congratulate him on his election to Pa rliament—we need more Cantabrians boosting
up the quality within this House—but I wa s puzzled at his c ontribution. I actually
thought he said at the start that he was standing in support of the legislation, and then he
rapidly moved on to explain why he was opposed  to it. I could not understand the logic.
Well, I actually could not find the logic in th e argument that he presented, to be honest.
I do think that this is something that is—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I am sorry to interrupt the
honourable member; her time has expired.

items.speaker: JOHN HAYES
items.text: Thank you, Mr Assistant Speaker Tisch,
for the opportunity to speak t onight on this bill, the Nationa l Animal Identification and
Tracing Bill, and I do so in support of the bill unequivocally. Reflecting on the
comments from colleagues across the House, and the importance that Jim Sutton and
Jim Anderton played in initiati ng this bill, I would like to inform the House that 2004,
when these people had these very original ideas , was the year that this sort of system
was introduced in the European Union. It  has a system called TRACES, the Trade
Control and Expert System, which tracks move ments of livestock both within the EU
and from third countries into the EU.
It is also worth reflecting that around this  time the Australians had their own system.
It is called the National Animal Identification System. It traces animals from birth to
slaughter. The Australians do this because—a s some members have already mentioned
tonight—having a system like this improve s access for Australian produce to export
markets and also contributes to food safety.
The Americans also have a system, and I reflect on Damien O’Connor’s list of
countries that he mentioned and that have systems, like Argentina, Mexico, and Korea.
All of those countries export into America. So if you want to do that, you have really
14 Feb 2012 National Animal Identification and Tracing Bill 393
got to abide by American rules, which cover cattle, poultry, horses, donkeys, sheep,
goats, pigs, and all other animals. It is wort h reflecting that we are talking about just
beef and deer in this legislation at this point, but other countries manage to include all of
their productive animals except household pets.
Of course, Jim Anderton was the Minist er of Agriculture who in 2004 said “Don’t
worry about the productive part of the ec onomy. Let’s microchi p dogs.”, and that
caused a furore, at least in my electorate. The goal in the American system is to be able
to trace within 48 hours of identifying an anim al that is unwell where that animal has
been and how it has been moved, and, therefor e, contribute to disease control. So I
support this bill because it is  critical for our export market s, and being critical for our
export markets it is going to give us higher export returns.
I would say to my colleague in the New Zealand First Party, w ho was standing to
oppose this bill and said we should be respon ding to market forces, that this system
already operates among many farmers in th e Wairarapa, in my electorate, and
particularly for exporting into the Amer ican market. Those farmers who supply
traceable meat right back from an individu al farm to the American market get a high
premium for doing so. So the returns are already there for the innovative and
progressive farmers who have introduced this system without legislation.
I think it is really important that we encourage farmers to engage with traceability,
because if you are going to get a higher pr ice for your product, you are going to get a
better return at your farm gate. If you do that, then you are going to contribute to
growing the economy, and that is a clear priority of this G overnment. We want to grow
this economy, we want the boat to  go faster, and we  want that because we want a better
standard of living for everybody in this country. We will all benefit from that outcome.
It is worth keeping in mind that this scheme will become compulsory for all
farmers—myself included—for their beef animals on 1 July of this year and next year, I
think on 1 March, for deer. I think it is probably inevitable that within the next few
years we will see this scheme being extended to other animals in this country,
particularly those that we need to push into export markets.
It is interesting for a second, too, to just recall the commen ts of my colleague in the
Labour Party Ruth Dyson talking about appl e traceability. She is absolutely right in
what she is talking about, but I have begun to get complaints  from apple growers in my
electorate who are complaining about the high  cost of meeting biosecurity requirements
in exporting products into the Australian market . Basically I am told  it costs you $200
to get an 18 kilogram carton of apples th rough into the Australian market. That is the
cost of meeting the biosecurity system.
We do not want to get into that situati on with beef and sheep meat exports, and I
think that this bill and the sy stem that is being implemented is really going to be very
cost efficient for livestock animals. It is going to increase the returns for export markets.
That will benefit all New Zealanders, and I have no hesitation in supporting the bill.
Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE
items.text: It gives me great pleasure to rise
to take this call on the National Animal Id entification and Tracing Bill, noting that the
MP for Wellington Central, Grant Robertson, previously took a call on the Labour side
to underscore that our support for this bill reflects our caucus pos ition right around the
country. So as the member for New Lynn in west Auckland, can I say that I am
delighted to be able to support it too, fo r a number of great reas ons, including that we
have plenty of animals in west Auckland to trace. Just watch Outrageous Fortune and
you will know what I mean.
Now, we did challenge earlier the member  for Auckland Central to take a call on
behalf of National, and we have yet to hear from her. We assume that National members
394 National Animal Identification and Tracing Bill 14 Feb 2012
in the inner city are similarly committed to this  bill, but we would love to hear from her
too.
It is a few years ago now that I visited the AgResearch institution at Ruakura and
was able to see some of the early devel opment of this project, then based on the
application of radio frequency ID tags to  livestock. It was around 2004, when the then
Labour Government first seriously kicked this  off with AgResearc h, and it is a delight
to see this now maturing to the point that we are passing legislation on a multipartisan
basis today in the House.
There are a number of really good reasons why we support the bill, and I could not
agree more strongly with the previous speaker, Mr Hayes, who said it is because we all
want to see the boat go faster. We all want to raise New Zealand’s standard of living
and we want to see our primary sector in particular increase in productivity and value. It
delivers that, because of quality assurance, because of pest and disease management,
because of a brand premium, and because of  the basis of further innovation in the
future.
Debate interrupted.

TUESDAY, 14 FEBRUARY 2012 
Mr Speaker took the Chair at 2 p.m.
