QUESTIONS FOR ORAL ANSWER 
QUESTIONS TO MINISTERS 
Economy, Rebalancing—Progress 
1. JOHN HAYES (National—Wairarapa)  to the Minister of Finance : What 
progress is being made in rebalancing New Zealand’s economy towards paying our way 
in the world? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Associ ate Minister of Finance) on behalf of the Minister 
of Finance: New Zealand is making steady progre ss rebalancing the economy with an 
improved merchandise trade result a nd improved household savings in 2011. 
Merchandise trade grew to a $3 billion surplus, notwithstanding the significant external 
challenges of a high dollar and, of course, weak global growth. Overall, our exports 
grew an impressive 9.7 percent by value in th e calendar year last year. There is still a 
long way to go, of course, bu t these early signs are enco uraging for exporters, and 
reinforce the Government’s commitment to helping build a platform from which our 
businesses can compete and trade in the wider world.  
John Hayes: How much did New Zealand’s merc handise trade with Australia and 
China grow in 2011? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE : New Zealand expanded expo rts to our key market, 
Australia, by 8.45 percent over the last year, to just under NZ$11 billion. This 
percentage increase is a very significant result given the higher volume of existing trade. 
It continues a trend evident over the last fe w years of strong yea r-on-year growth. In 
addition, New Zealand’s exports  to China grew by over $1 b illion in the calendar year 
last year. That is 22 percent annual grow th, which is a fantastic achievement for 
exporters, and reinforces the importance of China as our second largest export market.  
John Hayes : What progress is being made on  increasing New Zealand’s national 
savings? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE: More good news. New Zealand’ s savings rates are steadily 
improving. Statistics New Zealand figures show household savings in the year to March 
last year were positive for the first time in a decade. This is quite a turn-round from 
2007, when households were spending about $1.11 for every dollar they earned. It 
remains early days, but it does show the importance that households are now placing on 
savings. The shift from net borrowing to savi ngs, if it continues, will help provide a 
stronger platform for faster economic growth. 
Hon David Parker : By how much are New Zealand’s net international liabilities 
projected to grow over the next 5 years? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE: I do not have the ne t international liabilities, but I do have 
the current account deficit, which, I think, al ludes to the same thing that the member 
means, in terms of that being expected to  widen out from March 2012 to the year to 
March 2016. That is due to, primarily, the Canterbury— 
Hon David Parker: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. My question was not about 
the current account deficit. I do have a question about the current account deficit, but 
this is not it.  
Mr SPEAKER : I appreciate the member’s point  of order. I think, though, the 
Minister indicated he did not ha ve the net liabilities figures with him, and he tried to be 
308 Questions for Oral Answer 14 Feb 2012 
helpful by at least providing some inform ation about the curren t account. But I do 
accept that is not exactly the same issue. 
Hon David Parker: I raise a point of order, Mr Sp eaker. This is question No. 1, it is 
the Government’s own question to the Minist er of Finance, it is  about progress on the 
economic growth agenda, and I have asked abou t one of the most basic indicators as to 
whether that is working. I would have thought that the Minister— 
Mr SPEAKER : Order! The member is quite corre ct. It is the Government’s own 
question, and asking about net lia bilities is not exactly way out of line; there is no 
question that the supplementary question is in line. But I take the Mi nister at his word 
that he does not have the figures. People can  make their own judgment about that, but 
that is what the Minister indicated to the House, and there is nothing I can do about that. 
Hon Trevor Mallard : I raise a point of order, Mr  Speaker. Could you at least ask 
the Minister whether he has general indica tions—for example, th e percentage of GDP 
liabilities. I mean, any Associate Minister— 
Mr SPEAKER : Order! That is not strictly a point—[ Interruption] Order! The 
Minister wants to speak to the point of order? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE : That was exactly what I was doing by referring to the 
increase in the balance of payments deficit— 
Mr SPEAKER : No, we are now debating the whole issue. New Zealand’s net 
liability is a reasonably standard figure, and it is not exactly the same as the current 
account deficit. The question was very specif ic about net liabiliti es, but I take the 
Minister at the Minister’s word: the Minist er does not have thos e figures. Members can 
be critical of the Minister for not having t hose figures—that is the situation we are in—
but I cannot ask the Minister to provide what he does not have with him. 
Hon David Parker : Given that the Minister in an swer to the last supplementary 
question acknowledged that New Zealand’s curren t account deficit is projected to grow 
over the next 5 years, from $5 billion this year to a $17 billion deficit in 2016, is he 
surprised to learn that over that period New Zealand’s net international liabilities are 
projected to grow from $140 billion to $200 billion—an increase of 10 percent of GDP? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE: I do understand that the current account deficit figures and 
the international liabilities figures—it woul d not surprise me at all, which I think 
underlines the point that we were making with the primary que stion, which is the 
importance of growing exports and the importance of also—[ Interruption] The 
importance of growing exports. The reality of it is that that is due to happen because of 
the Canterbury rebuild—[Interruption]  
Mr SPEAKER: Order! I apologise to the Minister. Look, the Labour spokesperson 
on finance asked a supplementary question. I pr esume he wants to hear the answer, and 
the Minister is answering this questi on. I think the interj ections are beyond 
reasonableness.  
Hon STEVEN JOYCE : The point I was making is that the member inadvertently 
underlines the exact point that I was making in the responses to the question. The way 
you deal with that is by improving domestic  savings and by improving our exports as 
we sell to the rest of the world. Those are the ways in which you primarily address those 
issues, and I was reporting to the House that  we are making some reasonable—in fact, 
good—progress in doing that. 
Hon David Parker : I seek leave to table two documents, both prepared by the 
Parliamentary Library. The first is a graph of  New Zealand’s increasing net liabilities; 
the second is the graph of the increase in the current account deficits every year to 2016. 
Mr SPEAKER: Leave is sought to table those documents. Is there any objection? 
There is no objection. 
14 Feb 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 309 
Documents, by leave, laid on the Table of the House. 
Rt Hon Winston Peters : Can I ask the Minister as to how he concludes that a 
seriously overvalued dollar, massive borrowing, and key asset sales to foreign 
ownership could do anything other than balance our economic position worse? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE : Although some people undoubtedly believe the New 
Zealand dollar to be overvalued, I think the point is that, actually, our total exports grew 
last year to $47.7 billion. So although it obviously had an impact on some exporters, it 
did not obviously have an impact on all exporters, because we had that growth in 
exports over the full calendar year of 2011. So the dollar is challenging, but it is good to 
see that our exporters are continuing to grow. 
Rt Hon Winston Peters: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I asked him about the 
seriously overvalued dollar and massive borrowing, which everybody admits. The third 
aspect was key asset sales to foreign ow nership. He answered one part of that 
question— 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! 
Rt Hon Winston Peters: —but I asked only one question. 
Mr SPEAKER: The Minister is required to answer only one part of a supplementary 
question. It has been a longstanding requirement in this House of Ministers— 
Rt Hon Winston Peters: Point of order— 
Mr SPEAKER : The member may resume his seat  while I am on my feet. Thank 
you. It has been a longstanding  practice in this House that a Minist er is required to 
answer only one part of a supplementary que stion. If members want to put more than 
one part to a question, that is the risk they run. 
Rt Hon Winston Peters: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I did not put more than 
one part to the question. The question was relating to the rebalancing of this country’s 
economy. I gave it three aspects and asked which one of thos e, or those collectively, 
would do what he said. I am not asking thre e questions; I am asking questions with a 
few details. Surely the Minister is capable of answering that. 
Mr SPEAKER: Well, the member just destroyed any merit his point of order had, 
because he does not make that kind of deroga tory comment under a point of order. I am 
sorry, but— 
Rt Hon Winston Peters: My point of order, Mr Speaker, is— 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! I have not recognised the memb er yet. Does he wish to raise 
a further point of order? 
Rt Hon Winston Peters: I do, Mr Speaker. 
Mr SPEAKER: I have ruled already that the Minister has answered that question, so 
it must be a further point of order and a different point of order. 
Rt Hon Winston Peters : I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. It is a different point 
of order. I want to know how it is that one  could ask a question like I have put, with 
facts a, b, and c. If I am to get b and c answered, how does one make that question work 
in this House? 
Mr SPEAKER: Very simply, questions do not contain facts; they seek facts. 
State-owned Assets, Sales—Prime Minister’s Statements on Current Estimated 
Revenue 
2. DAVID SHEARER (Leader of the Opposition) to the Prime Minister: Does he 
stand by his statement made with regard to the revenue from asset sales “I don’t know 
the exact number that they have in their books today”? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY (Prime Minister) : I stand by the full statement I made in 
November 2011 when asked what value Tr easury had put on the mixed-ownership 
assets. The exact quote was: “I don’t know the exact number  that they have in their 
310 Questions for Oral Answer 14 Feb 2012 
books today. But I know the estimations they gave to us—if we release 49 percent in the 
equity markets there’s five to seven billion.” 
David Shearer: Did he state when announcing thes e asset sales 1 year ago that $10 
billion would be realised, and if he does not  stand by that figure, how does he justify 
this much lower figure? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : In terms of the latter part, that is the best estimates we have, 
and—as I said yesterday—in the end, obviously, it will be what the market is prepared 
to pay, and it will depend how much of the 49 percent we sell. But the best estimates we 
have at the moment would be in the order of about $6 billion, maybe a little more. 
David Shearer: Did he state that the figure could be up to $10 billion? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: Probably, and it could be; you never know. 
David Shearer: In light of his description of th e Solid Energy account as “ropy”, is 
it his opinion that some of the other Stat e-owned enterprises up for sale are also 
significantly overvalued in the audited accounts; and if so, which ones? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : The leader’s own member ha s been making that point—that 
there is quite a range of valuations, which was, as Clayton Cosgrove said, a commercial 
value for Solid Energy of $3.5 billion, an upda ted board valuation of $2.8 billion, and a 
Crown Ownership Monitoring Unit valuation of $1.7 billion. As I have said on 
numerous occasions, there is a variety of  reasons why companies have different 
valuations, and they depend on whether they  look at net asset value, book value, or 
equity value. In the end the value that actua lly matters is the one that the market will 
pay, and in our view it is in the order of about $5 billion to $7 billion. 
David Shearer: Is there a bottom line below whic h he would not se ll our profitable 
assets; and if so, what is that bottom line? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: The bottom line is that it has got to be the right thing for New 
Zealand, and it is. 
David Shearer: How much less will the Crown receiv e as a result of the uncertainty 
around the Treaty clause? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: Well, that would depend on th e consultation process and what 
the final Treaty clause looks like. In my view we will find our way, through an elegant 
solution, which will mean that private se ctor shareholders will be happy about the 
outcome.  
David Shearer: What is his elegant solution for dealing with the Treaty clause? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : It is one that makes it clear to M āori that the Crown is bound 
by the Treaty, but the specific obligations around  consultation of sale would not be the 
case for a private sector shareholder. What I can say is that what we do in the end will 
be clear—just like when the Labour Party was proud of itself it was clear because those 
members came to the House with boxes with the name “Labour” all over them, and now 
they have ripped the name off.  
Overseas Investment Rules—China Free-trade Agreement and Sale of Crafar 
Farms 
3. Dr RUSSEL NORMAN (Co-Leader—Green) to the Minister for Land 
Information: Did New Zealand’s Free Trade Agreement with China influence his 
decision to approve the sale of the Crafar farms to the Shanghai Pengxin Group? 
Hon MAURICE WILLIAMSON (Min ister for Land Information) : Ministers 
were satisfied that Milk New Zealand Holdi ngs met all the releva nt criteria under the 
Overseas Investment Act 2005. Ministers can have regard only to the criteria and factors 
that are outlined in that Act. Every applica tion is decided on its individual merits, and 
the outcome would be the same even if New Zealand did not have a free-trade 
agreement with China. The Overseas Invest ment Act requires the Overseas Investment 
14 Feb 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 311 
Office to treat all applications  on an equal basis, regardless of the country of origin of 
the applicants.  
Dr Russel Norman : I raise a point of order, Mr Sp eaker. That was, I think, a fine 
statement of general principles, but I wa s asking about a specific Minister—this one—
and his decision in a specific case. He did not address that primary question. 
Mr SPEAKER: I must have misheard the answer, but I thought I heard the Minister 
say that the outcome would have been the same, regardless of whether New Zealand

7. Dr CAM CALDER (National) to the Minister of Justice: What are her priorities 
in regard to bail laws over the coming three years? 
Hon JUDITH COLLINS (Minister of Justice) : This Government is committed to 
bail laws that will help make New Zealand safer, protect the public, and keep victims at 
the heart of our criminal justice system. We will change bail laws to extend the reverse 
burden of proof requirement for people with previous serious convi ctions to people 
charged with kidnapping, sexual conduct wi th a child under 12, sexual conduct with 
young persons under 16, aggravated burglary, and assault with intent to rob, in addition 
to the existing offences already covered. The reverse burden of proof will also apply to 
people charged with murder, or  serious class A drug offences  such as manufacturing or 
dealing in methamphetamine, regardless of  any previous offending. This means that 
they must prove that they are not a risk to the public or to the trial process. 
Dr Cam Calder: Why is the Government making these changes? 
Hon JUDITH COLLINS: We know that more than one-third of defendants arrested 
for these crimes commit further crimes while on bail. This is why it is so important to 
deal with them properly. These changes w ill build on the work this Government has 
already achieved, and we are reversing Labou r’s decision, which made it easier for 
defendants to get bail. These changes will get the balance right between public safety 
and a defendant’s right to be considered innocent until proven guilty.

Urbanisation, however, was not without its downsides. On the one hand, many Māori

the steady growth of a Māori middle class.

authorities—Māori land trusts and incorporations, a nd iwi authorities. It has been my

 For me, M āori development, as M āori conceive of the idea, has always been about

Dr JACKIE BLUE (National) : I am pleased to be speaking to the third reading of

which I am no longer on, well on its future deliberations and business in the future.  
This bill has been amended to ensure that  it is enduring because, quite frankly, the 
current system is outdated. It is really last  century and it was well  and truly overdue for 
an overhaul. This bill will modernise the road-user charges system. It will reduce 
compliance costs for operators, eliminate the scope for error and fraud in the purchase 
of road-user charges licences, and si mplify enforcement and administration 
requirements. It is very important. We must have a fair system, a balanced system, and a 
well-managed system. This is what this law will do. The road-user charges—or RUC—
system was established in 1978. It is a long time ago, and this review is very timely. All 
the revenue from the road-user charges system goes to the National Land Transport 
Fund, and the fund is used mainly for road  construction and maintenance, along with 
other activities benefiting road users.  
 The bill is a result of the recommendations of the Independent Review of the New 
Zealand Road User Charging System, and it brings about the most significant reform of 
road-user charges since it was introduced—i t is a very significant reform. Diesel 
vehicles are very popular in New Zealand—di esel is cheaper than petrol—and more 
economical to run. Fuel consumption tests generally give results between 20 percent 
and 30 percent better for a diesel-engine ca r compared with the same model with a 
petrol engine. But also you have got to know that up to 36 percent of diesel is used off-
road, such as on farms; in manufacturing, industrial, and commerc ial ventures; and on 
boats.  
But back to this bill. This bill is about bringing the road-user charges system into the 
21st century, from 1978 to 2012. This bill  addresses the conc ern about road-user 
charges evasion, which is conservatively estim ated to be $30 million per year, which is 
not an insignificant sum. This  bill will remove the evas ion opportunities and encourage 
timely payment, making a fairer system for all.  
The main provisions of the bill are, first of  all, a change in th e definition of vehicle 
weight. Currently, road-user charges are base d on the distance travelled and the weight 
carried. The system is complicated, and it ha s been open to error.  An operator has to 
guess the actual gross weight to be carried, and it can be difficult for an operator to 
predict in advance the actual weight to be carri ed. It is also very difficult, of course, to 
recover the charges owing after the fact. The bill changes the definition of vehicle 
weight to a fixed road-user charge, so that operators do not have to guess in advance, 
and so that Government authorities do no t have to deal w ith recovering money 
afterwards. Inevitably this will result in lower administrative costs for the industry and 
the Government, and, of course, it will m ean that fewer road-user charges are lost 
through evasion, so it is a win-win.  
There are a number of other provisions. Ot hers are removal of a time licence system 
and modernisation of the list of vehicles exempted from road-user charges. There is also 
14 Feb 2012 Road User Charges Bill 369 
an improvement to the regulatory framewor k for electronic management systems, and 
this really shows how far we have come from 1978 through to 2012. Really, back in 
1977 when the Road User Charges Act came into power, we did not have electronic 
systems and we did not have the internet. N one of this would have been dreamt of all 
that time ago. So, really, we have brought the system into the 21st century, and it means 
much more efficiency and much more fairne ss. It means that road-user charges can be 
purchased electronically, and that a distance licence can be displayed electronically on 
an on-board unit situated in the vehicle. And, of course, the distance travelled by the 
vehicle is measured electronically. It is all done electronically, something which no one, 
and certainly not our parents, would have thought of back in 1977. Quite frankly, the 
Road User Charges Bill of 1977 never would have dreamt of such a possibility, that in 
2012 we would be going to such a modern system.  
Another provision in the bill is that it is a fairer, simpler, and less costly structure in 
relation to offences—penalties —particularly for light vehicles. I cannot emphasise the 
fact that, really, a fixed road -user charges weight means that the distance-based evasion 
will be the main focus of compliance management, and will, obviously, save money and 
save time.  
Really, this bill, I cannot stress enough, is about bringing road-user charges into the 
21st century. It is about reducing compliance cost s for transport operators, and, 
ultimately, reducing transport costs for our businesses and exporters. These changes will 
make it easier and fairer to all those who pay road-user charges, and that has to be good.

businesses, simplify the administrative pr ocesses for industry and Government, and

Agency will also be able to  take greater advantage of mo dern internet technology in 
administering road-user charges payment channels.  
This bill addresses concerns about the ev asion, which I mentioned before, which has

who have been evading the system and w ho have not been paying their road-user 
charges as they should be. This bill will  remove a number of evasion opportunities, 
encourage timely payment, and make the system fairer for all. I commend this bill to the 
House.

Hon DAVID CARTER (Minister for Primary Industries) : I move, That the 
National Animal Identification and Tracing Bill be now read a third time. Agriculture is 
a key industry driving our econom y. We must maintain our reputation as world leaders 
in the production of top quality animal pr oducts. The Crown and industry have started 
to work together since 2004 to ensure that we have the quality information we need 
about livestock. In that regard, I would like to acknowledge and pay tribute to the earlier 
work of Ian Corney, who chaired the initial working-group. His absolute commitment is 
one of the reasons that this legislation is before the House tonight.  
The National Animal Identification and Tracing (NAIT) scheme will support the 
electronic recording of locations, the people in  charge of animals, and the movement of 
animals between properties, along with ot her attributes. With NAIT we can give 
378 National Animal Identification and Tracing Bill 14 Feb 2012 
assurances to domestic consumers and our tr ade partners that the product is healthy and 
disease-free. We can manage a disease more effectively and rapidly reopen markets if 
they are closed. Furthermore, the NAIT scheme  allows for other information to be held 
in conjunction with mandatory data and ca n further support improved productivity and 
on-farm management.  
The National Animal Identification and Tracing Bill sets out the legal framework for 
the collection of information on livestock, and their location and movement history 
throughout their lifetime. It also outlines  the governance arrangements and powers for 
the NAIT organisation that will manage  the NAIT scheme. NAIT needs to be 
mandatory to be effective. The bill will support the introduction of the NAIT scheme, 
scheduled for July 2012 for cattle and March 2013 for deer.  
It was agreed early on in the NAIT scheme’s development that the Government and 
the industry would share its co sts as well as its benefits . The Government funded the 
building of the database and is to fund a continuing contri bution of 35 percent of the 
system’s operational costs. The livestock industry groups have provided financial 
support during the scheme’s development and will do so once the bill has passed.  
During the bill’s passage th rough the House I have spoke n about the history of the 
project and how we got to this point. Ini tially, there was a substantial battle with 
Federated Farmers, which were difficult,  and that led to unnecessary scepticism 
amongst many farmers. Thankfully, with the new leadership of Federated Farmers, 
realism now prevails. With the establishment of NAIT, farmers now have the ability to 
manage stock at the level of an individual animal rather than as a herd. Farmers are able 
to invest in automated systems to weigh and draft animals according to the criteria that 
farmers themselves set, rather than having to assess an animal’s condition by eye. 
Modern farming systems are able to provide labour savings and more accurate 
responses to market demand. I also expect  the NAIT organisati on to respond to the 
demands from its levy-paying farmers. Once the NAIT scheme is well settled and 
functioning, the NAIT organisation and th e Animal Health Board will begin to 
consolidate their governance and functions. I look forward to the efficiencies and cost 
savings that will result at the level of both individual levy-paying farmers and the 
livestock industries themselves.  
I am pleased that most of the parties repr esented in this House have recognised the 
importance of this bill and of the NAIT sche me. I tonight acknowledge the work of the 
previous Labour Government in devel oping the NAIT scheme, and Labour’s ongoing 
support for the NAIT legislation. I also ac knowledge the long-term commitment and 
dedication to a successful NAIT scheme by a ll the industry parties that have been 
involved in NAIT Ltd itself, which is now in charge of delivering the scheme. I 
commend the National Animal Identification and Tracing Bill to the House.

have not looked to enough is th e future potential of this le gislation, not just across deer 
and cattle, which it will currently cover, but  across a much broader area: positioning 
New Zealand to be at the cutting edge and leading in what consumers actually want. I 
think it was Jonathan Young, who just resume d his seat, who mentioned this fact as 
well. I think more could be made of it. It  is really important for the New Zealand 
economy that we are seen not to be followi ng other countries—as we unfortunately are 
in this particular tracking process—but actually leading a response to what consumers 
want, because they are the people who are going  to make us successful or not. If we are 
not providing product in a way that consumers want and look to in the future—if we are 
not what they seek—we will have much harsher competition than we already have.  
What consumers want to know is where the product comes from. They want to know 
that it is safe, they want to know, if we are talking about meat , that it has been raised in 
a way that meets their ethical standards, a nd they want to know that it has not been 
raised in a way that causes huge damage to the envir onment. That point, I think, we 
miss out on quite substantially. We already do it in other ar eas. We do it in respect of 
apples. If you buy an apple overseas, eat it, and say “I think this apple is contaminated. I 
think it might have some residual spray on it.”,  you can take that apple in, get it tested 
for the residual spray, and our New Zealand marketers can trace the apple back, not just 
to New Zealand, but actually to  the very row of the orchard that that apple came from. 
That can give overseas consumers huge confidence in the safety of our product, and that 
is the sort of marketing that we could use for the National Animal Identification and 
Tracking system, and apply it to what consumers will want now and in the future.  
My colleague Grant Robertson talked about a project that he worked on with the Hon 
Simon Upton some years ago at a very  pleasant university in Dunedin, Otago 
University, doing what I think was a partic ularly tastelessly named project called 
Paddock to Plate—but as a vege tarian, I would see that as a little bit tasteless. But 
actually it was very, very substantial and good work that Grant Robertson and Simon 
Upton did, and again it was looking at the traceability of various products, and how that 
could be used to give consumers both with in New Zealand but also overseas a higher 
392 National Animal Identification and Tracing Bill 14 Feb 2012 
level of confidence in the ethical standa rds, the safety, the security, and the 
environmental standards of the product that they were eating. 
 We can do the same with Icebreaker. Icebreaker can tell you where the wool came 
from for any garment that you purchase from it, and it says that is a huge marketing tool 
for overseas customers. And we know, tragically, that Fonterra is very well aware of the 
importance of being able to trace the source of its milk and milk products, due to the 
disastrous situation that we had in China not very many years ago. So this is a model 
that is initially set up to provide just basic safety standards.  
We know how important this industry is to us. If we do have—and heaven forbid that 
we ever do have—an outbreak of foot-and-m outh disease or any other sort of disease 
within this farming area, we will want to  know as quickly as possible where each 
animal has been, and any of these traceability elements are, of course, important to that. 
But from my perspective, this is much more important in looking at future opportunities 
and the needs of consumers.  
Members of the House will recall last year or the year before a programme on 
television that has been quite harshly re viewed since its initial outburst into the 
conversation, particularly in the social medi a. It snuck filming equipment in to a pig 
farm and exposed some of what we would cal l the more unethical practices in farming 
pigs. What every single consumer—according to reports, anyway, but jolly near every 
single consumer—of pork after that programme asked their butcher or their supermarket 
was “How are these pigs raised? Are they ra ised like in that dreadful programme on 
television?”. So even in the New Zealand context—where we are very familiar with our 
own farms, we know the high standards that are kept on most farms, and we are familiar 
with farming, even if we are city-based people—having that familiarity raised an 
important ethical issue, and people started saying “Where did this come from?”.  
In conclusion, I am a little surprised at the contribution from Richard Prosser. I want 
to congratulate him on his election to Pa rliament—we need more Cantabrians boosting 
up the quality within this House—but I wa s puzzled at his c ontribution. I actually 
thought he said at the start that he was standing in support of the legislation, and then he 
rapidly moved on to explain why he was opposed  to it. I could not understand the logic. 
Well, I actually could not find the logic in th e argument that he presented, to be honest. 
I do think that this is something that is—

JOHN HAYES (National—Wairarapa) : Thank you, Mr Assistant Speaker Tisch, 
for the opportunity to speak t onight on this bill, the Nationa l Animal Identification and 
Tracing Bill, and I do so in support of the bill unequivocally. Reflecting on the 
comments from colleagues across the House, and the importance that Jim Sutton and 
Jim Anderton played in initiati ng this bill, I would like to inform the House that 2004, 
when these people had these very original ideas , was the year that this sort of system 
was introduced in the European Union. It  has a system called TRACES, the Trade 
Control and Expert System, which tracks move ments of livestock both within the EU 
and from third countries into the EU.  
It is also worth reflecting that around this  time the Australians had their own system. 
It is called the National Animal Identification System. It traces animals from birth to 
slaughter. The Australians do this because—a s some members have already mentioned 
tonight—having a system like this improve s access for Australian produce to export 
markets and also contributes to food safety.  
The Americans also have a system, and I reflect on Damien O’Connor’s list of 
countries that he mentioned and that have systems, like Argentina, Mexico, and Korea. 
All of those countries export into America. So if you want to do that, you have really 
14 Feb 2012 National Animal Identification and Tracing Bill 393 
got to abide by American rules, which cover cattle, poultry, horses, donkeys, sheep, 
goats, pigs, and all other animals. It is wort h reflecting that we are talking about just 
beef and deer in this legislation at this point, but other countries manage to include all of 
their productive animals except household pets. 
 Of course, Jim Anderton was the Minist er of Agriculture who in 2004 said “Don’t 
worry about the productive part of the ec onomy. Let’s microchi p dogs.”, and that 
caused a furore, at least in my electorate. The goal in the American system is to be able 
to trace within 48 hours of identifying an anim al that is unwell where that animal has 
been and how it has been moved, and, therefor e, contribute to disease control. So I 
support this bill because it is  critical for our export market s, and being critical for our 
export markets it is going to give us higher export returns.  
I would say to my colleague in the New Zealand First Party, w ho was standing to 
oppose this bill and said we should be respon ding to market forces, that this system 
already operates among many farmers in th e Wairarapa, in my electorate, and 
particularly for exporting into the Amer ican market. Those farmers who supply 
traceable meat right back from an individu al farm to the American market get a high 
premium for doing so. So the returns are already there for the innovative and 
progressive farmers who have introduced this system without legislation.  
I think it is really important that we encourage farmers to engage with traceability, 
because if you are going to get a higher pr ice for your product, you are going to get a 
better return at your farm gate. If you do that, then you are going to contribute to 
growing the economy, and that is a clear priority of this G overnment. We want to grow 
this economy, we want the boat to  go faster, and we  want that because we want a better 
standard of living for everybody in this country. We will all benefit from that outcome.  
It is worth keeping in mind that this scheme will become compulsory for all 
farmers—myself included—for their beef animals on 1 July of this year and next year, I 
think on 1 March, for deer. I think it is probably inevitable that within the next few 
years we will see this scheme being extended to other animals in this country, 
particularly those that we need to push into export markets.  
It is interesting for a second, too, to just recall the commen ts of my colleague in the 
Labour Party Ruth Dyson talking about appl e traceability. She is absolutely right in 
what she is talking about, but I have begun to get complaints  from apple growers in my 
electorate who are complaining about the high  cost of meeting biosecurity requirements 
in exporting products into the Australian market . Basically I am told  it costs you $200 
to get an 18 kilogram carton of apples th rough into the Australian market. That is the 
cost of meeting the biosecurity system.  
We do not want to get into that situati on with beef and sheep meat exports, and I 
think that this bill and the sy stem that is being implemented is really going to be very 
cost efficient for livestock animals. It is going to increase the returns for export markets. 
That will benefit all New Zealanders, and I have no hesitation in supporting the bill. 
Thank you. 
Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE (Labour—New Lynn) : It gives me great pleasure to rise 
to take this call on the National Animal Id entification and Tracing Bill, noting that the

to underscore that our support for this bill reflects our caucus pos ition right around the 
country. So as the member for New Lynn in west Auckland, can I say that I am 
delighted to be able to support it too, fo r a number of great reas ons, including that we 
have plenty of animals in west Auckland to trace. Just watch Outrageous Fortune and 
you will know what I mean.  
Now, we did challenge earlier the member  for Auckland Central to take a call on 
behalf of National, and we have yet to hear from her. We assume that National members

It is a few years ago now that I visited the AgResearch institution at Ruakura and 
was able to see some of the early devel opment of this project, then based on the 
application of radio frequency ID tags to  livestock. It was around 2004, when the then 
Labour Government first seriously kicked this  off with AgResearc h, and it is a delight 
to see this now maturing to the point that we are passing legislation on a multipartisan 
basis today in the House.  
There are a number of really good reasons why we support the bill, and I could not

because of a brand premium, and because of  the basis of further innovation in the
